cards.front:
GDP (Gross Domestic Product) measures the value of all final goods and services produced:

(A) By Indian residents anywhere in the world
(B) Within a country's geographic boundaries during a given period
(C) Only by Indian citizens abroad
(D) By the government only
cards.back:
(B) Within a country's geographic boundaries during a given period

GDP & National Income — GDP — based on geography (where produced). GNP (Gross National Product) — based on nationality of producer (Indian residents anywhere in world). GNP = GDP + NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad). NFIA can be positive (Saudi Arabia, US — get income from abroad) or negative (India — net outflow as we have more foreign investment than Indians earning abroad). Most countries report GDP as the primary aggregate.
cards.option1: By Indian residents anywhere in the world
cards.storedExplanation: GDP — based on geography (where produced). GNP (Gross National Product) — based on nationality of producer (Indian residents anywhere in world). GNP = GDP + NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad). NFIA can be positive (Saudi Arabia, US — get income from abroad) or negative (India — net outflow as we have more foreign investment than Indians earning abroad). Most countries report GDP as the primary aggregate.

cards.front:
The relation between 'GDP at Market Price' (GDPmp) and 'GDP at Factor Cost' (GDPfc) is:

(A) GDPmp = GDPfc + Indirect taxes − Subsidies
(B) GDPmp = GDPfc + Subsidies − Indirect taxes
(C) GDPmp = GDPfc − Profits
(D) GDPmp = GDPfc + Depreciation
cards.back:
(A) GDPmp = GDPfc + Indirect taxes − Subsidies

GDP & National Income — Net Indirect Taxes (NIT) = Indirect taxes − Subsidies. GDPmp = GDPfc + NIT. The 'wedge' between the two reflects taxes (which add to market price) and subsidies (which lower it). GDPfc is sometimes called 'income approach' GDP (sum of factor incomes — wages, rent, interest, profit). Net vs Gross — subtract depreciation to get NDP / NNP from GDP / GNP.
cards.storedExplanation: Net Indirect Taxes (NIT) = Indirect taxes − Subsidies. GDPmp = GDPfc + NIT. The 'wedge' between the two reflects taxes (which add to market price) and subsidies (which lower it). GDPfc is sometimes called 'income approach' GDP (sum of factor incomes — wages, rent, interest, profit). Net vs Gross — subtract depreciation to get NDP / NNP from GDP / GNP.

cards.front:
Since 2015, India's primary headline national-income measure as published by MoSPI is:

(A) GDP at factor cost (old base)
(B) GDP at constant market prices + GVA at basic prices (2011-12 base)
(C) GNP only
(D) Per-capita income
cards.back:
(B) GDP at constant market prices + GVA at basic prices (2011-12 base)

GDP & National Income — MoSPI revised the base year to 2011-12 (from 2004-05) in January 2015. Headline became GDP at MARKET PRICES (constant) for international comparability. Sectoral analysis switched to GVA at BASIC PRICES — 'basic price' = factor cost + production taxes − production subsidies (excludes net product taxes). Relationship: GVA basic prices + Net product taxes = GDP market prices. Quarterly + advance estimates released regularly. Latest 2024-25 GDP growth ~7.6% (real).

Sectoral analysis switched to GVA at BASIC PRICES — 'basic price' = factor cost + production taxes − production subsidies (excludes net product taxes). cards.front:
The 'GDP deflator' is best described as:

(A) Same as CPI
(B) Ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP — broadest measure of economy-wide inflation
(C) Always equals 100
(D) Inflation in foreign-trade goods only
cards.back:
(B) Ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP — broadest measure of economy-wide inflation

GDP & National Income — GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. It captures price changes across ALL goods/services in the economy (not just consumer basket like CPI). Nominal GDP at current prices → reflects both volume + price changes. Real GDP at base-year prices → reflects only volume change. Wider than CPI (consumer-only) and WPI (wholesale only). Implicit measure — derived rather than directly polled. Useful for cross-country comparisons of long-term inflation trends.
cards.storedExplanation: GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100. It captures price changes across ALL goods/services in the economy (not just consumer basket like CPI). Nominal GDP at current prices → reflects both volume + price changes. Real GDP at base-year prices → reflects only volume change. Wider than CPI (consumer-only) and WPI (wholesale only). Implicit measure — derived rather than directly polled. Useful for cross-country comparisons of long-term inflation trends.

cards.front:
By nominal GDP rank in 2025-26 (per IMF / Economic Survey), India is the:

(A) 5th largest economy
(B) 4th largest economy (overtook Japan in FY 2024-25)
(C) 3rd largest economy
(D) 10th largest economy
cards.back:
(B) 4th largest economy (overtook Japan in FY 2024-25)

GDP & National Income — India overtook Japan to become the 4th largest economy by nominal GDP in FY 2024-25 (~USD 4 trillion). The order: USA (~28T) > China (~18T) > Germany (~4.5T) > India (~4T) > Japan (~4T very close). On PPP basis India is already 3rd (after US, China). Aim — 3rd largest by 2027-28 when India would overtake Germany (~$5 T projected). Per-capita GDP however is much lower — India ~$2,800 vs Germany $54,000 (2024).

cards.front:
Three approaches to compute GDP — Production / Income / Expenditure — should all give:

(A) Different numbers
(B) The same total (income earned = output produced = expenditure on output)
(C) Average of two methods
(D) Maximum of the three
cards.back:
(B) The same total (income earned = output produced = expenditure on output)

GDP & National Income — Three sides of the same coin (Circular Flow of Income): (1) Production / Output / Value-Added = sum of GVA across all industries. (2) Income = sum of factor payments — wages + rent + interest + profit + mixed income. (3) Expenditure = C (consumption) + I (investment) + G (government) + X − M (net exports). All three measure the same economy → same total. In practice, statistical discrepancy arises but is reconciled. India officially uses Output approach for GDP and Expenditure-side for double-checking.

(2) Income = sum of factor payments — wages + rent + interest + profit + mixed income. (3) Expenditure = C (consumption) + I (investment) + G (government) + X − M (net exports). All three measure the same economy → same total. In practice, statistical discrepancy arises but is reconciled. India officially uses Output approach for GDP and Expenditure-side for double-checking.

cards.front:
Net National Product at factor cost (NNPfc) — popularly called 'National Income' — is calculated as:

(A) GNPmp − Depreciation − Indirect taxes + Subsidies
(B) GDP at market price + Indirect taxes
(C) GDP at factor cost − Subsidies
(D) Per-capita income × population
cards.back:
(A) GNPmp − Depreciation − Indirect taxes + Subsidies

GDP & National Income — Hierarchy from GDP to National Income: GDP at market price → +NFIA → GNP at market price → −Depreciation → NNP at market price → −Indirect taxes + Subsidies → NNP at factor cost (= National Income). Per-capita income = NNPfc / population. India's per-capita NNI (2024-25) ≈ ₹2.0 lakh at current prices.
cards.option1: GDP at market price + Indirect taxes
cards.storedExplanation: Hierarchy from GDP to National Income: GDP at market price → +NFIA → GNP at market price → −Depreciation → NNP at market price → −Indirect taxes + Subsidies → NNP at factor cost (= National Income). Per-capita income = NNPfc / population. India's per-capita NNI (2024-25) ≈ ₹2.0 lakh at current prices.

cards.front:
The currency of BHUTAN is the:

(A) Rupee
(B) Ngultrum
(C) Taka
(D) Baht

cards.front:
Consider the following about GOODS AND SERVICES TAX (GST). 1. It subsumed Central excise, service tax, VAT, entry tax, octroi, and many cesses. 2. GST is a destination-based tax. 3. The GST Council is chaired by the Finance Minister and votes follow a weighted system. 4. Petrol, diesel, ATF, crude oil and natural gas are PROVISIONALLY outside the GST net. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 2 and 4 only
(D) 1 and 3 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

GDP & National Income — All four correct. GST effective 1 July 2017 via 101st Amendment. Destination-based (tax accrues to consuming state). GST Council — FM chairs; 1/3 weight to Centre, 2/3 total to all States. Petroleum products are constitutionally included but kept OUTSIDE the GST net by Council decision — to be added later.

GST Council — FM chairs; 1/3 weight to Centre, 2/3 total to all States. Petroleum products are constitutionally included but kept OUTSIDE the GST net by Council decision — to be added later.

cards.front:
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in which year?

(A) 2012
(B) 2015
(C) 2014
(D) 2017
cards.back:
(B) 2015

GDP & National Income — NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) constituted on 1 January 2015 by a Cabinet resolution, replacing the 1950-established Planning Commission. PM is ex-officio chairperson; Vice-Chairman and CEO appointed by PM. Not a constitutional body.

cards.front:
A government runs a FISCAL DEFICIT of 5% of GDP. Which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. The fiscal deficit equals the sum of revenue deficit and capital expenditure. 2. Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments. 3. A higher fiscal deficit, financed by borrowing, tends to increase public debt as a % of GDP over time. 4. In India, FRBM Act targets a fiscal deficit of 3% of GDP under normal conditions.

(A) 2, 3 and 4 only
(B) 1, 2 and 3 only
(C) All four
(D) 1 and 4 only
cards.back:
(A) 2, 3 and 4 only

GDP & National Income — Statement 1 is WRONG as a definition. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total revenue (excluding borrowings). It is NOT 'revenue deficit + capital expenditure' — that conflates different concepts. The other three are correct: primary deficit subtracts interest payments; higher fiscal deficit → higher debt; FRBM (2003, amended 2018) targets 3% of GDP normally.
cards.storedExplanation: Statement 1 is WRONG as a definition. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total revenue (excluding borrowings). It is NOT 'revenue deficit + capital expenditure' — that conflates different concepts. The other three are correct: primary deficit subtracts interest payments; higher fiscal deficit → higher debt; FRBM (2003, amended 2018) targets 3% of GDP normally.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a BRETTON WOODS institution?

(A) International Monetary Fund (IMF)
(B) International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank)
(C) Asian Development Bank (ADB)
(D) International Development Association (IDA)
cards.back:
(C) Asian Development Bank (ADB)

GDP & National Income — ADB was founded in 1966 (Manila) separately. Bretton Woods (1944, New Hampshire) created IMF and the World Bank (originally IBRD; IDA is now a part of the WB Group). The ITO was proposed but never formed — its successor is the WTO (1995).
cards.option2: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank)
cards.storedExplanation: ADB was founded in 1966 (Manila) separately. Bretton Woods (1944, New Hampshire) created IMF and the World Bank (originally IBRD; IDA is now a part of the WB Group). The ITO was proposed but never formed — its successor is the WTO (1995).

cards.front:
ASSERTION (A): India's CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT (CAD) is widened by persistent crude-oil imports. REASON (R): India imports over 80% of its crude oil requirements, exposing the current account to oil-price shocks.

(A) Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation
(B) Both A and R are true, R is NOT the correct explanation
(C) A is true, R is false
(D) A is false, R is true
cards.back:
(A) Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation

GDP & National Income — India imports ~85% of its crude. A $10/barrel rise in crude adds roughly $15 bn to the annual oil import bill. This directly widens the merchandise trade deficit and thus the CAD. Classic textbook vulnerability — reflected in every Economic Survey.
cards.option1: Both A and R are true, R is NOT the correct explanation
cards.option2: A is true, R is false
cards.option3: A is false, R is true
cards.storedExplanation: India imports ~85% of its crude. A $10/barrel rise in crude adds roughly $15 bn to the annual oil import bill. This directly widens the merchandise trade deficit and thus the CAD. Classic textbook vulnerability — reflected in every Economic Survey.

The PRADHAN MANTRI JAN DHAN YOJANA (PMJDY) was launched in:

(A) 2010
(B) 2014
(C) 2016

cards.front:
The money value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year is the:

(A) Gross National Product (GNP)
(B) Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
(C) Net National Product (NNP)
(D) Per capita income
cards.back:
(B) Gross Domestic Product (GDP)

GDP & National Income — GDP — production within the geographical boundaries of a country, regardless of whether the producer is domestic or foreign. GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA). NFIA = income Indians earn abroad − income foreigners earn in India. India typically has negative NFIA (more money goes out as repatriated MNC profits than comes in via NRIs), so GNP < GDP.
cards.storedExplanation: GDP — production within the geographical boundaries of a country, regardless of whether the producer is domestic or foreign. GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA). NFIA = income Indians earn abroad − income foreigners earn in India. India typically has negative NFIA (more money goes out as repatriated MNC profits than comes in via NRIs), so GNP < GDP.

cards.front:
Net National Product (NNP) is calculated as:

(A) GNP + depreciation
(B) GNP − depreciation
(C) GDP + net exports
(D) GDP − indirect taxes
cards.back:
(B) GNP − depreciation

GDP & National Income — NNP = GNP − depreciation of capital. Depreciation represents wear and tear of existing capital used up in production. 'Net' means 'after subtracting depreciation'. NNP at factor cost = 'National Income' (the income accruing to factors of production — labour, capital, entrepreneurship). NNP at market price = NNP at factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies.
cards.storedExplanation: NNP = GNP − depreciation of capital. Depreciation represents wear and tear of existing capital used up in production. 'Net' means 'after subtracting depreciation'. NNP at factor cost = 'National Income' (the income accruing to factors of production — labour, capital, entrepreneurship). NNP at market price = NNP at factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies.

cards.front:
In India, national income statistics are compiled by the:

(A) Reserve Bank of India
(B) Central Statistics Office (NSO)
(C) NITI Aayog
(D) Ministry of Finance
cards.back:
(B) Central Statistics Office (NSO)

GDP & National Income — The Central Statistics Office — reorganised in 2019 as the National Statistical Office (NSO) under MoSPI (Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation) — compiles national income accounts. P. C. Mahalanobis is often called the architect of India's official statistics (he founded ISI and the NSSO). NITI Aayog is the planning think-tank (replaced the Planning Commission in 2015). RBI compiles monetary and financial statistics.

P. C. Mahalanobis is often called the architect of India's official statistics (he founded ISI and the NSSO). NITI Aayog is the planning think-tank (replaced the Planning Commission in 2015). RBI compiles monetary and financial statistics.

cards.front:
The difference between 'nominal GDP' and 'real GDP' is that:

(A) Nominal is for goods, real is for services
(B) Nominal uses current-year prices, real uses base-year prices
(C) Nominal is for India, real is for the world
(D) Real excludes the informal economy
cards.back:
(B) Nominal uses current-year prices, real uses base-year prices

GDP & National Income — Nominal GDP = measured at current-year (market) prices — inflated by price changes. Real GDP = measured at constant prices of a chosen base year — strips out inflation. Real growth rate is the most widely reported measure of economic growth. The GDP deflator = (Nominal / Real) × 100 is itself an inflation measure. India's current base year is 2011-12; a revision to 2020-21 or 2022-23 is being prepared.
cards.option1: Nominal is for goods, real is for services
cards.option2: Nominal is for India, real is for the world
cards.storedExplanation: Nominal GDP = measured at current-year (market) prices — inflated by price changes. Real GDP = measured at constant prices of a chosen base year — strips out inflation. Real growth rate is the most widely reported measure of economic growth. The GDP deflator = (Nominal / Real) × 100 is itself an inflation measure. India's current base year is 2011-12; a revision to 2020-21 or 2022-23 is being prepared.

cards.front:
Per capita income of a country is calculated as:

(A) GDP × population
(B) National income ÷ total population
(C) GDP − taxes
(D) NNP + subsidies
cards.back:
(B) National income ÷ total population

GDP & National Income — Per capita income = National Income / Population. Gives the average income per person per year. India's nominal per capita income was about ₹2.0 lakh in 2023-24 (approximately US$ 2,500). Rich countries often measure it at PPP (purchasing-power parity) as well — on that basis India is higher (~US$ 10,000 at PPP). Per capita income masks inequality — a Gini coefficient or decile distribution supplements it.

India's nominal per capita income was about ₹2.0 lakh in 2023-24 (approximately US$ 2,500). cards.front:
Which method does NOT measure national income?

(A) Production (Value-Added) method
(B) Nielsen survey of consumer brand preference
(C) Income method
(D) Expenditure method
cards.back:
(B) Nielsen survey of consumer brand preference

GDP & National Income — Three equivalent approaches to national income — (i) Production / value-added method — sum of value added at each stage of output. (ii) Income method — sum of factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit). (iii) Expenditure method — sum of C + I + G + (X−M). All three must, in principle, give the same total. Consumer brand surveys are market-research tools, not national-income accounting.

cards.front:
The first estimate of India's national income was prepared by:

(A) P. C. Mahalanobis
(B) Dadabhai Naoroji
(C) V. K. R. V. Rao
(D) D. R. Gadgil
cards.back:
(B) Dadabhai Naoroji

GDP & National Income — Dadabhai Naoroji — 'Grand Old Man of India' — gave the first estimate of India's national income in his book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901), using it to articulate the 'Drain Theory'. The first scientific estimate came from V. K. R. V. Rao in 1931-32. Mahalanobis designed the National Income Committee (1949) and India's planning models. D. R. Gadgil was the first Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission.

cards.front:
GDP at MARKET PRICE differs from GDP at FACTOR COST by:

(A) Net foreign income from abroad to residents
(B) Net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies)
(C) Depreciation of capital stock during the year
(D) Inflation rate of the country in that period
cards.back:
(B) Net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies)

GDP & National Income — GDP at MARKET PRICE = GDP at FACTOR COST + (Indirect Taxes − Subsidies) = GDP at FC + NET INDIRECT TAXES. Market price includes taxes (paid by buyer); factor cost reflects what producers actually receive. India officially uses GVA (Gross Value Added) at basic prices = GDP at FC since 2015 (CSO methodology revision). Distractor 1 = difference between GDP and GNP (NFIA). Distractor 3 = difference between gross + net (depreciation). Distractor 4 = nominal vs real adjustment.
cards.option1: Net foreign income from abroad to residents
cards.option2: Depreciation of capital stock during the year
cards.option3: Inflation rate of the country in that period

Market price includes taxes (paid by buyer); factor cost reflects what producers actually receive. India officially uses GVA (Gross Value Added) at basic prices = GDP at FC since 2015 (CSO methodology revision). Distractor 1 = difference between GDP and GNP (NFIA). Distractor 3 = difference between gross + net (depreciation). Distractor 4 = nominal vs real adjustment.

cards.front:
GNP differs from GDP by which adjustment?

(A) Subtracting depreciation from gross value
(B) Adding net factor income from abroad (NFIA)
(C) Adding all indirect taxes minus subsidies
(D) Multiplying by current inflation rate level
cards.back:
(B) Adding net factor income from abroad (NFIA)

GDP & National Income — GNP = GDP + NFIA. NFIA = factor income earned by Indians abroad − factor income earned by foreigners in India. GDP is TERRITORIAL (within India's borders); GNP is NATIONAL (Indians anywhere). For India, NFIA is usually slightly NEGATIVE (we're a net debtor; pay more interest abroad than we earn) → GNP slightly < GDP. NDP = GDP − depreciation. NNP = GNP − depreciation. NI (National Income) = NNP at factor cost.
cards.option2: Adding all indirect taxes minus subsidies
cards.option3: Multiplying by current inflation rate level
cards.storedExplanation: GNP = GDP + NFIA. NFIA = factor income earned by Indians abroad − factor income earned by foreigners in India. GDP is TERRITORIAL (within India's borders); GNP is NATIONAL (Indians anywhere). For India, NFIA is usually slightly NEGATIVE (we're a net debtor; pay more interest abroad than we earn) → GNP slightly < GDP. NDP = GDP − depreciation. NNP = GNP − depreciation. NI (National Income) = NNP at factor cost.

cards.front:
REAL GDP differs from NOMINAL GDP because Real GDP:

(A) Includes net factor income from abroad too
(B) Adjusts for inflation using a base-year price
(C) Is always larger than the nominal GDP value
(D) Is calculated only by central planning bodies
cards.back:
(B) Adjusts for inflation using a base-year price

GDP & National Income — NOMINAL GDP — at current-year prices. REAL GDP — at base-year prices (CONSTANT PRICES). Adjusts for inflation to show genuine production change. India base year: 2011-12 (will be revised to 2022-23 around 2025-26). Real growth = (Nominal growth − Inflation) approximately. GDP DEFLATOR = (Nominal/Real) × 100 → broad price-level measure. Comparing 2024 GDP to 1990 GDP only meaningful in REAL terms. During inflation, nominal > real.

cards.option2: Is always larger than the nominal GDP value
cards.option3: Is calculated only by central planning bodies

cards.front:
PER CAPITA INCOME of a country is calculated as:

(A) GDP divided by total area of the country
(B) National Income divided by total population
(C) Total tax revenue divided by population
(D) Imports plus exports divided by population
cards.back:
(B) National Income divided by total population

GDP & National Income — Per Capita Income = National Income / Population. India's per capita income (FY24): ~₹2.13 lakh (~$2,500). World average: ~$13,000. Per capita gives a sense of average prosperity but hides inequality. INDIA's per capita is much lower than China's (~$13,000), Bangladesh's ($2,800 — recently overtook India in some years). Income inequality measured by GINI coefficient (0 = perfect equality, 1 = max inequality). Distractor 1 = density-related concept. Distractors 3, 4 are unrelated.

The first SCIENTIFIC ESTIMATE of national income for India was made by:

(A) Mahalanobis at the Indian Statistical Institute
(B) Dadabhai Naoroji, in his 1867-68 estimates
(C) VKRV Rao, in his 1925 doctoral thesis
(D) Indian National Income Committee in 1949

Post-independence, the National Income Committee (1949, chaired by P.C. Mahalanobis) put national income estimation on a scientific basis. CSO (Central Statistics Office, now NSO) handles current estimates.

cards.front:
The PRIMARY SECTOR in national income accounting refers to:

(A) Manufacturing industries and construction sectors
(B) Agriculture, fishing, forestry, mining (raw extraction)
(C) Banking, insurance, IT services and trade
(D) Government welfare-spending and subsidy schemes
cards.back:
(B) Agriculture, fishing, forestry, mining (raw extraction)

GDP & National Income — Three-sector classification (Clark, Fisher): PRIMARY = extraction of raw materials from nature (agriculture, fishing, forestry, mining, quarrying). SECONDARY = manufacturing, construction, electricity (transformation of raw materials). TERTIARY = services (trade, transport, banking, IT, hospitality, government). India's GVA share (FY24): primary ~17%, secondary ~28%, tertiary ~55%. Trend — India is becoming services-led without going through full industrialisation (unusual development path; some call it 'premature deindustrialisation').

cards.front:
Three METHODS of measuring national income are:

(A) Direct, indirect and via household surveys
(B) Production (value-added), Income, and Expenditure
(C) Random sampling, full census and modelling
(D) Top-down, bottom-up and meta-aggregation
cards.back:
(B) Production (value-added), Income, and Expenditure

GDP & National Income — Three EQUIVALENT methods (yielding same result in theory): (1) PRODUCTION / VALUE-ADDED method — sum of Gross Value Added across all sectors; avoids double-counting by counting only value added at each stage. (2) INCOME method — sum of factor incomes (wages + rent + interest + profit) earned by residents. (3) EXPENDITURE method — sum of final demand: C + I + G + (X−M) (consumption + investment + govt. + net exports). India uses combination — value-added for production estimates, expenditure as cross-check. CSO publishes via all three. Discrepancies adjusted in final accounts.

cards.option2: Random sampling, full census and modelling

cards.front:
GDP stands for:

(A) Gross Development Product
(B) Gross Domestic Product
(C) Gross Domestic Price
(D) Gross Deflationary Product
cards.back:
(B) Gross Domestic Product

GDP & National Income — GDP — Gross Domestic Product — market value of all final goods and services produced WITHIN a country's borders in a year. GNP includes NET factor income from abroad (GNP = GDP + NFIA).
cards.storedExplanation: GDP — Gross Domestic Product — market value of all final goods and services produced WITHIN a country's borders in a year. GNP includes NET factor income from abroad (GNP = GDP + NFIA).

cards.front:
The relationship between GDP and GNP is:

(A) GNP = GDP − Depreciation
(B) GNP = GDP + NFIA
(C) GNP = GDP + Indirect taxes
(D) GNP = GDP × Inflation
cards.back:
(B) GNP = GDP + NFIA

GDP & National Income — GNP = GDP + NFIA. NFIA = income from abroad by citizens − income paid to foreigners for their work/investments here. For India, NFIA is typically NEGATIVE (more repatriated out than brought in), so GNP < GDP. NDP = GDP − depreciation. NNP = GNP − depreciation. Net Factor Income from Abroad.

cards.front:
PER CAPITA INCOME is calculated as:

(A) GDP × population
(B) National Income / Total population
(C) GDP / GNP
(D) Population / GDP
cards.back:
(B) National Income / Total population

GDP & National Income — Per capita income = National Income (or GDP) / Population. Useful indicator of individual prosperity; but hides inequality. India's per capita income (2024): around $2,500-2,700 (nominal). Much higher in PPP terms.

India's National Accounts / National Income estimates are published by:

GDP & National Income — NSO — under MoSPI (Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation). Combines the former CSO (Central Statistics Office) + NSSO. cards.front:
REAL GDP vs NOMINAL GDP: the difference is:

(A) Real GDP includes inflation effects; nominal does not
(B) Nominal GDP is at current prices; Real GDP is adjusted for inflation
(C) Both are the same
(D) Real GDP measures imports
cards.back:
(B) Nominal GDP is at current prices; Real GDP is adjusted for inflation

GDP & National Income — Nominal GDP — in current prices (inflated). Real GDP — deflated using a GDP deflator or base year prices, reflects actual output change. Real growth is the more meaningful measure of economic expansion. at constant/base-year prices.

India is the world's ___ LARGEST economy (nominal GDP, 2024-25):

(A) 10th
(B) 5th
(C) 15th

(B) 5th

cards.front:
'PPP' (Purchasing Power Parity) adjustment is used to:

(A) Measure inflation
(B) Compare national incomes by adjusting for cost-of-living differences
(C) Calculate corporate tax
(D) Set interest rates
cards.back:
(B) Compare national incomes by adjusting for cost-of-living differences

GDP & National Income — PPP — equalises the purchasing power of different currencies by comparing what a basket of goods costs in each country. Famous 'Big Mac Index' (Economist magazine). India's GDP is much larger in PPP terms than in nominal USD because costs are lower.

cards.front:
In India, which sector contributes the LARGEST share of GDP currently?

(A) Agriculture (primary)
(B) Industry / manufacturing (secondary)
(C) Services (tertiary)
(D) Mining
cards.back:
(C) Services (tertiary)

GDP & National Income — Services sector contributes >50% of India's GDP. Industry ~26%, Agriculture ~15%. But agriculture still EMPLOYS ~44% of the workforce — the classic 'structural mismatch' of India's economy.

cards.front:
Under MGNREGA (2005), each rural household is guaranteed at least ___ days of wage employment a year:

(A) 50

(C) 150

cards.back:

GDP & National Income — MGNREGA — Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (2005), effective 2006. Guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage labour per rural household per year, within 5 km of the home or travel allowance. Now extended to 150 days in some drought-hit districts.

cards.back:

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), the central bank of the country, was established in:

(A) 1925

cards.back:

cards.front:
The 'Repo Rate' set by the RBI is the rate at which:

(A) Commercial banks lend to the RBI
(B) The RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks
(C) Banks lend to each other
(D) Banks charge customers for savings accounts
cards.back:
(B) The RBI lends short-term money to commercial banks

Banking & RBI — Repo ('repurchase') rate — RBI lends short-term (1-day) money to banks against collateral (government securities); 'repo' means the bank agrees to repurchase the securities at a higher price. Reverse repo rate — banks park surplus cash with RBI; lower than repo. Bank Rate — longer-term RBI lending, largely symbolic now. MSF — marginal standing facility, slightly above repo.

cards.option3: Banks charge customers for savings accounts

cards.front:
The proportion of a bank's deposits that it must keep as cash with the RBI (not earning interest) is called the:

(A) Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
(B) Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)
(C) Repo Rate
(D) Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL)
cards.back:
(B) Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)

Banking & RBI — CRR — cash the bank must hold with the RBI, in proportion to its NDTL. SLR — additional liquid assets (cash, gold or approved govt. securities) held with the bank itself. Both tighten / loosen the money supply. Raising CRR pulls liquidity out, cooling inflation; cutting CRR releases funds, supporting growth. Interest-free; currently around 4.5 % (SLR ~18 %).

cards.front:
In banking terminology, an 'NPA' (Non-Performing Asset) is a loan on which principal or interest repayments are overdue for:

(A) 30 days
(B) More than 90 days
(C) 6 months
(D) 1 year
cards.back:
(B) More than 90 days

Further categories — Sub-standard (NPA up to 12 months), Doubtful (NPA over 12 months), Loss (unrecoverable). Which of the following is NOT a function of the Reserve Bank of India?

cards.front:
The REPO RATE is the rate at which:

(A) Banks borrow from each other
(B) RBI LENDS short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities
(C) Savings account interest is computed
(D) Cross-border currency conversion
cards.back:
(B) RBI LENDS short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities

Banking & RBI — REPO RATE (REPURCHASE RATE) — rate at which RBI LENDS short-term funds to commercial BANKS against pledged government securities with agreement to repurchase. BENCHMARK POLICY RATE set by the MONETARY POLICY COMMITTEE (MPC), 6 members (3 RBI + 3 external), since 2016 amendment to RBI Act. Meets BI-MONTHLY. repo ↑ → banks' cost ↑ → lending rates ↑ → dampens inflation. repo ↓ → stimulates growth. CURRENT (Apr 2026): ~6.50%. RELATED RATES: (1) REVERSE REPO RATE — rate RBI pays banks for parking surplus. (2) MSF (Marginal Standing Facility) — emergency overnight at repo + 25bps. (3) CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) — % deposits banks must keep with RBI as cash; currently 4.5%; NO interest. (4) SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio) — % deposits in Gsecs + gold + cash; currently 18%; earns interest. (5) LAF (Liquidity Adjustment Facility). RBI's CPI INFLATION TARGET: 4% ± 2% (i.e., 2-6%) — statutory since 2016. repurchase agreement.

cards.front:
In 1969 the Indian Government NATIONALISED how many commercial banks?

(A) 6
(B) 14 BANKS on 19 July 1969 by PM Indira Gandhi
(C) 21
(D) 4
cards.back:
(B) 14 BANKS on 19 July 1969 by PM Indira Gandhi

Banking & RBI — 1969 BANK NATIONALISATION — defining moment in Indian economic history. DATE: 19 JULY 1969 ('Bank Nationalisation Day'). PM INDIRA GANDHI used an OVERNIGHT ordinance to nationalise 14 PRIVATE commercial banks with deposits > ₹50 crore, bringing 40% of commercial banking under direct govt control. BANKS NATIONALISED: Central Bank of India, Bank of India, Punjab National Bank, Bank of Baroda, UCO Bank, Canara Bank, United Bank of India, Dena Bank, Syndicate Bank, Union Bank of India, Allahabad Bank, Indian Bank, Indian Overseas Bank, Bank of Maharashtra. LEGAL CHALLENGE: R.C. COOPER v. UNION OF INDIA (1970) — SC struck down the ordinance 10-1 on compensation grounds; Parliament re-enacted as a law with adequate compensation — upheld. SECOND ROUND (1980): 6 more banks nationalised (deposits > ₹200 crore) — Andhra, Corporation, New Bank of India, Oriental Bank of Commerce, Punjab + Sind, Vijaya. Since 2017-2020 merger wave: ~12 PSBs today; 21 private; 43 foreign; 12 small finance; 6 payments banks. banks with deposit > ₹50 crore.

cards.front:
UPI, India's instant mobile payment system launched in 2016, is operated by:

(A) RBI directly
(B) NPCI
(C) SEBI
(D) SBI
cards.back:
(B) NPCI

Banking & RBI — UPI (UNIFIED PAYMENTS INTERFACE) — INSTANT, 24/7, real-time inter-bank mobile payment system. LAUNCHED: 11 April 2016 by then RBI Governor RAGHURAM RAJAN. OPERATOR: NATIONAL PAYMENTS CORPORATION OF INDIA (NPCI) — a not-for-profit Sec-8 company set up 2008 under RBI + IBA (Indian Banks' Association). FEATURES: (1) single mobile app accesses multiple bank accounts; (2) VPA like name@bank — no need to share bank details; (3) instant transfer 24/7; (4) 2FA. 2024 stats: ~12 BILLION transactions/MONTH; ₹20 lakh crore monthly value; UPI accounts for ~50% of real-time global retail payments. MAJOR UPI apps: PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm, BHIM, WhatsApp Pay, Amazon Pay, Cred. OTHER NPCI products: IMPS (2010), RuPay (2012 card network), NACH, BBPS, AePS (Aadhaar-enabled Payment System), FASTag (NETC), CTS. UPI has gone GLOBAL: linked with Singapore's PayNow, UAE, Mauritius, Bhutan, Nepal, France, Sri Lanka.

cards.front:
The SARFAESI Act (2002) empowers banks to:

(A) Fix interest rates
(B) Recover NPAs by SEIZING + SELLING secured assets of defaulters WITHOUT court intervention
(C) Print currency
(D) Grant business licences
cards.back:
(B) Recover NPAs by SEIZING + SELLING secured assets of defaulters WITHOUT court intervention

Banking & RBI — SARFAESI ACT 2002 — SECURITISATION + RECONSTRUCTION of FINANCIAL ASSETS + ENFORCEMENT of SECURITY INTEREST ACT. Based on Narasimham-II (1998) + Andhyarujina Committee (1999). POWERS: (1) banks can issue 60-DAY NOTICE to defaulter; then take POSSESSION of the pledged asset + auction; NO court intervention needed. (2) creation of ASSET RECONSTRUCTION COMPANIES (ARCs) to purchase stressed loans. Minimum loan: ₹1 lakh. EXCLUSIONS: agri land, amounts <20% of loan. APPEAL: DRT → DRAT → HC (must deposit 50% before appealing). PRE-SARFAESI, banks had to file civil suits taking 10-15 years. NPA (Non-Performing Asset) — loan where interest/principal remains unpaid >90 days. Gross NPA ratio fell from ~11% (2018) to ~3% (2024) through IBC + SARFAESI + govt recapitalisation + AQR. Complementary law: IBC (Insolvency + Bankruptcy Code, 2016) — covers corporate insolvency via NCLT. for secured loans > ₹1 lakh.

cards.front:
PRADHAN MANTRI JAN DHAN YOJANA (PMJDY), launched 28 August 2014, aims at:

(A) LPG subsidies
(B) UNIVERSAL FINANCIAL INCLUSION
(C) Housing loans
(D) Health insurance
cards.back:
(B) UNIVERSAL FINANCIAL INCLUSION

Banking & RBI — PMJDY — 'NATIONAL MISSION for FINANCIAL INCLUSION'. LAUNCHED: 28 AUGUST 2014 by PM Narendra Modi; Guinness Record — 1.8 crore accounts in one week. FEATURES: (1) ZERO balance savings a/c (BSBDA); (2) RuPay debit card with ₹1-2L accident insurance; (3) ₹30,000 life cover (2014-15 enrollees); (4) ₹10,000 overdraft facility after 6 months; (5) no minimum balance; (6) free Aadhaar seeding. PROGRESS (Nov 2024): ~53 CRORE accounts; ₹2.33 lakh crore total deposits; 36 crore RuPay cards; 55% female account-holders; 67% rural/semi-urban. IMPACT: backbone of DBT — LPG (PAHAL), PM-KISAN, MGNREGA wages, COVID relief. JAM TRINITY = Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile = foundational architecture of India's DPI. Today ~95% Indian adults have bank account (World Bank Findex 2021, up from 35% in 2011). Related schemes: PMJJBY (life, ₹2L at ₹436/yr), PMSBY (accident, ₹2L at ₹20/yr), APY (pension, max ₹5000/month after 60 yr age). zero-balance account + RuPay card + ₹2L accident cover + overdraft facility for every household.

cards.front:
CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) differs from SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio) in that:

(A) Both are held with RBI
(B) CRR is kept with RBI in CASH (no interest)
(C) Both earn interest
(D) SLR is for only private banks
cards.back:
(B) CRR is kept with RBI in CASH (no interest)

Banking & RBI — CRR — Cash Reserve Ratio (Sec 42 of RBI Act 1934) — % of a bank's NDTL (net demand + time liabilities) to be kept WITH RBI IN CASH, earning NO INTEREST. Current: 4.5%. SLR — Statutory Liquidity Ratio (Sec 24 of Banking Regulation Act 1949) — % of NDTL kept by the bank itself in Gsecs + SDLs + gold + cash. EARNS INTEREST. Current: 18%. PURPOSE: liquidity buffer + force banks to hold safe assets. Historical peaks: CRR 15% (1992); SLR 38.5% (1991). MNEMONIC: CRR = Cash with RBI; SLR = Securities within bank. Other key ratios: LCR (Liquidity Coverage, Basel III) 100%; NSFR 100%; CAR (Capital Adequacy) ≥ 9% (+ Capital Conservation Buffer); PSL (Priority Sector Lending) 40% of net bank credit (agriculture, MSME, housing, education, weaker sections). SLR is kept BY THE BANK ITSELF in Gsecs + gold + cash.
cards.option3: SLR is for only private banks

cards.front:
NABARD, India's apex rural + agricultural development bank, was established in:

(A) 1969
(B) 12 July 1982, on the recommendation of the SIVARAMAN (CRAFICARD) Committee
(C) 1991
(D) 1955
cards.back:
(B) 12 July 1982, on the recommendation of the SIVARAMAN (CRAFICARD) Committee

Banking & RBI — NABARD — NATIONAL BANK FOR AGRICULTURE AND RURAL DEVELOPMENT. Established 12 JULY 1982 by the NABARD Act 1981, on recommendations of the CRAFICARD Committee (chaired by B. SIVARAMAN). HQ: Mumbai. Owner: 100% GoI (since 2018). REPLACED: ARDC + ACD of RBI + RPCC. Current Chairman: Shaji K.V. FUNCTIONS: (1) REFINANCE to cooperative banks, RRBs, commercial banks, NBFCs for ag term loans. (2) DIRECT FINANCE to large rural infrastructure projects. (3) RIDF (Rural Infrastructure Development Fund, 1995) — funds state projects; funded by PSB priority-sector shortfalls. (4) Supervision of state + district cooperative banks + RRBs. (5) SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (1992) — ~1.5 crore SHGs — world's largest microfinance programme. (6) Kisan Credit Card scheme. Rural banking structure: (a) RRBs (est. 1975 per Narasimham Committee I); (b) Cooperative banks (3-tier: PACS → DCCB → StCB); (c) SFBs (Small Finance Banks 2015 — AU, Equitas, Ujjivan, Suryoday, etc.).

cards.front:
The NARASIMHAM COMMITTEES (1991 + 1998) are associated with reforms in:

(A) Taxation
(B) Banking / financial sector
(C) Administrative services
(D) Foreign policy
cards.back:
(B) Banking / financial sector

Banking & RBI — NARASIMHAM COMMITTEES — chaired by M. NARASIMHAM (former RBI Governor, 1977). (1) NARASIMHAM-I (1991) — post 1991 BoP crisis + LPG reforms. REC: (a) reduce SLR 38.5→25% + CRR progressively; (b) DEREGULATE interest rates; (c) allow FOREIGN + NEW PRIVATE banks (led to ICICI, HDFC, Axis, IndusInd entry 1993-94); (d) adopt CAPITAL ADEQUACY NORMS (Basel 8%); (e) introduce ASSET CLASSIFICATION + income recognition (NPAs); (f) structure supervision under Board for Financial Supervision (BFS, RBI). (2) NARASIMHAM-II (1998) — deeper reforms. REC: (a) raise CAR from 8 to 9% (now Basel III+); (b) reduce PSB govt shareholding to 33%; (c) bank MERGERS (seed for 2017-20 merger wave); (d) creation of ASSET RECONSTRUCTION COMPANIES (led to SARFAESI 2002); (e) tech modernisation. Other banking committees: HILTON YOUNG (1926) → RBI Act; CHAKRAVARTY (1985); KHAN (1997); TARAPORE (1997, 2006); RAGHURAM RAJAN (2008) → financial sector reforms; MOR Committee (2014) → financial inclusion. CAR, NPA norms, deregulation of rates, bank consolidation, entry of private banks.

Banking & RBI — Per RBI's Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning (IRAC), an account becomes NPA if interest/principal remains overdue for MORE THAN 90 DAYS for term loans (was 180 days before 2004; aligned with international norms). cards.front:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) was enacted in which year and what is the target resolution period?

(A) 2013; 180+180 days
(B) 2016; 180+90 days
(C) 2017; 360 days max
(D) 2018; 120 days
cards.back:
(B) 2016; 180+90 days

Banking & RBI — IBC 2016 (effective 28 May 2016) unified India's bankruptcy laws. Under Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP): 180-day initial period + one-time 90-day extension = MAX 270 days (extended to 330 days by 2019 amendment, including litigation time). Key institutions: IBBI (regulator), NCLT (adjudicating authority for corporates), NCLAT (appellate), IPAs (Insolvency Professional Agencies), Information Utilities. cards.front:
Under Basel III norms implemented in India, what is the minimum Capital Adequacy Ratio (CRAR) required for a Scheduled Commercial Bank (SCB)?

(A) 8%
(B) 9%
(C) 11.5%
(D) 12%
cards.back:
(B) 9%

Banking & RBI — Basel III (global regulatory framework, implemented in India from 2013 onwards by RBI) prescribes MINIMUM CAR/CRAR = 9% for SCBs (higher than Basel's own 8% — India applied a stricter buffer). Additional requirement: Capital Conservation Buffer of 2.5% (so effective minimum 11.5%) + Counter-Cyclical Capital Buffer 0-2.5%. Tier 1 + Tier 2 capital / Risk Weighted Assets. For SFBs: 15% (with Tier 1 ≥ 7.5%). For UCBs: 9% (Tier 1) + 12% (Total, for Tier-2/3/4).

cards.front:
The SARFAESI Act, 2002, empowers banks to recover bad loans WITHOUT court intervention. What does SARFAESI stand for?

(A) Securities and Reconstruction of Financial Assets & Enforcement of Security Interest
(B) State Audit and Recovery Finance Act for Enforcement of Secured Instruments
(C) Secured Assets Recovery and Financial Enforcement of Special Instruments
(D) Scheduled Accounts Recovery by Financial Establishments & Secured Interest
cards.back:
(A) Securities and Reconstruction of Financial Assets & Enforcement of Security Interest

Banking & RBI — SARFAESI = Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002. Allows banks/FIs to: (1) securitise assets; (2) set up Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs); (3) enforce security interest WITHOUT court intervention — attach and sell defaulter's mortgaged assets after 60-day notice. Applies to loans above ₹1 lakh (now ₹20 lakh by 2021 amendment). Not applicable to: agricultural land, loans ≤ ₹1 lakh, and where 80% of loan is repaid. Critical tool alongside IBC 2016 for NPA resolution.

The Narasimham Committee (I, 1991), whose recommendations reshaped Indian banking in the 1990s, was headed by:

(A) M. Narasimha Rao (former PM)

(C) N. Narasimhan (former Cabinet Secretary)
(D) PVN Narasimhan (first NABARD chairman)

cards.front:
Which Indian bank was the first to be established and is considered the oldest surviving bank?

(A) State Bank of India
(B) Bank of Hindustan
(C) Allahabad Bank (1865)
(D) State Bank of India via its predecessor Bank of Calcutta (1806)
cards.back:
(D) State Bank of India via its predecessor Bank of Calcutta (1806)

Banking & RBI — SBI's family tree: Bank of Calcutta (2 June 1806) → renamed Bank of Bengal (1809) → merged with Bank of Bombay (1840) and Bank of Madras (1843) to form Imperial Bank of India (1921) → nationalised as STATE BANK OF INDIA by SBI Act 1955. So SBI is the OLDEST surviving bank via Bank of Calcutta (1806). Bank of Hindustan (1770) was EARLIER but defunct by 1832. Allahabad Bank (1865) was India's first FULLY INDIAN-MANAGED joint-stock bank; it merged into Indian Bank in 2020. Punjab National Bank (1894) — first bank fully managed by Indians.

cards.front:
Bank nationalisation in India happened in two phases. Which year did the SECOND phase of bank nationalisation occur?

(A) 1969
(B) 1980
(C) 1991
(D) 1993
cards.back:
(B) 1980

Banking & RBI — FIRST phase: 19 July 1969 — Indira Gandhi nationalised 14 major private banks (those with deposits > ₹50 crore) via the Banking Companies Ordinance 1969. Banks included: Central BoI, BoI, PNB, BoB, UCO, Canara, Dena, Syndicate, Union, Allahabad, Indian, Indian Overseas, BoM, United Bank. SECOND phase: 15 April 1980 — 6 more private banks with deposits > ₹200 crore nationalised (Andhra Bank, Corporation, New Bank of India merged later with PNB, Oriental Bank, Punjab & Sind, Vijaya). Result: ~91% of banking system became public sector by 1980. Liberalisation in 1991 allowed new private banks (HDFC, ICICI, Axis etc.).

cards.front:
Which of the following is a regulator of NBFCs in India?

(A) SEBI
(B) RBI
(C) IRDAI
(D) PFRDA
cards.back:
(B) RBI

Banking & RBI — NBFCs (Non-Banking Financial Companies) are regulated by RBI. Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) framework (effective Oct 2022) classifies NBFCs into 4 layers: (1) BASE Layer — smaller NBFCs (<₹1000 Cr assets) — minimum NOF ₹10 Cr by March 2027; (2) MIDDLE Layer; (3) UPPER Layer (identified by RBI as systemically important); (4) TOP Layer (reserved for extreme systemic risk cases). Types: AFC (Asset Finance), LC (Loan), ICC (Investment & Credit), IFC (Infrastructure Finance), MGC (Mortgage Guarantee), MFI (MicroFinance), HFC (Housing Finance — now regulated by RBI from NHB since 2019). SEBI regulates mutual funds/stock markets; IRDAI regulates insurance; PFRDA regulates pensions.

cards.front:
An asset is classified as a 'Non-Performing Asset' (NPA) by RBI if interest / principal remains overdue for:

(A) 30 days
(B) 90 days
(C) 180 days
(D) 1 year
cards.back:
(B) 90 days

Banking & RBI — NPA — overdue beyond 90 days (one quarter). Sub-classifications: Standard (paying), Sub-standard (NPA up to 12 months), Doubtful (NPA 12-36 months), Loss (over 36 months — written off / negligible recovery expected). Banks must make 'provisions' (set aside profits) for NPAs — Standard 0.4%, Sub-standard 15%, Doubtful 25-100%, Loss 100%. Twin-balance-sheet problem (2014-18) was driven by surge in corporate NPAs. Net NPA ratio of scheduled commercial banks dropped to ~0.7% by 2024 (peak ~12% in 2018).

cards.front:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, India was passed in:

(A) 2013
(B) 2016
(C) 2019
(D) 2020
cards.back:

Apex authority — IBBI (Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India). Major resolutions — Essar Steel (sold to ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel, 2019), Bhushan Steel (sold to Tata Steel), Jet Airways. cards.front:
The 'Basel III' norms — international banking regulation framework — focus primarily on:

(A) Country credit ratings
(B) Bank capital adequacy, leverage ratio, liquidity standards (LCR, NSFR)
(C) Currency exchange rates only
(D) Income tax for banks
cards.back:
(B) Bank capital adequacy, leverage ratio, liquidity standards (LCR, NSFR)

Banking & RBI — Basel III — agreed by Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS, 27 jurisdictions) post-2008 financial crisis. Key requirements: minimum CET-1 capital 4.5%, Tier 1 capital 6%, total capital 8% of RWA + Capital Conservation Buffer 2.5% + Counter-cyclical buffer 0-2.5%. Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) ≥ 100% (30-day stress). Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) ≥ 100% (1-year horizon). Leverage Ratio ≥ 3%. India implemented Basel III through RBI guidelines, fully phased in by 2019.

cards.front:
The 'repo rate' is the rate at which the:

(A) Government borrows from the public
(B) RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities
(C) Banks lend to retail customers
(D) RBI exchanges foreign currency
cards.back:
(B) RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities

Banking & RBI — Repo (repurchase) — RBI lends overnight to banks against G-Sec collateral; banks 'sell with a repurchase agreement'. Repo is the policy rate; sets the floor for short-term interest rates. As of Apr 2025: Repo = 6.00% (after a 25 bp cut in Apr-25 MPC). Reverse repo — RBI borrows from banks (currently 3.35%, rarely used since SDF was introduced in Apr 2022). SDF — Standing Deposit Facility (3.50% in Apr 2025) is the lower-bound; MSF — Marginal Standing Facility (6.25%) is the upper-bound. Bank Rate (now aligned to MSF). LAF (Liquidity Adjustment Facility) corridor: SDF (lower) – Repo (mid) – MSF (upper).

cards.front:
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in India was formed under the amended RBI Act, 1934. Its composition is:

(A) All members nominated by RBI
(B) 6 members — 3 from RBI (incl. Governor as Chair, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer) + 3 external members appointed by the Centre
(C) All members from the Finance Ministry
(D) 12 members from various banks
cards.back:
(B) 6 members — 3 from RBI (incl. Governor as Chair, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer) + 3 external members appointed by the Centre

Banking & RBI — MPC — created in 2016 by an amendment to the RBI Act 1934. 6 members: (1) RBI Governor (ex-officio Chairperson, casting vote in case of tie); (2) Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy; (3) one RBI officer nominated by Central Board; (4-6) three external members appointed by the Centre (typically economists). Term of external members — 4 years, non-renewable. Decisions by majority; if 3-3 tie, Governor's casting vote. Meets at least 4 times a year (usually 6 — every 2 months). Mandate: maintain headline CPI inflation at 4% ± 2% (i.e., 2-6% band) — 'flexible inflation targeting'; review every 5 years (current term till Mar 2026).

cards.front:
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is:

(A) Loans banks must give to priority sectors
(B) The proportion of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that must be kept with the RBI in cash, earning no interest
(C) Foreign exchange reserves of the RBI
(D) Money kept in ATMs
cards.back:
(B) The proportion of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that must be kept with the RBI in cash, earning no interest

Banking & RBI — CRR — % of NDTL kept as cash with RBI; no interest paid. Currently 4% (Apr 2025). Reducing CRR — releases liquidity to banks (more lending capacity, expansionary). SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio) — % of NDTL kept in liquid assets (G-Sec, gold, cash with the bank itself); currently 18% (Apr 2025). Earns interest. Quantitative tools of monetary policy: CRR, SLR, OMO (Open Market Operations — RBI buys/sells G-Sec to manage liquidity), LAF, MSF. Qualitative tools: margin requirements, moral suasion, credit rationing. CRR floor was earlier 3% (statutory), but the floor was removed by amendment.

VRR (Variable Rate Repo) and VRRR (Variable Rate Reverse Repo) — variable-rate auctions for liquidity management.

cards.front:
RBI's primary inflation target under the flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework is:

(A) WPI between 0-2%
(B) Headline CPI (Consumer Price Index, combined) at 4% ± 2% (i.e., a 2-6% band)
(C) Core inflation at exactly 5%
(D) GDP deflator at 6%
cards.back:
(B) Headline CPI (Consumer Price Index, combined) at 4% ± 2% (i.e., a 2-6% band)

Banking & RBI — FIT framework — operationalised by the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) → MPC Act amendments (2016). Target: 4% ± 2% headline CPI (combined). Set by the Centre in consultation with RBI; reviewed every 5 years (current target valid till 31 Mar 2026). FAILURE — if CPI is outside the 2-6% band for 3 consecutive quarters, RBI must submit a report to the Centre explaining reasons + remedial action + expected return-to-target horizon. (RBI failed in 2022 — submitted such a report for the first time.) WPI (Wholesale Price Index) — was the main inflation measure pre-2014; RBI now uses CPI as the headline target. Core inflation = CPI excluding food & fuel.

cards.front:
The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) was introduced in 2011 as:

(A) A loan facility for SMEs
(B) An emergency overnight borrowing window for banks at a rate higher than the repo rate (currently repo + 25 bp)
(C) A subsidy for marginal farmers
(D) A tax on banks
cards.back:
(B) An emergency overnight borrowing window for banks at a rate higher than the repo rate (currently repo + 25 bp)

Banking & RBI — MSF — introduced 9 May 2011. Banks can borrow OVERNIGHT from RBI by dipping into their SLR holdings (up to 2% of NDTL — increased to 3% temporarily during COVID). Rate = repo + 25 bp (currently 6.25% in Apr 2025 with repo at 6.00%). Used as the upper bound of the LAF corridor. MSF is a 'penalty' window for emergency liquidity; banks rarely use it heavily — it's a signalling tool. Bank Rate is now aligned with MSF. The corridor (lower bound = SDF since 2022; upper bound = MSF) helps RBI keep call money rates close to the repo rate.

cards.front:
When the RBI INCREASES the repo rate, the typical (textbook) effect on the economy is:

(A) Inflation rises immediately
(B) Borrowing becomes costlier → demand cools → inflation expected to ease over time (contractionary)
(C) Government deficit decreases
(D) Currency value always falls
cards.back:
(B) Borrowing becomes costlier → demand cools → inflation expected to ease over time (contractionary)

Banking & RBI — Repo hike (contractionary monetary policy): banks face higher cost of borrowing from RBI → pass-through to lending rates (home, auto, business loans cost more) → loan demand falls → consumer + business spending eases → demand-side inflation reduces. Lag — typically 6-9 months for full transmission. Side-effects: GDP growth tends to slow (inflation-growth tradeoff); savings yields rise (good for senior citizens); rupee may strengthen marginally (higher rates attract foreign investment). REVERSE — repo cut: stimulus, cheaper credit, growth-friendly. RBI's stance shifts from 'accommodative' (cut bias) to 'neutral' to 'tight' (hike bias) depending on inflation-growth balance. April 2025 — 25 bp cut, stance maintained at 'neutral'.

cards.front:

(A) Currency with the public + demand deposits
(B) Currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI

(D) Savings bank deposits

M1 = M0 + demand deposits; M2 = M1 + post-office savings deposits; M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks ('broad money' — the most commonly reported aggregate). RBI targets broad money (M3) in its monetary policy framework.

cards.front:
The 'money multiplier' of an economy is approximately the reciprocal of:

(A) The repo rate
(B) The cash reserve ratio (CRR)
(C) The bank rate
(D) The inflation rate
cards.back:
(B) The cash reserve ratio (CRR)

Banking & RBI — Basic money-multiplier model — if banks keep fraction 'r' (CRR) of deposits as reserves and lend the rest, the total money created from a new deposit is 1/r. If CRR = 4 %, the multiplier is 25 (ignoring other leakages like cash in hand). Real-world multipliers are lower due to cash preferences, excess reserves, and the SLR constraint. Still the simplest link between reserve ratio and broad-money growth.

cards.front:
'Gresham's law' in monetary economics states that:

(A) High taxes drive out investment
(B) Bad money drives out good money from circulation
(C) Too much money causes inflation
(D) Savings rise with interest rates
cards.back:
(B) Bad money drives out good money from circulation

Banking & RBI — Gresham's law (attributed to Sir Thomas Gresham, 16th c.) — 'Bad money drives out good' — when two currencies circulate at the same legal value but have different intrinsic values, people hoard the more valuable (good) one and spend the less valuable (bad) one. Classic case — when debased silver coins circulated alongside pure silver coins, pure ones disappeared from daily use.

The rate at which the RBI lends SHORT-TERM funds to commercial banks against government securities is called:

(A) Bank Rate
(B) Repo Rate
(C) Reverse Repo Rate

(B) Repo Rate

cards.front:
CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) refers to:

(A) % of bank's net demand and time liabilities kept as cash reserve with RBI
(B) % of deposits banks lend at repo rate
(C) Minimum ratio of NPA to total loans
(D) Gold holding required by the central bank
cards.back:
(A) % of bank's net demand and time liabilities kept as cash reserve with RBI

Banking & RBI — CRR = cash with RBI (no interest earned). SLR = proportion of NDTL held in safe liquid assets (gold, cash, approved securities) with the bank itself. Both are monetary-policy tools: higher CRR/SLR → less money to lend → tighter liquidity.

cards.front:
The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) in India refers to:

(A) Portion of banks' deposits kept as gold reserves
(B) Percentage of banks' Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) to be held as cash reserves WITH THE RBI
(C) Amount banks can borrow from the RBI overnight
(D) Reserves banks keep in foreign currencies
cards.back:
(B) Percentage of banks' Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) to be held as cash reserves WITH THE RBI

Banking & RBI — CRR = % of bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL = deposits + borrowings less inter-bank liabilities) that it must keep as CASH RESERVES WITH THE RBI — earns NO interest. Currently ~4.5% (since May 2022). Purpose: controls liquidity; raising CRR reduces lending capacity, tightens money supply. SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio, Sec 24 of Banking Regulation Act) = different % kept as LIQUID ASSETS (G-secs, gold, approved securities) — currently ~18%; this earns interest. Banks must maintain BOTH CRR and SLR. Higher CRR/SLR = tighter monetary policy. Repo Rate = interest on short-term borrowing from RBI. Reverse Repo = interest RBI pays on overnight deposits from banks.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a 'quantitative' (general) credit control tool of the RBI?

(A) Margin requirements
(B) Open Market Operations (OMO)
(C) Consumer credit controls
(D) Moral suasion
cards.back:
(B) Open Market Operations (OMO)

Banking & RBI — Credit control tools fall into two categories: QUANTITATIVE (general, affect ALL credit): (1) Bank Rate; (2) Open Market Operations (OMO — RBI buys/sells G-secs to inject/absorb liquidity); (3) CRR; (4) SLR; (5) Repo & Reverse Repo; (6) MSF. QUALITATIVE (selective, target specific sectors): (1) Margin requirements (% down-payment for specific-purpose loans); (2) Moral suasion (informal persuasion — 'please lend more to priority sector'); (3) Consumer credit controls; (4) Direct action (penalties on errant banks); (5) Credit rationing (ceilings on specific sectors); (6) Publicity. OMO is the most MARKET-BASED tool, actively used in the US Fed too.

cards.front:
The RBI's 'Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS)' allows resident individuals to remit abroad up to what annual limit (as of 2024)?

(A) US$ 25,000 per year
(B) US$ 2,50,000 per financial year
(C) US$ 10,00,000 per year
(D) US$ 5,000 per trip only
cards.back:
(B) US$ 2,50,000 per financial year

Banking & RBI — LRS (Liberalised Remittance Scheme, introduced Feb 2004) allows Indian resident individuals to freely remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year (April-March) for any permitted capital or current account transaction — studies abroad, travel, gifts, investments in foreign securities, immovable property, etc. Initial limit was $25,000 (2004) → raised progressively to $250,000 (2015). TCS (Tax Collected at Source) rules apply: 20% TCS on most LRS remittances > ₹7 lakh (effective Oct 2023) — except medical, education. Not available to HUFs/corporates/partnership firms. Can't be used for trading in forex abroad, lottery, margin trading, or sending funds to FATF-flagged countries.

cards.front:
RBI's 'Payments Vision 2025' is built around FIVE anchor goals. Which among the following is NOT one of them?

(A) Integrity
(B) Inclusion
(C) Infrastructure
(D) Innovation
cards.back:
(C) Infrastructure

Banking & RBI — Payments Vision 2025 (released June 2022) articulates RBI's roadmap with FIVE 'I' anchors: (1) INTEGRITY; (2) INCLUSION; (3) INNOVATION; (4) INSTITUTIONALISATION; (5) INTERNATIONALISATION. 'Infrastructure' is NOT one of the five (it is part of the foundation but not a named anchor). Key targets: triple digital payments, raise the number of digital payment transactions from ~100 Cr/day to ~270 Cr/day, roll out UPI internationally, CBDC (e₹ — retail and wholesale pilot from Dec 2022), rupee-denominated global payments (via RTGS linking with other countries). Earlier iterations: Payments Vision 2018, 2021-25 mid-point review.

cards.front:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was established under the RBI Act of:

(A) 1947, the year of Indian independence
(B) 1934, taking over from the Imperial Bank of India
(C) 1955, after nationalisation of major banks

cards.front:
The RBI manages India's foreign-exchange reserves under which Act?

(A) FERA (Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973)
(B) FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999)
(C) PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002)
(D) RBI Act, 1934, as the original parent statute
cards.back:
(B) FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999)

Banking & RBI — FEMA, 1999 — replaced the older FERA (1973). FEMA is regulatory + facilitative; FERA was restrictive (criminal prosecution-based). India holds the 4th-largest FX reserves globally (~$700+ billion as of 2025), comprising foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs, IMF reserve position. RBI's reserve-management goals: liquidity, safety, return (in that order). Reserves provide an import cushion (~10-11 months of imports) and a buffer against currency volatility. PMLA — Enforcement Directorate's key statute, separate domain. RBI Act founded the bank but FX regulation came under FEMA later.
cards.option3: RBI Act, 1934, as the original parent statute

cards.front:
Which entity was carved OUT of the RBI in 1982 to focus on rural credit?

(A) SIDBI, the Small Industries Development Bank of India
(B) NABARD, the apex bank for agriculture and rural sectors
(C) EXIM Bank, the Export-Import Bank of India for trade
(D) NHB, the National Housing Bank for housing finance
cards.back:
(B) NABARD, the apex bank for agriculture and rural sectors

Banking & RBI — NABARD — established 12 July 1982, on the recommendations of the Sivaraman Committee. Took over the Agricultural Credit Department (ACD) and Rural Planning + Credit Cell (RPCC) from RBI. Functions: refinance facility for cooperative banks + RRBs, financial inclusion, supervision of cooperative + regional rural banks (RRBs). HQ Mumbai. Distractor 1 — SIDBI (1990) is for MSMEs. Distractor 3 — EXIM Bank (1982, separately) for export-import credit. Distractor 4 — NHB (1988) for housing finance, also created within RBI's framework.

cards.front:
The RBI is sometimes called the 'BANKER's BANK' because it:

(A) Owns shares in commercial banks across the country
(B) Holds banks' reserves and lends to them as lender of last resort

cards.front:
The RBI's primary objective under the amended RBI Act (post-2016) is to:

(A) Maximise the Government's annual fiscal revenue
(B) Maintain price stability while keeping growth in mind
(C) Direct subsidised credit to all priority sectors
(D) Manage the public debt-to-GDP ratio of the country
cards.back:
(B) Maintain price stability while keeping growth in mind

Banking & RBI — RBI Act amendment (2016) — formalised FLEXIBLE INFLATION TARGETING (FIT). Primary objective: maintain PRICE STABILITY (CPI inflation 4% ± 2%, i.e. 2-6% band) while keeping in mind the OBJECTIVE OF GROWTH. Earlier 'multiple indicators' approach replaced. Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) operationalises this. Distractor 1 — fiscal revenue is the Centre's domain (CBDT, CBIC). Distractor 3 — priority-sector lending is a subsidiary objective. Distractor 4 — debt management is shared with Centre but not the PRIMARY objective.

Which of the following is NOT a function of the Reserve Bank of India?

(A) Issuer of currency notes (except ₹1)
(B) Banker to the Government of India and state governments (most)
(C) Direct lender to industries and individuals
(D) Lender of last resort to commercial banks

Real RBI functions: (1) Issue of currency (notes ≥ ₹2; ₹1 notes + coins issued by Govt of India, but RBI distributes); (2) Banker / debt manager to the Centre + most states (J&K and Sikkim used to be exceptions, now also under RBI); (3) Banker's bank — maintains CRR/SLR with itself, lender of last resort; (4) Custodian of forex reserves; (5) Monetary policy + regulation of banks; (6) Promotional roles (DICGC, NABARD set-up).

The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of RBI, set up by the 2016 amendment to RBI Act, has how many members?

(A) 4 (all RBI)
(B) 6 — 3 from RBI + 3 external (appointed by Govt)
(C) 8
(D) 12
cards.back:

Banking & RBI — MPC — 6 members. From RBI: Governor (chairperson), Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one officer of RBI nominated by Central Board. Mandate: maintain CPI inflation at 4% ±2% (revised by Govt every 5 years). MPC sets the REPO RATE — RBI's main policy rate. Meets at least 6 times a year.

cards.front:
The 'Repo Rate' is the rate at which:

(A) Commercial banks lend to RBI
(B) RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities (sale-and-repurchase)
(C) Banks lend among themselves overnight
(D) RBI buys forex from the market
cards.back:
(B) RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities (sale-and-repurchase)

Banking & RBI — Repo (repurchase agreement) — bank sells G-secs to RBI today and repurchases at a higher price tomorrow; the difference = interest = repo rate. REVERSE repo — opposite direction (RBI borrows from banks). Other RBI rates: MSF (Marginal Standing Facility, repo + 0.25%), Bank Rate (= MSF normally), CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio), SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio). When RBI hikes repo → cost of funds for banks rises → lending rates rise → demand cools → inflation falls (textbook effect).

cards.front:
The 'Cash Reserve Ratio' (CRR) is the minimum fraction of:

(A) A bank's net worth that must be retained as gold
(B) A bank's NDTL (Net Demand and Time Liabilities) that must be kept with RBI in cash, earning no interest
(C) Bank capital lent to government
(D) Money parked in mutual funds
cards.back:

Banking & RBI — CRR — kept as cash with RBI (no interest paid). Stipulated under Section 42 of RBI Act, 1934. Currently 4% (subject to MPC revisions). Distinct from SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio, ~18%) — kept in cash, gold, or government securities WITH THE BANK ITSELF, not with RBI; SLR earns interest. Higher CRR → less money for banks to lend → cools credit growth. CRR was once as high as 15% in early 1990s; gradually reduced as part of liberalisation.

RBI follows the 'Minimum Reserve System' to issue currency. Under this system, the minimum reserve required to be maintained is:

(A) ₹100 crore — of which ₹85 crore in foreign securities, ₹115 crore in gold
(B) ₹200 crore — ₹115 crore in gold + ₹85 crore in foreign securities

cards.front:
The UNION BUDGET is presented every year on:

(A) Last day of February (traditional)
(B) 1 FEBRUARY
(C) 31 March
(D) 15 August
cards.back:
(B) 1 FEBRUARY

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — UNION BUDGET of INDIA ('Annual Financial Statement' per Art 112 of Constitution) — presented by FINANCE MINISTER in LOK SABHA annually. DATE: 1 FEBRUARY (since 2017; before that, last working day of February as inherited from British colonial practice). REASONS FOR SHIFT: (a) earlier presentation → earlier passage → implementation from 1 April; (b) benefits agri + state budgets. RAIL BUDGET — separately presented since 1924 (Acworth Committee); MERGED with Union Budget from 2017 (first merged = Arun Jaitley 2017 budget). CALENDAR: (1) 1 FEB — FM presents budget speech ~2 hours; tabled documents. (2) 2 Feb – next ~10 days — general discussion in both Houses. (3) Feb-Mar (1-month recess) — STANDING COMMITTEES scrutinise DEMANDS FOR GRANTS ministry-wise. (4) 2nd half of March – early April — voting on Demands + passage of APPROPRIATION BILL + FINANCE BILL. (5) FINANCIAL YEAR starts 1 APRIL. BUDGET DOCUMENTS (14+ key ones): (1) Annual Financial Statement (Art 112 — main document). (2) Demands for Grants. (3) Finance Bill (Art 110). (4) Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement (FRBM Act). (5) Medium Term Fiscal Policy Statement. (6) Macroeconomic Framework Statement. (7) Expenditure Budget Vol-I/II. (8) Receipts Budget. (9) Budget at a Glance. (10) Memorandum explaining tax proposals. (11) Output Outcome Framework. (12) Key Features of Budget. cards.front:
The FRBM Act 2003 set targets for FISCAL CONSOLIDATION. It stipulates:

(A) Surplus budget every year
(B) Fiscal deficit target of 3% of GDP (originally 2008-09, missed), revenue deficit target 0%; debt target 40% of GDP for Centre, 20% for states
(C) No deficit allowed
(D) Fiscal deficit 10% of GDP
cards.back:
(B) Fiscal deficit target of 3% of GDP (originally 2008-09, missed), revenue deficit target 0%; debt target 40% of GDP for Centre, 20% for states

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — FRBM ACT (Fiscal Responsibility + Budget Management Act) 2003 — aimed at FISCAL DISCIPLINE + prudent debt management. ENACTED 2003, effective 5 July 2004. Operationalised the 2000 K.P. Geethakrishnan Committee + 2003 Kelkar Task Force. ORIGINAL TARGETS (to be met by 2008-09): (1) FISCAL DEFICIT ≤ 3% of GDP. (2) REVENUE DEFICIT = 0 (balanced revenue account — subsequently dropped; replaced with 'effective revenue deficit' concept). (3) Pre-decided reductions: FD 0.3%/yr, RD 0.5%/yr. (4) No RBI FINANCING (ad hoc treasury bills) of deficit post 2006. TARGETS MISSED: 2008-09 global financial crisis + counter-cyclical spending; 2020-21 COVID. FD was 3.4% in 2018-19; shot up to 9.2% in 2020-21 (COVID); now gradually declining. REVISED TARGETS (N.K. Singh Committee 2017 recommendations adopted in 2018 amendments): (a) FISCAL DEFICIT — 3% by 2020-21 (missed); (b) REVENUE DEFICIT — 2.1% by 2019-20 (missed); (c) GENERAL GOVERNMENT DEBT = 60% of GDP (40% Centre + 20% states) by 2024-25. CURRENT STATUS (FY 2024-25 Budget): FD = 4.9% (Centre); all-India (Centre + States) ~9-10%. GDP-to-debt ratio ~58% (Centre) + ~28% (states) = ~86% total (includes public sector enterprises too). BUDGET 2024-25 (Nirmala Sitharaman): (a) FD target 4.9% for FY25; 4.5% for FY26; (b) Capex push continues; (c) gross borrowings ₹14.01 lakh crore. KEY FISCAL CONCEPTS: (1) FISCAL DEFICIT (FD) = Total Expenditure – Total Revenue Receipts (exc. borrowings). Measures total govt borrowing need. (2) REVENUE DEFICIT (RD) = Revenue Expenditure - Revenue Receipts. Indicates dis-saving. (3) PRIMARY DEFICIT (PD) = FD - Interest payments. Indicates NEW borrowing (minus servicing old debt). (4) EFFECTIVE REVENUE DEFICIT (ERD) — introduced 2011; = RD - Grants for creation of capital assets. (5) GROSS FISCAL DEFICIT (GFD) vs NET (net of net lending). SOURCES OF FD FINANCING: (a) MARKET BORROWING (dated G-Secs via RBI auctions); (b) small savings (NSSF); (c) external borrowings (concessional — World Bank, ADB); (d) draw-down of cash balances. KEY ISSUE: CROWDING-OUT of private investment — govt borrowing increases interest rates + absorbs loanable funds. COUNTER-CYCLICAL fiscal policy OK during recessions (2008, 2020) but must consolidate during growth phases.

cards.front:
The GST (Goods + Services Tax) was rolled out in India on:

(A) 1 April 2016
(B) 1 JULY 2017
(C) 26 January 2018
(D) 15 August 2017
cards.back:
(B) 1 JULY 2017

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — GST (GOODS + SERVICES TAX) — INDIA's BIGGEST INDIRECT TAX REFORM since Independence. ROLLED OUT midnight 30 Jun / 1 JULY 2017 in Parliament's CENTRAL HALL by President Pranab Mukherjee + PM Modi. 'ONE NATION, ONE TAX, ONE MARKET'. 101ST CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT ACT 2016 created legal basis (Art 246A, 269A, 279A — GST Council). PATH: proposed 2000 (Atal Bihari Vajpayee), Empowered Committee (Asim Dasgupta), 115th CAB 2011 lapsed, 122nd CAB 2014 passed in 2016 as 101st CAA. STRUCTURE — 'DUAL GST': (1) CGST (Central GST) — central component; (2) SGST (State GST) — state component; (3) IGST (Integrated GST) — on inter-state supply + imports, collected by Centre, apportioned to destination state; (4) UTGST (Union Territory GST) — for UTs without legislature. PRINCIPLE: DESTINATION-based tax (where consumed, not produced — benefits consuming states). SLABS: (a) 0% — essential goods (fresh food, milk, educational services, healthcare, unbranded atta/dal/rice, sanitary pads since 2018, cereals, natural honey); (b) 5% — mass consumption (packaged food, tea, coffee, sugar, edible oil, medicines, transport); (c) 12% — processed food, butter, ghee, ayurvedic medicines, mobile phones (some); (d) 18% — most services + mid-range goods (toothpaste, hair oil, shoes >₹500, hotel 1000-7500); (e) 28% — luxury + demerit (cars, refrigerators, washing machines, tobacco, aerated drinks, cement); PLUS GST COMPENSATION CESS on tobacco + luxury cars + coal (max 15% cess; 200%+ on cigarettes). SPECIAL RATES: Gold 3%, Rough diamond 0.25%. ABSORBED ~17 indirect taxes: Central Excise Duty, Service Tax, Additional Customs Duty, VAT, Entry Tax, Octroi, Luxury Tax, Entertainment Tax, Purchase Tax, Central Sales Tax, State Surcharges, etc. NOT under GST: Alcohol (states' revenue), Petroleum (petrol, diesel, ATF, crude oil, natural gas — states' revenue), Electricity duty, Stamp duty. THRESHOLD: exempt for businesses with turnover <₹40 lakh (services ₹20 lakh in North-East). COMPOSITION SCHEME — ₹1.5 cr turnover. GST COUNCIL — constitutional body (Art 279A); chaired by Finance Minister; all state FMs + 2 Union Ministers; Centre has 1/3 vote weight, states 2/3 collectively; decisions by 3/4 majority. Meets periodically. GSTN (GST Network) — IT backbone for returns, invoicing, input tax credit. GST MONTHLY COLLECTIONS: crossed ₹1 lakh crore regularly since 2019, ₹2 lakh crore first in April 2024; FY24-25 estimated ₹22-24 lakh crore. GST COMPENSATION to states: Centre compensated for 5 years (2017-2022) for revenue shortfall below 14% growth (Compensation Cess fund). 5-year guarantee ended June 2022 + not extended. Some states (TN, Kerala, WB) demand further support. 'One Nation, One Tax'; 101st Constitutional Amendment 2016; 4 slabs 5%, 12%, 18%, 28%; CGST + SGST + IGST + UTGST components.

cards.front:
India's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth rate in FY 2023-24 was:

(A) ~3%
(B) 8.2%
(C) Over 15%
(D) Negative
cards.back:
(B) 8.2%

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — INDIA's GDP GROWTH — fastest among major economies. RECENT FY FIGURES (real GDP growth): (a) FY 2019-20: 3.9% (pre-COVID slowdown); (b) FY 2020-21: -5.8% (COVID contraction); (c) FY 2021-22: 9.7% (rebound); (d) FY 2022-23: 7.0%; (e) FY 2023-24: 8.2% (second advance estimate; provisional 8.2%); (f) FY 2024-25: 6.5-7% (projection). Nominal GDP FY 2023-24: ₹295 LAKH CRORE (~$3.5 TRILLION). India = 5TH LARGEST ECONOMY by nominal GDP (overtook UK 2022); 3RD LARGEST by PPP (after China + USA). Projected to be 3rd largest nominal by 2028. BASIC GDP CONCEPTS: (1) GDP — total value of all goods + services produced WITHIN country's borders in a year. (2) GNP — GDP + net factor income from abroad (NFIA) = GDP + (income earned by Indians abroad) - (income earned by foreigners in India). For India, GNP typically SLIGHTLY LESS than GDP (more foreign investment in India than Indian investment abroad, generating net factor income outflow). (3) NDP / NNP — subtract DEPRECIATION. (4) NOMINAL vs REAL: (a) Nominal = current-year prices; (b) Real = base-year prices (measures true output growth, excludes inflation). India's base year 2011-12 (pending change to 2020-21). (5) MARKET PRICES vs FACTOR COST: Market price = Factor cost + Indirect taxes - Subsidies. 3 METHODS to calculate GDP: (1) PRODUCTION / VALUE ADDED — sum of GVA across sectors (agri + industry + services). (2) INCOME — wages + rent + interest + profits. (3) EXPENDITURE — C + I + G + (X - M). In INDIA, MAIN method is Production method; from Jan 2015, new series with GVA at basic prices central metric. SECTORAL CONTRIBUTION to GVA (FY24): AGRICULTURE 17% (but 46% workforce — low productivity), INDUSTRY 27% (Manufacturing 14% — LOW by Asian standards; Make in India aims 25%), SERVICES 56% (IT + finance + tourism + retail). INDIA UNIQUE — service-led growth bypassing manufacturing-intensive phase (contrast with China, Vietnam). PER CAPITA INCOME (FY24): ~$2,700 = ₹2.30 lakh/year. Still relatively LOW (WORLD avg $12,000; USA $80,000). India's GDP per capita PPP ~$10,000. CENTRAL STATISTICS OFFICE (CSO) / NSO — under Ministry of Statistics + Programme Implementation (MoSPI) — releases GDP data. National Accounts Statistics (NAS) annual publication. Quarterly GDP data released 2 months after quarter end. POVERTY: ~10% multidimensional poor (NITI Aayog MPI 2023, from 29% in 2013-14); 13.5 CRORE people lifted from MPI 2015-16 to 2019-21. making India the FASTEST-growing major economy; real GDP growth consistently 6-8% over 2013-2025 except COVID dip; provisional estimate.
