cards.front:
In a PROGRESSIVE income tax system (like India's), the tax RATE:

(A) Decreases as income rises
(B) INCREASES as income rises
(C) Stays constant
(D) Is uniform flat tax
cards.back:
(B) INCREASES as income rises

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — PROGRESSIVE TAX SYSTEM — tax rate INCREASES as taxable income rises. Principle: those with GREATER ABILITY TO PAY bear HIGHER proportional tax burden. Higher tax brackets on richer earners. INDIA's INCOME TAX system is PROGRESSIVE. TYPES of TAXATION: (1) PROGRESSIVE — most income tax (India, USA, UK, most countries); social equity favoured. (2) REGRESSIVE — rate DECREASES with higher income (e.g., sales tax + GST hurts poor more as share of income); demerit taxes (on tobacco, fuel) fall harder on poor proportionally. (3) PROPORTIONAL / FLAT — uniform rate regardless of income (e.g., 20% on everyone); simpler but less equitable. INDIA INCOME TAX REGIMES (AY 2024-25): NEW TAX REGIME (default from FY 2023-24, simplified, fewer deductions): (a) ₹0-3 LAKH: NIL; (b) ₹3-7 LAKH: 5%; (c) ₹7-10 LAKH: 10%; (d) ₹10-12 LAKH: 15%; (e) ₹12-15 LAKH: 20%; (f) >₹15 LAKH: 30%. STANDARD DEDUCTION: ₹75,000. Total REBATE u/s 87A: up to ₹25,000 (so effective NIL tax up to ₹7 LAKH income). PLUS 4% Health + Education Cess. SURCHARGE on HNI: 10% (>₹50L), 15% (>₹1 Cr), 25% (>₹2 Cr), 37% (>₹5 Cr) — max marginal rate ~42.7% under old regime; REDUCED to 25% maximum surcharge under new regime (max marginal ~39%). OLD TAX REGIME (optional; more deductions — 80C ₹1.5 L, 80D medical, HRA, LTA, home loan interest ₹2L u/s 24b, NPS 80CCD, etc.): (a) ₹0-2.5 L NIL; (b) ₹2.5-5 L 5%; (c) ₹5-10 L 20%; (d) >₹10 L 30%. TAX on INDIVIDUALS + HUFs + firms + corporates. CORPORATE TAX: (a) Domestic companies — 22% (new regime, no deductions) + 4% cess = ~25% effective; 25% (regime 1 with deductions); 15% for new manufacturing companies. (b) Foreign companies — 40% + surcharge + cess. TYPES OF TAXES IN INDIA: (1) DIRECT (Individual / Corp / Wealth / Gift / Securities Transaction Tax) — paid directly; progressive; IMPOSED by CENTRE (incl income tax), administered by CBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes). (2) INDIRECT (GST, Customs, Excise on alcohol/petroleum, Stamp Duty) — consumer ultimately pays via price; often regressive. CBIC (CBEC renamed 2018) = Central Board of Indirect Taxes + Customs. DIRECT TAX CODE (DTC) — proposed comprehensive overhaul; pending. TDS (Tax Deducted at Source) + TCS (Tax Collected at Source) — collection mechanisms. ITR (Income Tax Return) FILING due 31 July (individuals), 31 Oct (companies). STATS: ~7.5 CRORE ITRs filed FY24; tax-to-GDP ratio ~12% (low; OECD avg 34%). DIRECT tax share has been growing; ~55% of Central tax revenue now direct. higher income → higher marginal tax rate; pro-redistribution; based on 'ability to pay' principle.

DIRECT tax share has been growing; ~55% of Central tax revenue now direct. higher income → higher marginal tax rate; pro-redistribution; based on 'ability to pay' principle.

cards.front:
The 15th FINANCE COMMISSION (Chair: N.K. Singh) recommended the SHARE of NET CENTRAL TAXES devolved to STATES (2020-2026) at:

(A) 35%
(B) 41% (down from 14th FC's 42%, to accommodate J&K UT out of state pool); states' collective share of divisible pool
(C) 50%
(D) 30%
cards.back:
(B) 41% (down from 14th FC's 42%, to accommodate J&K UT out of state pool); states' collective share of divisible pool

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — FINANCE COMMISSION (FC) — constitutional body under Article 280, constituted by PRESIDENT every 5 years (or earlier); recommends DEVOLUTION of resources + transfers between Centre + States. COMPOSITION: 1 Chairman + 4 members (qualifications specified). FUNCTIONS: (1) Distribution of NET PROCEEDS of taxes between Centre + States (vertical devolution). (2) Distribution among states (horizontal — based on formula). (3) Principles governing GRANTS-IN-AID to states (Art 275). (4) Measures to augment state consolidated funds for local bodies (panchayats + municipalities) since 73rd + 74th CAAs. (5) Any other matter in interests of sound finance. FCs SO FAR: (1) 1st FC (K.C. Neogy, 1952): states got 10%. (2) 10th FC (KC Pant, 1995-2000): started sharing all taxes (80th CAA 2000 after recommendations). (3) 13th FC (Vijay Kelkar, 2010-15): 32% devolution. (4) 14th FC (Y.V. Reddy, 2015-2020): 42% devolution (BIGGEST JUMP — 10 percentage points); major shift towards state autonomy. (5) 15th FC (N.K. SINGH, 2020-21 + 2021-26): recommended 41% devolution for 2020-26 (reduced by 1% to accommodate J&K becoming a Union Territory, which reduced state pool). Also HORIZONTAL formula. (6) 16th FC (ARVIND PANAGARIYA, appointed Dec 2023) — constituted for 2026-31 period; will submit 2025. 15TH FC's HORIZONTAL DEVOLUTION FORMULA (among states): (a) INCOME DISTANCE 45% — per capita income gap from highest-income state (Haryana) — REWARDS POORER states (equity); (b) POPULATION (2011 census) 15% — used 2011 census (earlier FCs used 1971 census for population — controversial as South with good family planning felt penalised; FC-15 switched to 2011 — controversial for South too); (c) AREA 15%; (d) FOREST + ECOLOGY 10%; (e) DEMOGRAPHIC PERFORMANCE 12.5% (penalises high fertility); (f) TAX EFFORT 2.5%. TOP BENEFICIARIES (highest share): UP (17.94%), Bihar (10.06%), MP (7.85%), West Bengal (7.52%), Maharashtra (6.32%). LEAST: Goa (0.39%), Sikkim (0.39%), Mizoram (0.50%). CRITIQUE: SOUTH STATES (Kerala, Karnataka, TN, AP, Telangana) feel penalised despite better governance + fiscal discipline + lower fertility — lost share under 15th FC despite good record. Inter-State Council + NITI Aayog also forums for cooperative federalism. 15th FC also recommended: (1) revenue deficit grants to 17 states; (2) grants for health (₹1.06 lakh cr); (3) grants for local bodies (₹4.36 lakh cr for rural + urban); (4) performance-based incentives; (5) disaster management grants. 16TH FC under Panagariya is studying above issues + GST reform + GST Council integration + state-specific concerns + Southern states' demand.

cards.front:
INFLATION, measured by the CONSUMER PRICE INDEX (CPI), is BASED on:

(A) Just food prices
(B) A BASKET of goods + services consumed by typical household
(C) Wholesale prices only
(D) Export prices
cards.back:
(B) A BASKET of goods + services consumed by typical household

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — INFLATION — general, sustained rise in prices of goods + services in an economy; reduces purchasing power of money. Opposite: DEFLATION (falling prices). INFLATION INDICES in INDIA: (1) CPI (Consumer Price Index) — reflects RETAIL prices; most relevant for consumers. INDIA uses CPI-Combined (urban + rural, 2012 base), published by NSO (National Statistical Office). WEIGHTS: FOOD + BEVERAGES 45.86%, miscellaneous 28.32%, housing 10.07%, fuel + light 6.84%, clothing + footwear 6.53%, pan/tobacco 2.38%. Since 2016 — RBI has STATUTORY inflation target of 4% ± 2% (i.e., 2-6% band) — FLEXIBLE INFLATION TARGETING; failure to stay in band for 3 consecutive quarters requires report to Centre. (2) WPI (Wholesale Price Index) — wholesale prices of goods (no services); OFFICE of ECONOMIC ADVISER, DPIIT; 2011-12 base, 697 items. WEIGHTS: manufactured products 64.2%, primary articles 22.6%, fuel + power 13.15%. WPI tends to be more VOLATILE than CPI (dominated by commodity prices); used for indexation of govt payments. (3) CPI-IW (Industrial Workers) — labour ministry; used for DA (Dearness Allowance) calculation for central govt employees. (4) CPI-AL (Agricultural Labourers), CPI-RL (Rural Labourers). INFLATION TYPES: (1) DEMAND-PULL — 'too much money chasing too few goods'; aggregate demand > supply; e.g., consumer boom, govt spending boost. (2) COST-PUSH — rising input costs (oil, raw materials, wages) pushed to consumer prices; e.g., oil price shocks 1973, Russia-Ukraine 2022. (3) STRUCTURAL — long-run supply bottlenecks (agri rigidities, infrastructure). (4) IMPORTED inflation — rupee depreciation → costlier imports → inflation. (5) HEADLINE vs CORE: Headline = overall CPI; Core = CPI excluding volatile food + fuel. CAUSES + REMEDIES: (a) Monetary — RBI raises repo rate to tame inflation; (b) Fiscal — cut government spending, raise taxes; (c) Supply side — boost production, reduce bottlenecks; (d) Trade — reduce import duties on inflation-sensitive items. MODERATE inflation (4-6%) considered HEALTHY — signals growing economy, gives small margin for adjustment. HYPER-inflation (>50%/month) = Zimbabwe 2008, Weimar Germany 1923, Venezuela 2018-22, Yugoslavia 1994 — catastrophic. STAGFLATION — stagnation + inflation together (1970s US + UK, 2022 worries). DISINFLATION — slowing inflation rate (still positive). DEFLATION — negative inflation (Japan 1990s-2010s). INDIA's CPI inflation: 6.7% (FY22-23), 5.4% (FY23-24, provisional), 4.5% (FY24-25 projection) — on downward path. FOOD PRICES are VOLATILE + key driver (tomato + onion spikes of 2023). MSP + buffer stocks + PDS moderate food inflation. India base 2012 with food 45.86% weight; RBI targets 4% ± 2%.

cards.front:
The INDIAN FIVE-YEAR PLANS ended with the 12th Plan (2012-17). They have been replaced by:

(A) Quarterly plans by RBI
(B) NITI Aayog's 3-YEAR ACTION AGENDAS / 7-year strategy / 15-year vision document + annual budgets; Planning Commission scrapped Jan 2015
(C) US-style fiscal-year plans
(D) No plans at all
cards.back:
(B) NITI Aayog's 3-YEAR ACTION AGENDAS / 7-year strategy / 15-year vision document + annual budgets; Planning Commission scrapped Jan 2015

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — INDIA'S PLANNING EVOLUTION: PLANNING COMMISSION (1950-2014) — set up by Nehru Cabinet resolution 15 March 1950; chaired by PM; produced 12 FIVE-YEAR PLANS. SCRAPPED 1 January 2015 by Modi govt; REPLACED by NITI AAYOG (National Institution for Transforming India). REASONS for SCRAPPING: (1) Outdated Soviet-style top-down planning; (2) weakening of states' autonomy; (3) inefficient bureaucracy; (4) poor coordination. NITI AAYOG — created by Cabinet resolution 1 Jan 2015. STRUCTURE: (1) Chairperson — PM; (2) VICE-CHAIRMAN (currently Suman K. Bery, 2022-); (3) CEO (B.V.R. Subrahmanyam, IAS, 2023-); (4) Governing Council = all state CMs + UT LGs + PM; (5) Regional Councils; (6) Full-time members + ex-officio members + special invitees. FUNCTIONS: (1) 'THINK-TANK' — research + policy analysis; (2) Cooperative + COMPETITIVE FEDERALISM; (3) facilitates states + Centre cooperation. NO allocatory power over centrally sponsored schemes (transferred to Finance Ministry). (4) Strategic + long-term direction. KEY DOCUMENTS by NITI Aayog: (1) '3-YEAR ACTION AGENDA' (2017-20). (2) '7-YEAR STRATEGY FOR NEW INDIA @ 75' — vision for 2022. (3) '15-YEAR VISION DOCUMENT' (long-term). (4) 'SDG INDIA INDEX' annual — state-wise performance on Sustainable Development Goals. (5) 'NATIONAL HEALTH INDEX' annual. (6) 'COMPOSITE WATER MANAGEMENT INDEX'. (7) 'ASPIRATIONAL DISTRICTS PROGRAMME' (115 districts, 2018; ~500+ blocks in 2023 expansion). (8) 'EXPORT PREPAREDNESS INDEX'. (9) 'ATAL INNOVATION MISSION' (Atal Tinkering Labs, incubators). (10) 'Multidimensional Poverty Index'. (11) 'AIM-Start-up India' linkage. PAST 5-YEAR PLANS (summary): (a) 1st (1951-56) — Mahalanobis-Harrod-Domar; agri + irrigation focus. Growth 3.6%. (b) 2nd (1956-61) — Mahalanobis model; heavy industry + PSUs (steel plants — Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur). Growth 4.1%. (c) 3rd (1961-66) — self-sustaining growth; failed due to Indo-China war, droughts. Growth 2.4%. Three ANNUAL PLANS (1966-69) 'plan holidays'. (d) 4th (1969-74) — Indira's 'Garibi Hatao'; Bank nationalisation; Green Revolution. Growth 3.3%. (e) 5th (1974-79) — Emergency era; truncated. (f) 6th (1980-85) — IRDP; MMGs. (g) 7th (1985-90) — productivity. (h) 8th (1992-97) — LPG reforms continued; Manmohan; growth 6.8%. (i) 9th (1997-2002) — infra. (j) 10th (2002-07) — Vajpayee; growth 7.8%. (k) 11th (2007-12) — UPA-II; growth 8.1%; inclusive. (l) 12TH PLAN (2012-17) — last. Growth 6.9% avg. Since 2015: ANNUAL BUDGETS + periodic strategy documents replace 5YP structure.

cards.front:
India's Foreign Exchange Reserves (FOREX), a major economic indicator, are maintained by:

(A) Finance Ministry directly
(B) RBI
(C) State Bank of India
(D) SEBI
cards.back:
(B) RBI

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — FOREX RESERVES (Foreign Exchange Reserves) — foreign currency holdings of central bank + government. INDIA's RBI manages them. CURRENT LEVEL (2024-25): ~$700 BILLION (record high; was $100 B in 2003, $300 B in 2015, $600 B in 2021). INDIA = 4TH LARGEST forex holder globally (after CHINA $3.3 T, JAPAN $1.3 T, SWITZERLAND ~$900 B; USA ~$250 B — low since USD is reserve currency). COMPONENTS of INDIA's forex reserves: (1) FOREIGN CURRENCY ASSETS (FCA) — ~$610 B; mostly USD (~60%), EUR, GBP, JPY, CAD, AUD. Held in US Treasury securities, AAA bonds, deposits with central banks + BIS. (2) GOLD — ~$60 B; 820+ TONNES (RBI holds 30%+ abroad — BoE Vaults London, BIS). (3) SDRs (Special Drawing Rights) — ~$18 B; IMF reserve asset, basket of 5 currencies. (4) RESERVE POSITION in IMF — ~$5 B. FORMULA: forex reserves should cover MINIMUM 3-6 MONTHS of imports (India's 2024 imports ~$720B → ~10 months of reserves = STRONG cushion). IMPORTANCE: (1) manage EXCHANGE RATE (RBI intervenes by buying/selling USD to prevent sharp rupee swings); (2) meet IMPORT needs (especially oil, gold); (3) SERVICE EXTERNAL DEBT; (4) investor CONFIDENCE signal; (5) meet contingencies (COVID, war, crisis); (6) prevent currency crises. HISTORIC CRISIS: 1991 BoP CRISIS — forex reserves fell to ~$1 BILLION (only 2 WEEKS of imports); India had to PLEDGE 47 TONNES OF GOLD to Bank of England + Union Bank of Switzerland in May-July 1991 to raise $400M for imports; PM Chandra Shekhar, FM Yashwant Sinha; triggered LPG REFORMS under Narasimha Rao + Manmohan Singh from July 1991. EXCHANGE RATE REGIMES: (1) FIXED — currency pegged to another (like Hong Kong Dollar to USD). (2) FLOATING — market-determined (US, UK, EU). (3) MANAGED FLOAT — India's system; market-determined but RBI intervenes to curb excess volatility. INR has been managed float since 1993. RUPEE HISTORY: 1947 — ₹1 = $1 (parity with USD); 1966 — ₹4.76/$ (devaluation); 1991 — ₹17.50 → 24.50 (devaluation); 2013 — ₹60; 2022-23 — ₹83; 2024 — ₹83-85. Rupee has depreciated ~35% since 2013 vs USD. CAPITAL ACCOUNT: India has PARTIAL capital account convertibility (Tarapore Committee 1997, 2006 roadmaps). Current account fully convertible since 1994 (LERMS abolished). FDI routes: automatic + government approval. FCRA (Foreign Contribution Regulation Act) for NGO forex receipts. FEMA 1999 replaced FERA 1973. BoP (Balance of Payments) = Current Account (trade + services + transfers) + Capital Account (FDI + FII + ECBs + banking). India typically runs CAD (Current Account Deficit) ~1-2% of GDP + capital surplus. hold reserves to stabilise Rupee + meet imports + investor confidence; INDIA has 4TH LARGEST reserves globally (~$650-700 B); Reserve Bank of India.

cards.front:
MUDRA scheme for small business financing was launched in 2015. What does MUDRA stand for?

(A) Micro Units Development + Refinance Agency
(B) Mutual Development + Reorganisation Agency
(C) Ministry of Urban Development + Rural Affairs
(D) Money Unit Deposit + Regulation Agency
cards.back:
(A) Micro Units Development + Refinance Agency

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — MUDRA — MICRO UNITS DEVELOPMENT + REFINANCE AGENCY. PMMY (PRADHAN MANTRI MUDRA YOJANA) LAUNCHED 8 APRIL 2015 by PM Modi. OBJECTIVE: 'FUND the UNFUNDED' — provide LOANS up to ₹10 LAKH to NON-CORPORATE, NON-FARM SMALL/MICRO ENTERPRISES without COLLATERAL. LOAN CATEGORIES: (1) SHISHU — up to ₹50,000 (small starters — street vendors, kirana shops, tailors, beauty parlours); (2) KISHOR — ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh (established small businesses); (3) TARUN — ₹5 lakh to ₹10 LAKH (expanding businesses). (4) TARUN PLUS — ₹10-20 LAKH added in Budget 2024-25 for existing Tarun beneficiaries who repaid previous loans. LENDERS: scheduled COMMERCIAL BANKS, REGIONAL RURAL BANKS, SMALL FINANCE BANKS, MFIs (Microfinance Institutions), NBFCs, Cooperative Banks. MUDRA itself REFINANCES these lenders. OWNERSHIP: MUDRA is a subsidiary of SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India, est. 1990, HQ Lucknow). PROGRESS (as of 2024): ~45 CRORE PMMY loans disbursed; ₹26+ lakh crore sanctioned. ~67% to women beneficiaries. ~50% to SC/ST/OBC. ~75% loans <₹50,000 (Shishu segment). BROAD IMPACT on informal sector. ELIGIBLE ACTIVITIES: Manufacturing, Trading, Service Sector, Agri (allied — dairy, poultry, fishery, bee-keeping). NOT for crop loans. INTEREST: varies by lender (not prescribed); typically 8-12% p.a. Collateral NOT required. Mudra Card = debit-card-like working-capital credit. OTHER SIMILAR SCHEMES: (1) STAND-UP INDIA (5 April 2016) — ₹10 lakh-1 CRORE loans for SC/ST + WOMEN entrepreneurs per bank branch. Over 2.5 lakh sanctioned. cards.front:
REVENUE EXPENDITURE includes:

(B) Salaries, subsidies, interest payments (recurring)
(C) Buying machinery for new factories here
(D) Investment in PSU equity here also too
cards.back:
(B) Salaries, subsidies, interest payments (recurring)

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — TWO TYPES of govt expenditure: (1) REVENUE expenditure — RECURRING, doesn't create assets; e.g., salaries of civil servants, defence personnel; subsidies (food, fertilizer, fuel); interest on past borrowings; pensions; grants to states (most are revenue); maintenance costs. (2) CAPITAL expenditure — creates assets / reduces liabilities; e.g., infrastructure (highways, railways, bridges, ports); buying machinery; loans to states; investments in PSU equity (shares); repayment of loans. INSIGHT: high revenue exp (esp. interest + subsidies) eats into capital exp room → less infrastructure investment. India's ratio: revenue ~80% + capital ~20% (govt aims to raise capex share — recent budgets have done so). REVENUE DEFICIT = Rev. Exp − Rev. Receipts (= 'living beyond means' — usually bad).

cards.front:
PRIMARY DEFICIT is computed as:

(A) Total expenditure minus total receipts
(B) Fiscal deficit minus interest payments
(C) Revenue expenditure minus receipts
(D) Capital deficit minus revenue gain
cards.back:
(B) Fiscal deficit minus interest payments

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — FOUR DEFICIT MEASURES (each tells different story): (1) FISCAL DEFICIT (FD) = Total Exp − Total Receipts excluding borrowings. (2) REVENUE DEFICIT (RD) = Rev Exp − Rev Receipts. (3) PRIMARY DEFICIT (PD) = FD − INTEREST PAYMENTS — shows the shortfall WITHOUT past-debt servicing burden; clean measure of CURRENT fiscal position. (4) EFFECTIVE REVENUE DEFICIT (ERD) = RD − grants for capital creation (introduced 2011-12). PRIMARY DEFICIT close to ZERO = govt's current spending matches current revenue (only borrowing for interest). NEGATIVE PD = primary surplus (revenue > non-interest spending) — desirable in long run for debt sustainability. India's PD has fluctuated; has worsened post-pandemic.

cards.front:
Indian financial year (FY) runs from:

(A) 1 January to 31 December (calendar year)
(B) 1 April to 31 March (existing convention)
(C) 1 July to 30 June (some countries follow)
(D) 1 October to 30 September (US-style)
cards.back:
(B) 1 April to 31 March (existing convention)

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — India FY = 1 APRIL to 31 MARCH. Inherited from BRITISH COLONIAL convention (1867); aligns roughly with rabi crop harvest. Different countries: USA Oct 1-Sep 30 (federal); JAPAN + UK April 1-Mar 31 (same as India); GERMANY + most EU + CHINA + CALENDAR YEAR (Jan-Dec). DEBATE: should India shift to calendar year? Considered occasionally (Shankar Acharya Committee, 2017) — but inertia + rabi alignment + transitional cost have kept status quo. UNION BUDGET — earlier presented LAST WORKING DAY OF FEBRUARY at 5 PM (British colonial timing); from 2017 shifted to 1 February at 11 AM (allows Parliament to pass before April 1 start). Railway budget (separate since 1924) merged with Union Budget from 2017.

Which fund's withdrawals require VOTING by Parliament?

(A) Public Account (PF, deposits etc.)
(B) Consolidated Fund of India
(C) Contingency Fund (President's hand)
(D) Personal accounts of ministers
cards.back:
(B) Consolidated Fund of India

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — THREE GOVT FUNDS (Articles 266, 267): (1) CONSOLIDATED FUND OF INDIA (CFI) — main fund; ALL receipts (taxes, borrowings, loans recovered) go in; ALL spending out NEEDS PARLIAMENT'S APPROVAL via APPROPRIATION + FINANCE Bills. EXCEPTIONS — 'CHARGED' expenditure (NOT voted but discussed): salary of Pres, VP, Speaker, judges, CAG, PSC chairmen; debt charges; emoluments of SC judges; pensions; sums needed to satisfy court judgements/arbitration awards. Also includes the Constitution's protected items. (2) CONTINGENCY FUND (Art 267) — President's discretion for unforeseen expenses; ~₹30,000 crore corpus (raised from ₹500 cr in 2021); replenished from CFI later by Parliament. (3) PUBLIC ACCOUNT (Art 266(2)) — money received in trust (PF, post office savings, judicial deposits, etc.) — withdrawals don't need Parliament approval.

When the Lok Sabha passes the Budget but new fiscal year is starting, an interim measure called VOTE ON ACCOUNT allows govt to:

(B) Spend up to 1/6 of estimates for 2 months till budget passes

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — VOTE ON ACCOUNT — provision (Article 116) for govt to draw from CFI to MEET ESSENTIAL EXPENSES (salaries, ongoing programmes) for 2-3 months while full budget is being debated + passed. Used in Feb 2024 by Modi-1 govt (since LS election in April-May 2024). Interim budget conventionally avoids major policy changes. After elections, Modi-2 presented full budget in July 2024.

cards.front:
The base corporate tax rate for domestic companies (NOT opting for 22% concessional regime, turnover > ₹400 cr) plus surcharge and cess is approximately:

(A) 15% (the new manufacturing rate)
(B) 30% base, with 22% concessional rate available under Section 115BAA (no exemptions)
(C) 40% (foreign companies only)
(D) 50%
cards.back:
(B) 30% base, with 22% concessional rate available under Section 115BAA (no exemptions)

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Domestic companies (turnover > ₹400 cr previous year): 30% base + cess + surcharge ≈ 34.94% effective. Companies opting for 115BAA (introduced Sep 2019): 22% + 10% surcharge + 4% cess = 25.17% effective, but they must forgo most exemptions and deductions. New manufacturing companies (incorporated after 1-Oct-2019, started mfg by 31-Mar-2024) under 115BAB: 15%+10%+4% = 17.16%. Smaller domestic companies (turnover ≤ ₹400 cr in PY 2022-23): 25% base. Foreign companies: 35% base (post Budget 2024, reduced from 40%) + surcharge + cess.

cards.front:
DTAA (Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement) is a bilateral treaty that:

(A) Doubles the tax rate for dual-resident individuals
(B) Prevents the same income from being taxed twice (in source country and residence country) and helps allocate taxing rights
(C) Allows tax evasion legally
(D) Imposes uniform tax rates worldwide
cards.back:
(B) Prevents the same income from being taxed twice (in source country and residence country) and helps allocate taxing rights

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — DTAA — bilateral; India has DTAAs with 90+ countries. Methods: (1) Exemption — income taxed only in one country; (2) Credit — both tax, but resident country gives credit for foreign tax paid. Mauritius DTAA was historically misused for round-tripping; renegotiated via Protocol 2016 (capital gains taxable in source country from 1-Apr-2017). India follows the OECD-modelled UN Model. GAAR (General Anti-Avoidance Rules) — overrides treaty if tax-avoidance is the main purpose. Section 90 of the Income Tax Act empowers the Government to enter into DTAAs.

(A) Higher slab rates and most deductions allowed
(B) Lower slab rates BUT most deductions/exemptions (80C, HRA, LTA, etc.) NOT allowed; standard deduction allowed
(C) Same as old regime
(D) Applicable only to corporates

cards.front:
The Finance Commission of India is a constitutional body established under:

(A) Article 275
(B) Article 280
(C) Article 356
(D) Article 148
cards.back:
(B) Article 280

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Article 280 — the President shall, within two years of the commencement of the Constitution and thereafter at the expiration of every fifth year (or earlier as required), constitute a Finance Commission. Chairman + 4 other members, appointed by the President. Its job: recommend distribution of net tax proceeds between Centre and States (vertical) and among States (horizontal). First FC in 1951 under K.C. Neogy.

The 15th Finance Commission recommended that States' share in the net divisible pool of Central taxes be:

(A) 32%
(B) 41%
(C) 42%

(A) Income distance
(B) Demographic performance
(C) Forest cover

cards.front:
Under the Constitution, a Finance Commission's recommendations are:

(A) Binding on the Union Government
(B) Recommendatory (advisory) in nature
(C) Subject to approval by the Supreme Court
(D) Binding only on State governments

Grants-in-aid to States under Article 275 and devolution under Article 270 are the two main channels.

cards.front:
The difference between the Finance Commission and the GST Council is that:

(A) FC recommends; GST Council's decisions are binding after notification
(B) Both are purely advisory
(C) Both are binding on Centre and States
(D) FC is statutory; GST Council is constitutional
cards.back:

GST Council (Art 279A, 101st Amendment, 2017) — constitutional and 'recommendatory' on paper, but Supreme Court in Union of India v. cards.front:
FISCAL POLICY refers to government use of:

(A) Interest rates set by the central bank
(B) Taxation + expenditure to influence economy
(C) Foreign exchange reserves only as tool
(D) Currency devaluation as the chief policy
cards.back:
(B) Taxation + expenditure to influence economy

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — FISCAL policy = Government's use of TAXATION + SPENDING to influence economy. Set by Finance Ministry / Govt. Tools: tax rates, subsidy, public spending, borrowing. EXPANSIONARY (boost growth): cut taxes, raise spending → stimulates demand, but raises deficit. CONTRACTIONARY (curb inflation): raise taxes, cut spending. Distractor 1 = MONETARY policy (RBI). Distractor 4 = exchange rate policy. Both fiscal + monetary policies are macroeconomic levers; ideally coordinated.

cards.front:
FISCAL DEFICIT (FD) is defined as:

(A) Revenue receipts minus revenue expenditure (revenue gap)
(B) Total expenditure minus total receipts (excluding borrowing)
(C) Capital receipts minus capital expenditure (capital gap)
(D) Tax revenue minus subsidy spending of govt budget
cards.back:
(B) Total expenditure minus total receipts (excluding borrowing)

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — FISCAL DEFICIT = Total Expenditure − Total Receipts (EXCLUDING BORROWINGS). i.e., the GAP that government fills by borrowing. India's FD target (FRBM) was 3% of GDP; suspended during pandemic; FY24 ~5.6%, glide path to 4.5% by FY26. Other deficits: REVENUE DEFICIT = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts (= 'living beyond means'); PRIMARY DEFICIT = FD − interest payments (true gap excluding past-debt servicing); EFFECTIVE REVENUE DEFICIT = RD − grants for capital creation. FD financed by: market borrowing (G-secs), small savings, foreign loans, RBI ways-and-means.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a DIRECT TAX in India?

(A) GST on goods + services bought
(B) Income tax (paid directly by taxpayer)
(C) Customs duty on imports + exports
(D) Excise duty on alcohol or fuel
cards.back:
(B) Income tax (paid directly by taxpayer)

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — DIRECT TAX = paid DIRECTLY by the person on whom it's levied; cannot be shifted. Examples: INCOME TAX (individuals + companies), CORPORATE TAX, CAPITAL GAINS TAX. Govt body: CBDT (Central Board of Direct Taxes). INDIRECT TAX = levied on goods/services; can be shifted to consumers (built into price). Examples: GST (replaced excise, service tax, VAT, etc., from July 2017), CUSTOMS DUTY (on imports — and few exports), STAMP DUTY (state-level). Govt body: CBIC (Central Board of Indirect Taxes + Customs). Indian taxes: ~50% direct + ~50% indirect (varies year to year).
cards.option3: Excise duty on alcohol or fuel

cards.front:
FRBM Act (Fiscal Responsibility + Budget Management Act, 2003) was enacted to:

(A) Increase government borrowing limits in budget
(B) Reduce + control fiscal deficit progressively
(C) Increase tax rates substantially every year
(D) Privatize all public sector banks (PSBs)
cards.back:
(B) Reduce + control fiscal deficit progressively

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — FRBM ACT, 2003 — enacted to bring fiscal discipline. Targets: (1) eliminate revenue deficit by FY09 (postponed); (2) reduce fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP. RBI ways-and-means lending to govt phased out by 2006. RBI cannot subscribe to PRIMARY auction of govt bonds (must buy in secondary market). Original targets often missed + RELAXED. Pandemic 2020 → suspended. Current glide path: FD to 4.5% of GDP by FY26 (FY24 actual ~5.6%). Critics argue FRBM is too rigid; defenders say discipline avoids crowding out + fiscal crisis. NK SINGH committee (2017) recommended 'debt rule' framework (debt-to-GDP target).

REVENUE RECEIPTS of the central government primarily come from:

(A) Sale of public sector enterprises in budget
(B) Tax revenue + non-tax revenue (interest etc.)
(C) Borrowing from Reserve Bank of India only
(D) Foreign aid + grants from foreign countries

cards.front:
The annual UNION BUDGET in India is presented by:

(A) Prime Minister of India in Parliament
(B) Finance Minister of Govt of India
(C) RBI Governor from the Mumbai office

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — UNION BUDGET = Annual Financial Statement (Article 112). Presented by FINANCE MINISTER in Lok Sabha, traditionally on the LAST WORKING DAY OF FEBRUARY at 5 PM, but from FY18 shifted to 1 FEBRUARY at 11 AM (allows Parliament to pass before April 1 fiscal year start). RAILWAY BUDGET (separate since 1924) merged with UNION BUDGET from 2017. Indira GANDHI (1969) — only PM to present budget (held FM portfolio briefly). MORARJI DESAI presented MOST budgets (10). NIRMALA SITHARAMAN (since 2019) — first full-time woman FM (Indira had been acting FM); has presented 6 budgets (FY 20-25). Special: 'KAR LAGE BAHI' (a tradition the PM once thanked her for, ditched in 2019).

(A) 18%

cards.front:
In the Union Budget, the 'Finance Bill' primarily deals with:

(A) Borrowing authority of the Union
(B) Imposition, abolition or change in taxes
(C) Allocation of funds to ministries
(D) Appointment of financial officers
cards.back:
(B) Imposition, abolition or change in taxes

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — The Finance Bill (Art 110 read with 117) gives effect to the Government's taxation proposals. It is introduced alongside the Budget; must be passed before the end of the relevant financial year. Allocation of funds happens through the Appropriation Bill (Art 114). cards.front:
The Laffer curve illustrates the relationship between tax rate and:

(A) Inflation rate
(B) Tax revenue collected
(C) Unemployment rate
(D) Exchange rate
cards.back:
(B) Tax revenue collected

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Laffer curve (Arthur Laffer, 1970s) — an inverted-U showing that tax revenue first rises, then falls as the tax rate increases past an optimum. At 0 % and at 100 %, revenue is zero (no tax; no incentive to work). The curve is invoked to argue for tax cuts when rates are above the optimum. The actual 'optimum' point is disputed and varies by economy and period.

cards.front:
Under India's direct tax code, the slab rates for individual income tax have historically been set by the:

(A) Reserve Bank of India
(B) Finance Act passed each year by Parliament
(C) Supreme Court
(D) Central Board of Direct Taxes alone
cards.back:
(B) Finance Act passed each year by Parliament

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Income-tax slab rates are not in the Income Tax Act 1961 itself — they are fixed each year through the Finance Act (after Parliament passes the Finance Bill). This is why 'Budget Day' every February-March is when new slabs take effect from the coming April 1. CBDT administers the law (framing rules, procedure), but cannot set the slab rates on its own.

cards.front:
An 'indirect tax' is levied on:

(A) Income earned by individuals
(B) Goods or services — burden can be shifted to the consumer
(C) Capital gains only
(D) Inheritance only
cards.back:
(B) Goods or services — burden can be shifted to the consumer

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Direct vs Indirect — DIRECT tax (income tax, corporate tax, capital gains, wealth tax) is paid directly by the assessee to the government; burden cannot be shifted. INDIRECT tax (GST, customs, excise) is levied on goods/services, collected by an intermediary (seller), but ultimately borne by the final consumer. India's tax mix has shifted — pre-GST, indirect taxes ~65% of total revenue. Post-GST, ratio became more direct-heavy. Capital tax = direct tax. Goods purchase = pays GST (indirect).

cards.front:
GST in India operates on the principle of:

(A) Cascading taxation (tax on tax)
(B) Value-added taxation with credit for input taxes (no cascading)
(C) Lump-sum fixed tax irrespective of value
(D) Income-based slabs
cards.back:
(B) Value-added taxation with credit for input taxes (no cascading)

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — GST = Value-Added Tax. Each link in the supply chain pays tax only on the VALUE ADDED at that stage; gets Input Tax Credit (ITC) for tax paid on its inputs. Eliminates cascading (tax-on-tax), which was a defect of pre-GST excise + state VAT + service tax + entry tax + octroi. India follows DESTINATION-based GST — tax accrues to the state where the good/service is consumed, not produced. Slabs: 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% (+cess on demerit goods). Petroleum products + alcohol kept outside GST.

cards.front:
GST has FOUR component sub-types in India. Which combination is correct?

(A) CGST, SGST, IGST, UTGST
(B) CGST only
(C) SGST and ITGST
(D) Income-GST, Sales-GST
cards.back:
(A) CGST, SGST, IGST, UTGST

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Four GSTs based on destination + transaction nature: CGST — Central GST, levied on intra-state transactions, accrues to Centre. SGST — State GST, accrues to State on the same intra-state transaction. IGST — Integrated GST on INTER-state transactions; later split between origin and destination via clearing mechanism. UTGST — for transactions in Union Territories without a state legislature. CGST + SGST = total intra-state rate (e.g., 18% = 9% + 9%). IGST = full rate (e.g., 18%) for inter-state.

Which of these is a CESS (not a regular tax) levied by the Centre?

(A) Income tax
(B) Health and Education Cess (4% on direct tax) + Swachh Bharat Cess (earlier)
(C) GST
(D) Customs duty

GST Compensation Cess on demerit goods (luxury cars, tobacco) — funds the GST compensation grant to states. Surcharge — different from cess; goes to general revenue.

cards.front:
Customs duty in India is levied on:

(A) Domestic sales of goods
(B) Goods crossing the international border (imports + a few exports)
(C) Personal income
(D) Property transfers
cards.back:
(B) Goods crossing the international border (imports + a few exports)

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Customs Duty — under Customs Act, 1962 + Customs Tariff Act, 1975. Levied at ports/airports/land borders by CBIC officers. Two main types: Basic Customs Duty (BCD), Integrated GST (IGST on imports), Compensation Cess, Anti-Dumping Duty (when foreign goods are dumped at low prices), Countervailing Duty (offsets export subsidies abroad), Safeguard Duty. Used for protectionism (raise BCD on certain goods to support domestic industry — e.g., 2024 increase on smartphones), revenue, regulating trade. Export duty is rare — mostly raw materials (e.g., iron ore).

cards.front:
An 'ad valorem' tax is one which is calculated as:

(A) A flat amount per unit (specific tax)
(B) A percentage of the value of the goods or transaction
(C) Based on weight only
(D) Lump sum on income
cards.back:
(B) A percentage of the value of the goods or transaction

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Ad valorem (Latin 'according to value') — tax = % × value. Examples: GST (5/12/18/28% of price), Customs ad valorem rate, Stamp duty on property, ad valorem excise on luxury goods. Specific tax = fixed amount per unit (tonne, litre, piece) — e.g., excise on tobacco per stick, road tax per vehicle. Most modern indirect taxes are ad valorem (revenue scales automatically with inflation/economy growth) — but 'sin tax' on cigarettes is sometimes specific to discourage consumption regardless of price.

cards.front:
The FISCAL DEFICIT is best defined as:

(A) The difference between revenue receipts and capital receipts
(B) Total expenditure minus total non-borrowed receipts
(C) Revenue expenditure minus tax-only revenue receipts
(D) The gap between corporate tax and direct tax collection
cards.back:
(B) Total expenditure minus total non-borrowed receipts

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Fiscal deficit = Total Expenditure − Total Receipts (excluding borrowing). It measures the total borrowing requirement of the government. Important for macro-stability — funded by market loans (G-Sec auctions), small savings, external loans. India's FY24 fiscal deficit ≈ 5.6% of GDP (target was 5.9%); FY26 budget targets 4.4%. Distractor 1 = a balance-sheet split, not deficit. Distractor 3 ≈ revenue deficit but excludes non-tax revenue. Distractor 4 = arbitrary, not a defined deficit.

cards.front:
REVENUE DEFICIT differs from fiscal deficit in that it covers only:

(A) All borrowings minus repayments to the central bank
(B) Revenue expenditure exceeding revenue receipts
(C) Capital expenditure minus capital receipts only
(D) Foreign loans subtracted from external grants
cards.back:
(B) Revenue expenditure exceeding revenue receipts

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Revenue Deficit = Revenue Expenditure − Revenue Receipts. Indicates that the government is borrowing for current consumption (not asset creation) — generally considered fiscally unhealthy. The FRBM Act, 2003 originally targeted ZERO revenue deficit but has been repeatedly missed. Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD) — excludes grants for capital-asset creation given to states. Distractor 1 = not a defined deficit. Distractor 3 ≈ capital deficit (rare term). Distractor 4 = arbitrary.

cards.front:
PRIMARY DEFICIT is calculated as:

(A) Fiscal deficit plus interest payments due in the year
(B) Fiscal deficit minus interest payments due in the year
(C) Revenue deficit minus capital expenditure on infrastructure
(D) Total tax revenue minus combined direct + indirect tax
cards.back:
(B) Fiscal deficit minus interest payments due in the year

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments. Strips out the legacy of past borrowings (interest on old debt) to show whether CURRENT government operations are themselves in deficit. A primary surplus means new borrowing is being used only to service old debt; revenue + spending are matched. India's primary deficit has historically been positive; budget targets aim to bring it to ~0%. Distractor 1 reverses sign. Distractors 3 and 4 are unrelated formulas.

The FRBM Act, 2003 was enacted to:

(A) Regulate foreign exchange transactions across the border
(B) Set fiscal targets and ensure inter-generational equity in public finances
(C) Bring all public sector banks under single government ownership
(D) Authorise direct cash transfers to below-poverty-line households
cards.back:
(B) Set fiscal targets and ensure inter-generational equity in public finances

Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP target instead of just fiscal-deficit target — debt anchor of 60% (Centre + States combined). Distractor 1 = FEMA, 1999. Distractor 3 = bank nationalisation (1969, 1980).

(B) Internal, borrowed largely through dated G-Sec auctions
(C) Equally split, roughly half internal and half external
(D) External, borrowed mostly from sovereign-wealth investors

The ratio of CESS + SURCHARGE in the Centre's gross tax revenue has RISEN sharply in recent years because:

(B) Customs duty
(C) Income Tax
(D) Service Tax

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — GST components: (1) CGST (Central GST) — on INTRA-state supplies; goes to CENTRE. (2) SGST (State GST) — on intra-state supplies; goes to STATE where consumed. CGST + SGST rate = GST rate (e.g., 18% GST = 9% CGST + 9% SGST). (3) UTGST (Union Territory GST) — same as SGST but for UTs without legislature (Chandigarh, A&N Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra & Nagar Haveli & Daman & Diu, Ladakh). Delhi, Puducherry, J&K have legislatures → use SGST. (4) IGST (Integrated GST) — on INTER-STATE supplies (goods moving between states) + IMPORTS; collected by CENTRE, then split between Centre + destination state. Rate = full GST rate (18% = 18% IGST, no split at collection). ORIGIN-BASED vs DESTINATION-BASED: GST is DESTINATION-BASED — tax goes where goods/services are consumed. This was a big shift from earlier origin-based taxes. REVERSE CHARGE MECHANISM (RCM): for specific goods/services, recipient pays GST instead of supplier.

cards.front:
The current (FY 2024-25) income tax slab under the NEW REGIME (default since 2023) for an individual, with the basic exemption limit at:

(A) ₹2.5 lakh
(B) ₹3 lakh
(C) ₹5 lakh
(D) ₹10 lakh
cards.back:
(B) ₹3 lakh

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — INCOME TAX in India — TWO REGIMES (since Budget 2020, further tweaked 2023/24): (A) OLD REGIME — higher slab rates but allows deductions (80C, 80D, HRA, LTA, home loan interest etc.). (B) NEW REGIME — lower rates + wider slabs, BUT NO most deductions (just standard deduction). DEFAULT switched to NEW REGIME from FY 2023-24. NEW REGIME SLABS (FY 2024-25, for individuals below 60): (1) ₹0 – ₹3 L = NIL; (2) ₹3-7 L = 5%; (3) ₹7-10 L = 10%; (4) ₹10-12 L = 15%; (5) ₹12-15 L = 20%; (6) > ₹15 L = 30%. REBATE u/s 87A: income up to ₹7 lakh → NO TAX under new regime (rebate up to ₹25k). STANDARD DEDUCTION ₹75k (raised from 50k in Budget 2024). SURCHARGE on income > ₹50L (10% → 37% progressive, but capped at 25% under new regime). CESS 4% (health + education). CORPORATE TAX RATES: domestic 22% (concessional, if foregoing exemptions) + 15% for new manufacturing companies (sunset). RATES CHANGE EVERY BUDGET — HIGH STALENESS. new regime FY 2024-25; rebate u/s 87A means no tax up to ₹7 lakh.

cards.front:
Which state in India was the FIRST to agree to implement GST, passing its resolution on 16 May 2017 (before 1 July rollout)?

(A) Gujarat
(B) Telangana
(C) Tamil Nadu
(D) Maharashtra
cards.back:
(B) Telangana

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — TELANGANA — FIRST STATE to pass its GST Bill on 16 May 2017 (before the national 1 July 2017 rollout). Followed closely by Bihar, Rajasthan, Gujarat, etc. GST was enabled by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 (September 2016) — longest-debated amendment, introduced as 115th Amendment Bill in 2011 by UPA, finally passed in 2016. Four GST Acts passed by Parliament (April 2017): CGST Act, IGST Act, UTGST Act, GST (Compensation to States) Act. GST implementation in India: July 2017 (18 years after Atal Bihari Vajpayee first proposed it in 2000, Kelkar Task Force endorsed in 2003). Modelled loosely on Canadian + French VAT systems. GST replaced: Central Excise, Service Tax, VAT, Entertainment Tax, Entry Tax, CST, Purchase Tax, Luxury Tax, Octroi, Advertising Tax, etc. GST Compensation Cess — for 5 years (extended) to compensate states for any revenue loss during transition. GST COUNCIL meets regularly to rationalise rates, handle issues. first, 16 May 2017.

cards.front:
Which Constitutional Amendment empowered the Union to tax incomes?

(A) Via original Constitution 1950
(B) 101st Amendment (GST)
(C) 82nd Amendment
(D) 42nd Amendment
cards.back:
(A) Via original Constitution 1950

Budget, Taxes & Fiscal Policy — Under the original INDIAN CONSTITUTION 1950, taxation powers are DIVIDED between Centre + States via the 7TH SCHEDULE (three lists): UNION LIST (Entry 82-92B for Union taxes): INCOME TAX (except agricultural income — state), CORPORATION TAX, CUSTOMS, EXCISE (historical — now mostly GST), SERVICE TAX (historical — now GST), wealth tax (abolished), estate duty (abolished). STATE LIST (Entries 45-63): AGRICULTURAL INCOME TAX, LAND REVENUE, STAMP DUTY (non-documents), EXCISE on ALCOHOL, TAXES ON VEHICLES, STATE EXCISE, ENTRY TAXES (now in GST), PROFESSIONAL TAX (capped at ₹2500/year via Art 276). CONCURRENT LIST: trade + commerce, stamp duty on certain documents. Fiscal federalism: FINANCE COMMISSION (Art 280) — every 5 years divides tax revenues between Centre-States. 15th FC period 2021-26 (chairman NK Singh) gave states 41% of divisible tax pool (down from 42% under 14th FC). 101st Amendment (2016) added Article 246-A overriding both Union + State lists to enable GST. IMPORTANT: INCOME from agriculture STILL tax-free at Centre but taxable by States — loophole for high-income farmers (though rarely enforced by states). 7th Schedule — Union List.

The THRESHOLD for GST registration for businesses dealing in GOODS is:

(A) ₹5 lakh annual turnover
(B) ₹40 lakh annual turnover (₹20 lakh for Special Category States); ₹20 lakh for services
(C) ₹1 crore
(D) No threshold — all must register
cards.back:
(B) ₹40 lakh annual turnover (₹20 lakh for Special Category States); ₹20 lakh for services

cards.front:
Which of the following best defines inflation?

(A) A one-time increase in the price of a single commodity
(B) A sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services in an economy
(C) A decrease in the production of goods
(D) An increase in the nominal value of currency
cards.back:
(B) A sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services in an economy

Inflation & Markets — Inflation is a SUSTAINED rise in the GENERAL price level — not a one-off change or a sectoral change. It erodes the purchasing power of money: the same rupee buys fewer goods over time. Measured via indices like CPI and WPI. A single commodity's price rise (e.g., tomatoes in monsoon) is NOT inflation if average prices are stable. An increase in nominal currency value is the opposite (deflation/currency strengthening).

cards.option2: A decrease in the production of goods
cards.option3: An increase in the nominal value of currency

cards.front:
In India, which of the following is the primary inflation index used by the RBI for its monetary policy decisions?

(A) WPI (Wholesale Price Index)
(B) CPI-Combined (Consumer Price Index)
(C) CPI-IW (Industrial Workers)
(D) IIP (Index of Industrial Production)
cards.back:
(B) CPI-Combined (Consumer Price Index)

Inflation & Markets — Since 2014 (Urjit Patel Committee + 2016 Monetary Policy Framework Agreement), the RBI targets HEADLINE CPI-Combined (released by NSO/MoSPI) with a central target of 4% ± 2%. WPI (Office of Economic Adviser, DPIIT) is used for deflating GDP at constant prices and tracking producer prices, but NOT as the RBI's policy target. CPI-IW (Labour Bureau) is used for DA calculations for govt employees, not RBI targeting.

cards.front:
Which of the following is an example of 'cost-push' inflation?

(A) A boom in consumer demand during a festival
(B) A sharp increase in crude oil prices raising transport and production costs
(C) Government printing excess money
(D) A stock market rally
cards.back:
(B) A sharp increase in crude oil prices raising transport and production costs

Inflation & Markets — COST-PUSH inflation arises when input costs (raw materials, wages, fuel) rise and producers pass this on to consumers. Classic example: oil shocks (1973 OPEC crisis, 2008 oil spike). DEMAND-PULL inflation arises when aggregate demand exceeds supply (option A — festival demand surge). Excess money printing is typically classified as demand-pull/monetary inflation (option C). A stock rally is asset-price inflation, not general inflation.

cards.front:
What is the current inflation target band set for the RBI under the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement?

(A) 2% ± 1% (i.e., 1% to 3%)
(B) 4% ± 2% (i.e., 2% to 6%)
(C) 5% ± 3% (i.e., 2% to 8%)
(D) 6% (hard ceiling)
cards.back:
(B) 4% ± 2% (i.e., 2% to 6%)

Inflation & Markets — The RBI's flexible inflation targeting framework sets a MEDIUM-TERM target of 4% CPI-Combined, with a tolerance band of ±2 percentage points (lower bound 2%, upper bound 6%). This was first set in 2016 (initial 5-year review) and was retained at the March 2021 review for another 5 years (2021-26). If inflation breaches the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the government explaining reasons and remedial actions.

cards.front:
Galloping inflation refers to inflation of:

(A) 0 to 3% annually
(B) 3 to 10% annually
(C) 10 to 1000% annually
(D) Below 0% (deflation)
cards.back:
(C) 10 to 1000% annually

Inflation & Markets — Inflation categories: (1) Creeping/Mild — <3%; (2) Walking/Trotting — 3-10%; (3) GALLOPING/Running — 10-1000%; (4) Hyperinflation — >1000% per year (e.g., Weimar Germany 1923, Zimbabwe 2008, Venezuela 2018). Galloping inflation disrupts business planning and wage contracts. Deflation is NEGATIVE inflation (falling prices) and is generally considered a warning sign of slump.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a MONETARY POLICY tool that the RBI uses to control inflation?

(A) Raising or lowering Income Tax rates
(B) Changing the Repo Rate
(C) Issuing Union Government bonds
(D) Adjusting MSP for agricultural commodities
cards.back:
(B) Changing the Repo Rate

Inflation & Markets — MONETARY policy tools are used by the CENTRAL BANK (RBI). Key tools: Repo Rate, Reverse Repo Rate, MSF, Bank Rate, CRR, SLR, OMO (Open Market Operations). Changing Repo Rate (lending rate for banks to RBI) influences bank interest rates → consumer borrowing/saving → aggregate demand → inflation. Income Tax is a FISCAL POLICY tool (Finance Ministry). Government bonds are fiscal. MSP is set by Cabinet on CACP recommendation — neither monetary nor a direct fiscal tool.

cards.front:
'Stagflation' refers to which economic condition?

(A) High growth with rising prices
(B) Low/stagnant growth accompanied by high inflation and unemployment
(C) Declining prices with rising output
(D) Stable prices combined with zero unemployment
cards.back:
(B) Low/stagnant growth accompanied by high inflation and unemployment

Inflation & Markets — STAGFLATION = STAGnation + inFLATION. It is the coexistence of (1) slow/zero economic growth, (2) high inflation, and (3) elevated unemployment. It challenges the classical Phillips-curve view that inflation and unemployment trade off. Famous example: US in 1970s during oil shocks. Policymakers face a dilemma: tightening money controls inflation but worsens unemployment; loosening controls does the opposite.

cards.front:
The business cycle typically consists of four phases. Which phase is characterized by declining output, rising unemployment, and falling prices?

(A) Expansion
(B) Peak
(C) Contraction/Recession
(D) Trough
cards.back:
(C) Contraction/Recession

Inflation & Markets — Business cycle phases: (1) EXPANSION — GDP rising, employment up, prices rising modestly; (2) PEAK — growth at maximum, economy overheated; (3) CONTRACTION/RECESSION — GDP falling, unemployment rising, prices falling or rising slowly; (4) TROUGH — economy at its bottom before recovery. A recession is technically defined as TWO consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth (NBER uses broader criteria). Great Depression (1929-33) was a severe contraction.

A recession is technically defined as TWO consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth (NBER uses broader criteria). Great Depression (1929-33) was a severe contraction.

cards.front:
Which of the following best describes 'core inflation'?

(A) Inflation in all goods and services
(B) Inflation excluding food and fuel
(C) Inflation only in essential commodities
(D) Inflation faced by rural consumers only
cards.back:
(B) Inflation excluding food and fuel

Inflation & Markets — CORE INFLATION strips out volatile items (food and fuel) from headline CPI to reveal underlying inflation trends driven by broader demand-supply conditions. Food/fuel are excluded because they swing due to monsoons, crude shocks, etc. — noise that obscures the inflation signal. Central banks watch core inflation closely since it responds more predictably to monetary policy. In India, core is often quoted alongside headline in RBI bi-monthly reviews. i.e., non-volatile components.

cards.front:
Who chairs the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which decides the repo rate?

(A) The Prime Minister
(B) The Finance Minister
(C) The Governor of the RBI
(D) The Chief Economic Advisor
cards.back:
(C) The Governor of the RBI

Inflation & Markets — The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has 6 members: 3 from RBI (Governor, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one officer nominated by RBI Central Board) + 3 external members (nominated by the Government of India for 4-year terms). The RBI Governor CHAIRS the MPC and has a CASTING VOTE in case of a tie. The MPC meets at least 4 times a year (usually 6) and decisions are made by majority vote. The PM and FM have no direct vote.

cards.front:
ASSERTION (A): When the RBI raises the REPO RATE, banks typically raise their lending rates, cooling aggregate demand. REASON (R): A higher repo rate makes it costlier for banks to borrow overnight from the RBI, so they pass the higher cost through to customers.

(A) Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation
(B) Both A and R are true, R is NOT the correct explanation
(C) A is true, R is false
(D) Both are false
cards.back:
(A) Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation

When the repo rises, banks' marginal cost of funds rises, and under the MCLR (and now EBLR for retail loans) regime, lending rates tend to follow. Higher borrowing cost → less credit-fuelled demand → cooling effect on inflation.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a quantitative tool of monetary policy in India?

(A) Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)
(B) Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
(C) Moral Suasion
(D) Open Market Operations (OMO)
cards.back:
(C) Moral Suasion

Quantitative tools are the levers that directly affect the overall volume of credit: CRR, SLR, repo/reverse repo, OMO, MSF, Bank Rate. Other qualitative tools: margin requirements, credit rationing, direct action.

cards.front:
If the CPI-Combined was 150 in March 2025 and 156 in March 2026 (base 2012 = 100), the year-on-year CPI inflation in March 2026 is closest to:

(A) 3.0 %
(B) 4.0 %
(C) 5.0 %
(D) 6.0 %
cards.back:
(B) 4.0 %

Inflation & Markets — YoY inflation = (new − old)/old × 100 = (156 − 150)/150 × 100 = 6/150 × 100 = 4.0 %. The trap is using (156 − 150)/100 = 6 % (wrong base). Always divide by the EARLIER index, not the index-base of 100.

cards.front:
Using the Fisher relation (real rate ≈ nominal − inflation), in which case does the NOMINAL rate UNDERSTATE the real return?

(A) Inflation is negative (deflation)
(B) Inflation is zero
(C) Inflation is positive
(D) Inflation equals the nominal rate exactly
cards.back:
(A) Inflation is negative (deflation)

Inflation & Markets — Real = nominal − π. If π < 0 (deflation), real > nominal → nominal UNDERSTATES the real return. If π > 0 (typical inflation), real < nominal → nominal OVERSTATES the real return. If π = 0, real = nominal exactly.
cards.option3: Inflation equals the nominal rate exactly

cards.front:
Inflation caused mainly by a rise in total demand that exceeds supply is called:

(A) Cost-push inflation
(B) Demand-pull inflation
(C) Imported inflation
(D) Structural inflation
cards.back:
(B) Demand-pull inflation

Inflation & Markets — Demand-pull — aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply at current prices. Cost-push — higher input costs (oil, wages) drive prices up. Imported — costlier imports or a weaker currency. Structural — bottlenecks in specific sectors such as food or housing.

cards.front:
The situation of simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment is called:

(A) Recession
(B) Stagflation
(C) Deflation
(D) Reflation
cards.back:
(B) Stagflation

Inflation & Markets — Stagflation — stagnant output with rising prices — breaks the classic Phillips curve relation. Best-known example: OECD economies in the 1970s after the oil shocks. Reflation = deliberate policy to push prices up after a deflationary spell; deflation = falling prices; recession = two quarters of negative GDP growth.

(C) Fuel and light

Housing weight applies only to the urban CPI. The rest of the basket is pan/tobacco, clothing, fuel and light, household goods, health, education, transport and miscellaneous.

cards.front:
Hyperinflation, in standard economic literature, is inflation typically exceeding:

(A) 5 % per year
(B) 50 % per month
(C) 10 % per year
(D) 100 % per year
cards.back:
(B) 50 % per month

Inflation & Markets — The classic Cagan threshold for hyperinflation is 50 % per month. Famous cases: Weimar Germany (1923), Hungary (1946, worst ever), Zimbabwe (2008), Venezuela (2016-19). Rough categorisation: creeping < 3 % p.a., walking 3-10 %, galloping 10-100 %, anything faster and accelerating = hyperinflation.

cards.front:
If the RBI wants to reduce inflation through monetary policy, it will typically:

(A) Cut the repo rate
(B) Raise the repo rate
(C) Cut the cash reserve ratio (CRR)
(D) Buy government bonds in the open market
cards.back:
(B) Raise the repo rate

Inflation & Markets — A higher repo rate raises banks' cost of funds, lifts lending rates, cools borrowing and demand, and eases inflation. Rate cuts, CRR cuts and open-market bond purchases are expansionary and add to inflationary pressure. The repo rate is decided by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), a six-member body that meets at least every two months.

cards.front:
Under India's inflation-targeting framework, the RBI has to keep CPI inflation (on average) at:

(A) 2 %, with a ±2 % tolerance band
(B) 4 %, with a ±2 % tolerance band
(C) 6 %, with a ±2 % tolerance band
(D) 5 %, with a ±1 % tolerance band
cards.back:
(B) 4 %, with a ±2 % tolerance band

Inflation & Markets — Since the 2016 amendment to the RBI Act, India runs a flexible inflation-targeting regime — CPI inflation target is 4 % with a tolerance band of ±2 %, i.e., between 2 % and 6 %. The target is reviewed by the Government in consultation with the RBI every five years; the 4 % target was retained for the 2021-26 period.

cards.front:
A fall in the overall price level over a sustained period is called:

(A) Disinflation
(B) Deflation
(C) Reflation
(D) Stagflation
cards.back:
(B) Deflation

Inflation & Markets — Deflation — sustained fall in the general price level. Disinflation is when inflation itself slows (prices still rising, just more slowly). Reflation is the policy effort to push prices back up after a deflationary period. Stagflation is high inflation combined with stagnant growth. Japan's 'lost decades' (1990s-2000s) are the textbook modern deflation example.

(A) Decrease in the general price level
(B) Sustained rise in the general price level / fall in purchasing power

cards.back:
(B) Sustained rise in the general price level / fall in purchasing power

The PHILLIPS CURVE suggests a trade-off between:

(B) Inflation and unemployment (short-run)
(C) Exports and imports
(D) Interest rate and savings
cards.back:
(B) Inflation and unemployment (short-run)

cards.front:
If prices rise by 8% while nominal wages rise by 3%, the REAL wage:

(A) Rises by 5%
(B) Falls by ~5%
(C) Stays the same
(D) Rises by 11%
cards.back:
(B) Falls by ~5%

(A) Cost-push inflation (supply-side)
(B) Demand-pull inflation (demand-side)
(C) Hyperinflation (very rapid > 50%/mo)
(D) Stagflation (stagnation + inflation)
cards.back:

cards.front:
DEFLATION is:

(A) Decreasing inflation rate (still positive figure)
(B) Falling general price level (negative inflation)
(C) Stable, zero inflation always for some periods
(D) Rising prices in only one sector of economy
cards.back:

Inflation & Markets — DEFLATION — sustained DECREASE in general price level (inflation rate < 0). DISINFLATION = decrease in inflation RATE (rate still positive but smaller). cards.front:
CORE INFLATION typically excludes which categories?

(A) Manufactured goods + services
(B) Food + fuel (most volatile)
(C) Housing + clothing categories
(D) Health + education services
cards.back:

Inflation & Markets — CORE INFLATION = headline inflation EXCLUDING food + fuel (the most volatile categories). Why exclude: food (weather, seasonality) + fuel (oil prices, geopolitical events) are highly variable, can mask underlying trend. Core inflation reveals UNDERLYING price pressure — better signal for monetary policy. Persistent high core inflation = entrenched inflation, harder to control. RBI looks at both headline + core CPI. cards.front:
Who BENEFITS during inflation?

(A) Lenders and savers benefit most from inflation
(B) Borrowers (loans repaid in cheaper currency)
(C) Pensioners on fixed income gain from inflation
(D) Salaried employees with no salary rise also gain
cards.back:

Inflation & Markets — Inflation effects: BENEFITS BORROWERS — they repay loans in money worth less than at borrowing time (real value of loan eroded). HURTS LENDERS + SAVERS — interest income may not keep up with inflation; real returns fall (especially fixed-deposit holders with rate < inflation). HURTS PENSIONERS + fixed-income earners — purchasing power of pension declines. HURTS salaried (without inflation-linked increments). REAL ESTATE + GOLD often gain (inflation hedges). EQUITY can be a hedge over LONG term (stocks of companies with pricing power).

cards.front:
The INDIAN STOCK MARKETS are regulated by:

(A) Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
(B) Finance Ministry directly
(C) SEBI — Securities and Exchange Board of India; set up 1988, given statutory powers by SEBI Act 1992; HQ Mumbai; also regulates mutual funds, FPIs, REITs, InvITs
(D) NITI Aayog
cards.back:
(C) SEBI — Securities and Exchange Board of India; set up 1988, given statutory powers by SEBI Act 1992; HQ Mumbai; also regulates mutual funds, FPIs, REITs, InvITs

Inflation & Markets — SEBI (SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE BOARD OF INDIA) — regulator of securities and capital markets in India. ESTABLISHED: (a) Non-statutory body on 12 APRIL 1988 by Government of India resolution; (b) Became STATUTORY (autonomous) under SEBI ACT 1992 after the HARSHAD MEHTA ‘1992 scam’ (fraudulent use of bank receipts on BSE — ₹5,000 crore); (c) HQ at MUMBAI (BKC); 4 regional offices (Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Ahmedabad). OBJECTIVES (‘mandate’): (1) PROTECT INTERESTS of investors in securities; (2) PROMOTE development of securities markets; (3) REGULATE securities market. POWERS: (a) quasi-legislative (frame rules/regulations — SEBI Takeover Code, LODR, ICDR etc.); (b) quasi-executive (investigate, issue orders); (c) quasi-judicial (adjudicate through SEBI whole-time members). COMPOSITION: Chairman + 2 whole-time + 2 part-time members (appointed by GoI). CURRENT CHAIRPERSON (as of Apr 2026): TUHIN KANTA PANDEY (ex-Finance Secretary, took office March 2025, replacing Madhabi Puri Buch who was India’s first female SEBI chair). ENTITIES SEBI REGULATES: (1) STOCK EXCHANGES — BSE, NSE, MSEI, commodity exchanges (MCX, NCDEX); (2) ISSUERS of securities (IPOs, FPOs, rights issues); (3) INTERMEDIARIES — merchant bankers, brokers, sub-brokers, registrars, depositories (NSDL, CDSL); (4) FOREIGN PORTFOLIO INVESTORS (FPIs); (5) MUTUAL FUNDS; (6) ALTERNATIVE INVESTMENT FUNDS (AIFs) — PE, VC, hedge funds; (7) REITs & InvITs (Real Estate + Infrastructure Investment Trusts); (8) CREDIT RATING AGENCIES (CRAs — CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, India Ratings); (9) INVESTMENT ADVISERS; (10) RESEARCH ANALYSTS; (11) PORTFOLIO MANAGERS. NOT REGULATED by SEBI: banks (RBI), insurance (IRDAI), pensions (PFRDA), government bond issuance (RBI on behalf of GoI). FSDC — Financial Stability and Development Council — apex inter-regulatory body (Finance Minister chairs) to coordinate among RBI-SEBI-IRDAI-PFRDA.

cards.front:
The BENCHMARK stock index representing 30 companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) is:

(A) NIFTY 50
(B) SENSEX
(C) NASDAQ Composite
(D) Dow Jones
cards.back:
(B) SENSEX

Inflation & Markets — SENSEX (‘SENSitive indEX’) — India's OLDEST benchmark stock market index; tracks 30 LARGE, WELL-ESTABLISHED, actively-traded, financially sound companies representing diverse sectors on the BOMBAY STOCK EXCHANGE (BSE). Full name: S&P BSE SENSEX. HISTORY: (1) BSE established 1875 — ASIA's OLDEST stock exchange; (2) SENSEX launched 1 Jan 1986; (3) Base year 1978-79, Base value 100; (4) methodology shifted to FREE-FLOAT market capitalisation weighting in Sept 2003. SIGNIFICANT MILESTONES: (a) First crossed 1,000 in 25 July 1990; 5,000 in Oct 1999; 10,000 in Feb 2006; 20,000 in Oct 2007 (pre-GFC peak); 25,000 in 2014; 50,000 in Jan 2021; 60,000 in Sep 2021; 75,000 in Apr 2024; 80,000+ by 2025. (b) Sensex touched ~85,000 in late 2024 before correction. COMPUTED EVERY 15 seconds during trading hours (9:15-15:30 IST). NIFTY 50 — India's other benchmark, on the NSE (NATIONAL STOCK EXCHANGE, founded 1992, operational 1994, now world's biggest derivatives exchange by volume). Nifty 50 is a 50-stock index launched 1996; base year 1995, base value 1000. Currently in the ~25,000 range (2026). OTHER INDIAN INDICES: (1) BSE SMALLCAP, MIDCAP, LARGECAP; (2) BSE 100, BSE 200, BSE 500; (3) NIFTY NEXT 50, NIFTY MIDCAP 50/100/150, NIFTY SMALLCAP; (4) SECTORAL — BANK NIFTY, NIFTY IT, NIFTY PHARMA, NIFTY AUTO, NIFTY FMCG, NIFTY METAL, NIFTY REALTY; (5) BSE DOLLEX (US-dollar version). GLOBAL INDICES: DOW JONES INDUSTRIAL AVERAGE (30 stocks, USA, oldest — 1896); S&P 500 (USA, 500 stocks); NASDAQ Composite (tech-heavy, USA); FTSE 100 (UK, London); DAX 40 (Germany); NIKKEI 225 (Japan); HANG SENG (Hong Kong); SHANGHAI COMPOSITE; KOSPI (Korea); STRAITS TIMES (Singapore); ASX 200 (Australia). free-float market-cap weighted; base year 1978-79, base value 100; launched 1986; also called BSE 30, or S&P BSE SENSEX.

cards.front:
An INITIAL PUBLIC OFFERING (IPO) is:

(A) A bond issue by the government
(B) The FIRST SALE of shares to the PUBLIC by a private company
(C) The buyback of shares by a company
(D) A central bank open-market operation
cards.back:
(B) The FIRST SALE of shares to the PUBLIC by a private company

Inflation & Markets — IPO (INITIAL PUBLIC OFFERING) — the FIRST TIME that a private company offers its SHARES to the PUBLIC to raise capital. After the IPO, the company becomes ‘PUBLIC / LISTED’ and its shares are traded freely on stock exchanges. CLASSIFICATION of markets: (1) PRIMARY MARKET — where securities are ISSUED for the first time (IPO, FPO, rights issue); company receives the money. (2) SECONDARY MARKET — where PREVIOUSLY-ISSUED securities are traded among investors (regular stock exchange trading); company doesn't receive proceeds, but buyers/sellers transact. IPO PROCESS (India, SEBI ICDR Regulations 2018): (a) appoint MERCHANT BANKERS (book-running lead managers — BRLMs); (b) DRHP (Draft Red Herring Prospectus) filed with SEBI; (c) SEBI approves after scrutiny; (d) RHP (Red Herring Prospectus) finalised; (e) SUBSCRIPTION period: 3-5 working days; (f) PRICE BAND set (e.g., ₹100-105); investors bid in BOOK-BUILDING process; (g) ALLOTMENT on pro-rata basis; (h) LISTING DAY — shares begin trading. Categories of investors in an Indian IPO: QIB (Qualified Institutional Buyers, 50% in book-built) - institutional investors like MFs, FIIs, banks, insurance; NIIs (Non-institutional investors, 15%) — individuals with application > ₹2 lakh; RETAIL (35%, typically) — individuals up to ₹2 lakh; EMPLOYEE reserve portion. Types of offering: FRESH ISSUE (new shares, cash goes to company) or OFFER FOR SALE (OFS, existing shareholders sell — cash goes to them, not to company). ANCHOR INVESTORS — get allotment 1 day before public subscription. IPO TERMS: (1) LISTING — inclusion on stock exchange; (2) LOCK-IN — existing shareholders may be restricted from selling for 6-18 months; (3) GREY MARKET PREMIUM (GMP) — informal pre-listing trading price; (4) LISTING GAIN — difference between IPO price and listing-day price. FAMOUS IPOs in India: (a) COAL INDIA 2010 (₹15,475 cr, was largest till 2021); (b) LIC 2022 (₹21,008 cr, India's largest IPO ever); (c) PAYTM 2021 (₹18,300 cr, notorious for post-listing losses); (d) ZOMATO 2021 (unicorn IPO era); (e) HDFC BANK, TCS (multi-decade wealth creators). FPO = Follow-on Public Offering (already-listed company raises more capital). OFS (Offer for Sale, separate mechanism for promoters to sell shares to public via SE). the company ‘lists’ on a stock exchange; raises primary-market capital; regulated by SEBI (ICDR Regulations).

cards.option2: The buyback of shares by a company

cards.front:
‘BULLISH’ in stock market parlance means:

(A) Falling prices, pessimistic outlook
(B) RISING prices, OPTIMISTIC outlook (vs BEARISH = falling, pessimistic); bull attacks by thrusting horns UPWARD, bear swipes paws DOWNWARD
(C) High interest rates
(D) Illegal insider trading
cards.back:
(B) RISING prices, OPTIMISTIC outlook (vs BEARISH = falling, pessimistic); bull attacks by thrusting horns UPWARD, bear swipes paws DOWNWARD

Inflation & Markets — BULL vs BEAR — classical stock market terms. BULL / BULLISH: (a) Market is RISING / prices are going UP; (b) investors OPTIMISTIC about future; (c) buying interest dominates. Etymology: a bull attacks by thrusting its HORNS UPWARD — stock prices move UP like a bull's strike. A ‘BULL MARKET’ = prolonged rise of 20%+ from lows; some last years. BEAR / BEARISH: (a) Market is FALLING / prices going DOWN; (b) investors PESSIMISTIC; (c) selling pressure dominates. Etymology: a bear attacks by swiping paws DOWNWARD. A ‘BEAR MARKET’ = prolonged decline of 20%+ from highs. OTHER MARKET ANIMAL ANALOGIES: (1) CHICKEN — panicky investor selling out of fear; (2) PIG — greedy investor taking excessive risk; ‘bulls make money, bears make money, pigs get slaughtered’; (3) SHEEP — herd-following investor; (4) OSTRICH — investor ignoring bad news (‘head in sand’); (5) DOVE / HAWK — policy stance of central banks (dove = accommodative, hawk = tight); (6) WOLF — aggressive predatory trader (‘Wolf of Wall Street’ book/film about Jordan Belfort); (7) WHALE — very large investor. OTHER STOCK MARKET TERMS: (a) BLUE CHIP — very well-established, high-market-cap, stable company (e.g., TCS, RIL, HDFC Bank, ITC, HUL); (b) PENNY STOCK — very low price (<₹10), small-cap, risky; (c) GROWTH STOCK — high earnings growth, reinvests; (d) VALUE STOCK — undervalued relative to fundamentals; (e) DIVIDEND STOCK — pays high/regular dividends; (f) MULTIBAGGER — returns multiples of investment (10-bagger = 10x return); (g) BOURSE — alternative term for stock exchange; (h) CIRCUIT BREAKER / CIRCUIT FILTER — automated trading halt when market moves beyond set % (SEBI: 10%, 15%, 20% levels in Sensex/Nifty); (i) UPPER CIRCUIT / LOWER CIRCUIT — when a single stock moves by a preset %; (j) SHORT SELLING — selling borrowed shares with expectation of buying back cheaper; (k) F&O — Futures & Options (derivatives). (l) VIX — Volatility Index (‘Fear Gauge’); Nifty VIX reflects expected volatility over next 30 days.

cards.front:
The DEPOSITORIES that hold Indian investors' shares in DEMATERIALISED (demat) form are:

(A) Only NSE's depository
(B) NSDL (National Securities Depository Ltd, promoted by IDBI/UTI/NSE, 1996) and CDSL
(C) Only SBI banks
(D) Physical vaults of RBI
cards.back:
(B) NSDL (National Securities Depository Ltd, promoted by IDBI/UTI/NSE, 1996) and CDSL

Inflation & Markets — DEPOSITORIES in India — institutions that hold securities (shares, bonds, ETFs, mutual fund units) in ELECTRONIC / DEMATERIALISED (‘DEMAT’) form, replacing physical paper share certificates. TWO depositories exist: (1) NSDL (National Securities Depository Limited) — established 1996 (India's FIRST depository); promoted by IDBI Bank, UTI, NSE; HQ Mumbai; (2) CDSL (Central Depository Services Limited) — established 1999; promoted by BSE and leading banks; HQ Mumbai. Both regulated by SEBI under the DEPOSITORIES ACT 1996. DEMAT ACCOUNT holds securities; investors access it via a DEPOSITORY PARTICIPANT (DP) — usually a broker (Zerodha, Groww, Angel One, ICICI Direct, HDFC Securities, Kotak) or bank. BENEFITS of DEMAT: (a) no forgery / theft / loss of certificates; (b) no stamp duty on transfer (except 0.015% for delivery); (c) fast settlement — T+1 (since Jan 2023) and T+0 in pilot (2024 onwards); (d) easy corporate actions (dividend auto-credit, bonus/split/rights auto-applied); (e) secure pledging/loan against shares. Securities TRACED end-to-end: issuer company → RTA (Registrar + Transfer Agent — KFintech, Link Intime) → Depository (NSDL/CDSL) → DP → investor's demat account. SETTLEMENT CYCLE — T+1 (trade date + 1 working day), moved from T+2 in 2023; T+0 same-day settlement in pilot phase for select stocks. GLOBALLY: T+1 is standard in USA (since May 2024), EU moving to T+1 by 2027. Depositories outside India: DTCC (USA), Euroclear + Clearstream (Europe), JASDEC (Japan), KSD (Korea). MARKET INFRASTRUCTURE INSTITUTIONS (MIIs) under SEBI: stock exchanges (BSE, NSE, MSEI, commodity exchanges), depositories (NSDL, CDSL), clearing corporations (ICCL, NSCCL) — they are ‘systemically important’. RECENT INDIAN MILESTONE: NSDL's IPO expected 2025-26; CDSL already listed in 2017 (the first Asian depository listed). DEMAT ACCOUNTS in India: crossed 20 CRORE in early 2025 (vs 4 crore in 2020), growth driven by fintechs + WFH trading. both regulated by SEBI; Central Depository Services Ltd, promoted by BSE, 1999.

cards.front:
A MUTUAL FUND pools money from many investors to invest in:

(A) Only government bonds
(B) Only equity shares
(C) A DIVERSIFIED PORTFOLIO of stocks, bonds, and other securities
(D) Real estate exclusively
cards.back:
(C) A DIVERSIFIED PORTFOLIO of stocks, bonds, and other securities

Inflation & Markets — MUTUAL FUND (MF) — investment vehicle that pools money from many investors to invest collectively in securities (stocks, bonds, money market, gold, derivatives). Managed by a professional FUND MANAGER on behalf of the investors; each investor owns UNITS (proportional shares) of the fund's portfolio. Indian MFs regulated by SEBI under the MUTUAL FUND REGULATIONS 1996. AMFI (Association of Mutual Funds in India) is the industry body. STRUCTURE: (1) SPONSOR — company that establishes the MF (e.g., HDFC, ICICI Prudential, SBI). (2) TRUSTEES — hold fund assets in trust for unitholders. (3) AMC (Asset Management Company) — manages the fund, takes investment decisions; licensed by SEBI. (4) CUSTODIAN — holds the actual securities. (5) RTA — maintains investor records. TYPES OF MFs: (A) BY STRUCTURE: (1) OPEN-ENDED — units can be bought/sold anytime at NAV; no fixed maturity (most common). (2) CLOSE-ENDED — fixed tenure, units issued at launch only, listed on exchange. (3) INTERVAL — hybrid. (B) BY ASSET CLASS: (1) EQUITY — primarily stocks (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, multi-cap, ELSS, sectoral, index); (2) DEBT — primarily bonds (liquid, gilt, corporate bond, credit risk, dynamic bond); (3) HYBRID — mix (balanced, aggressive hybrid, conservative hybrid, multi-asset); (4) SOLUTION-ORIENTED — retirement, children; (5) OTHER — GOLD ETFs, international, FoF (fund of funds). cards.front:
‘DERIVATIVES’ in financial markets include instruments like futures and options, whose VALUE is DERIVED FROM:

(A) The price of the paper on which they are printed
(B) The performance of the regulator
(C) An UNDERLYING ASSET
(D) The market capitalisation of all listed stocks
cards.back:
(C) An UNDERLYING ASSET

Inflation & Markets — DERIVATIVES — financial CONTRACTS whose VALUE is DERIVED FROM an UNDERLYING ASSET (stock, index, commodity, currency, bond, interest rate, or another derivative). They allow investors to: (1) HEDGE — reduce risk of adverse price moves in the underlying; (2) SPECULATE — bet on future price movements with leverage; (3) ARBITRAGE — exploit price differences across markets. FOUR MAIN TYPES: (I) FORWARDS — OVER-THE-COUNTER (OTC), CUSTOMISED contract between two parties to buy/sell an asset at a fixed price on a future date; unregulated; counterparty risk. (II) FUTURES — standardised, EXCHANGE-TRADED version of forwards; mark-to-market daily; margin-based; eliminates counterparty risk via CLEARING HOUSE. Types: STOCK FUTURES (on individual shares), INDEX FUTURES (Nifty 50, Sensex), CURRENCY FUTURES, COMMODITY FUTURES, INTEREST RATE FUTURES. (III) OPTIONS — contract giving BUYER the RIGHT (not obligation) to buy/sell an asset at a STRIKE price on/before an EXPIRY date; SELLER has the OBLIGATION. CALL OPTION = right to BUY; PUT OPTION = right to SELL. Buyer pays a PREMIUM to seller. TYPES: European (exercise only on expiry), American (any time up to expiry). IN-THE-MONEY (ITM), AT-THE-MONEY (ATM), OUT-OF-THE-MONEY (OTM). The OPTIONS GREEKS: Delta (sensitivity to underlying), Gamma, Vega (volatility), Theta (time decay), Rho (interest rate). (IV) SWAPS — contracts to EXCHANGE future cash flows; INTEREST RATE SWAP (fixed for floating), CURRENCY SWAP, CREDIT DEFAULT SWAP (CDS — famously at centre of 2008 GFC). INDIAN DERIVATIVES MARKET: (a) Equity F&O introduced June 2000; NSE now the world's LARGEST derivatives exchange by volume (2022, overtook CME). (b) Currency F&O — USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR, JPY/INR. (c) Commodity exchanges: MCX (metals + energy — gold, silver, crude, natural gas), NCDEX (agri — wheat, soybean, cotton); regulated by SEBI since 2015 (earlier by FMC). (d) SEBI reforms 2024 — weekly expiries reduced to 1 per exchange per week to curb retail speculation. (e) 2024 DATA: retail F&O traders LOST ₹1.8 lakh crore cumulatively over 3 years (SEBI study). (f) STT (Securities Transaction Tax) on F&O. LEVERAGE — derivatives allow control of large positions with small margin; hence high gain potential but equally high loss potential. Famous derivative disasters: Barings Bank (Nick Leeson, 1995), LTCM (1998), Lehman Brothers (2008), Archegos (2021). value fluctuates based on underlying's price; used for hedging, speculation, arbitrage; stock, index, commodity, currency, bond, interest rate.
