cards.front:
The ABBREVIATION ‘P/E’ (as in ‘this stock has a P/E of 25’) stands for:

(A) Price-to-Employees ratio
(B) PRICE-to-EARNINGS ratio
(C) Profit-to-Equity ratio
(D) Performance-to-Expectation index
cards.back:
(B) PRICE-to-EARNINGS ratio

Inflation & Markets — PRICE-TO-EARNINGS RATIO (P/E or PE ratio) — one of the most widely used STOCK VALUATION metrics. Formula: P/E = CURRENT SHARE PRICE / EPS (Earnings Per Share). EPS = Net Profit / No. of outstanding shares. Interpretation: (a) P/E = 25 means investors are paying ₹25 for every ₹1 of annual earnings the company generates; (b) equivalently, at current earnings, it would take 25 years for the company to ‘earn back’ the purchase price; (c) HIGH P/E (say 40-50+) — expensive vs earnings; may indicate GROWTH expectations (market expects future earnings to explode); or OVER-VALUATION; (d) LOW P/E (say 8-10) — cheap; UNDER-VALUATION, OR slow-growth/risky company; (e) NEGATIVE P/E — company has losses. USE: (i) COMPARE a stock to its PEERS within the same sector (Banking stocks typically trade at lower P/E than IT/Pharma); (ii) compare with HISTORICAL AVERAGE P/E of the same stock; (iii) compare with the INDEX P/E (Nifty 50's long-run average P/E ~20-22; if above 28 seen as expensive). TYPES: (A) TRAILING P/E — uses past 12 months actual EPS; (B) FORWARD P/E — uses estimated next-year EPS; (C) SHILLER P/E (CAPE) — cyclically adjusted, uses 10-year average inflation-adjusted earnings — popular for long-term macro valuation. OTHER key FINANCIAL RATIOS for investors: (1) P/B (Price-to-Book) — share price / book value per share; for banks this is often more used than P/E; <1 = potentially undervalued; (2) DIVIDEND YIELD = DPS / share price (%); (3) ROE (Return on Equity) = Net Profit / Shareholders' Equity; measures profitability on investor capital; >15% = good; (4) ROCE (Return on Capital Employed); (5) EV/EBITDA — Enterprise Value / Earnings Before Interest-Tax-Depreciation-Amortisation; for capital-intensive companies; (6) DEBT-TO-EQUITY — borrowings / equity; high = risky; (7) CURRENT RATIO — short-term assets/liabilities, liquidity; (8) QUICK RATIO — excludes inventory; (9) INTEREST COVERAGE — EBIT/Interest expense. PEG RATIO (P/E divided by annual earnings growth %): <1 = fair; 1-2 = okay; >2 = expensive. Peter Lynch popularised it. MARKET CAP = share price × total shares; categories: LARGE (top 100 in India ~>₹20,000 cr), MID (101-250), SMALL (beyond). market price per share ÷ earnings per share (EPS); indicates how many years of earnings investors are willing to pay for the stock; high P/E = growth expectation or over-valuation.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the OLDEST stock exchange in Asia?

(A) NSE (1992)
(B) BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange) — founded 1875 as ‘The Native Share & Stock Brokers' Association’ under a banyan tree on Dalal Street, Mumbai; Asia's OLDEST
(C) Tokyo Stock Exchange
(D) Hong Kong Stock Exchange
cards.back:
(B) BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange) — founded 1875 as ‘The Native Share & Stock Brokers' Association’ under a banyan tree on Dalal Street, Mumbai; Asia's OLDEST

Inflation & Markets — BSE (BOMBAY STOCK EXCHANGE) — ASIA'S OLDEST stock exchange; located at DALAL STREET, MUMBAI. HISTORY: (1) Founded in 1875 by PREMCHAND ROYCHAND and 21 others as ‘THE NATIVE SHARE AND STOCK BROKERS' ASSOCIATION’; initial gatherings were under a BANYAN TREE opposite Mumbai's Town Hall (later at Dalal Street). (2) Recognised under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 — became India's FIRST exchange to be granted permanent recognition by the GoI. (3) Corporatised and demutualised in 2005 (Demutualisation Scheme). (4) Listed on itself in 2017. CURRENT FACTS: ~5,300 listed companies (most of any exchange globally), market cap > $5 trillion. CEO: Sundararaman Ramamurthy. Trading platform: BOLT (BSE on-Line Trading, now BOLT Plus and new-gen). SENSEX is BSE's flagship index. BSE has also launched: INDIA INX (India International Exchange) at GIFT City, Gujarat (2017) — India’s first international financial services exchange. NSE (NATIONAL STOCK EXCHANGE) — India's larger and technologically more advanced exchange. FOUNDED: 1992 (under HARSHAD MEHTA scam aftermath — replacing open outcry with electronic trading); commenced operations 1994. INITIATIVES: (a) first to introduce SCREEN-BASED, ORDER-DRIVEN, anonymous trading (NEAT — National Exchange for Automated Trading) — revolutionised Indian markets; (b) first to launch DERIVATIVES in India (2000); (c) introduced NIFTY 50 in 1996; (d) NSE-promoted: NSDL (depository), NSCCL (clearing), NSE IFSC (GIFT IFSC, 2017). NSE holds ~93% market share of equity cash volumes in India, and is the WORLD'S LARGEST derivatives exchange by contracts traded (2022 onwards, overtook CME Group). NSE IPO: planned but delayed due to SEBI disputes (co-location scandal resolved 2023); expected 2026. OTHER EXCHANGES GLOBALLY: NYSE (New York, 1792 — founded under ‘Buttonwood Tree’ agreement, oldest in world), LSE (London, 1698), Tokyo (1878), Shanghai (1866, re-opened 1990), Hong Kong (1891), Nasdaq (1971, world’s first electronic exchange), Euronext (Paris-Amsterdam-Brussels merger). By MARKET CAP: NYSE (~$27T) > Nasdaq ($24T) > Shanghai, Tokyo, Euronext, HKEX, NSE India (~$4-5T, rising). In 2024, India briefly overtook HK to become 4th-largest market by cap.

cards.front:
BONDS (G-Secs, corporate bonds) are DEBT securities that REPRESENT:

(A) Ownership stake in a company
(B) A LOAN given BY the investor TO the issuer
(C) A derivative contract
(D) Units of a mutual fund
cards.back:
(B) A LOAN given BY the investor TO the issuer

Inflation & Markets — BONDS — DEBT SECURITIES that represent a LOAN from an investor to a borrower (government, company, or municipality). The issuer agrees to: (a) pay PERIODIC INTEREST (‘coupon’) — usually semi-annually or annually; (b) return the PRINCIPAL (‘face value’/‘par value’) at MATURITY. Bonds are ‘FIXED-INCOME securities’. Unlike stocks (EQUITY — ownership stake), bondholders are LENDERS, NOT owners; they get priority over equity in case of liquidation. KEY BOND TERMS: (1) FACE VALUE (par) — principal to be repaid (often ₹1,000 or ₹10,000 in India); (2) COUPON — stated interest rate; (3) MATURITY — date of principal repayment; (4) YIELD TO MATURITY (YTM) — total return if held to maturity (incorporates coupon + price gap vs face); (5) CREDIT RATING — AAA (highest), AA, A, BBB (investment grade) ... D (default). Rated by CRAs: CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, India Ratings (S&P, Moody's, Fitch globally). TYPES of bonds: (I) BY ISSUER: (a) SOVEREIGN / G-SECS — issued by Govt of India (via RBI); considered risk-free; T-bills (up to 1 year), Dated G-Secs (up to 40 years); regulated by RBI; traded on NDS-OM platform; cut-offs auctioned weekly. (b) STATE DEVELOPMENT LOANS (SDLs) — state govt bonds. (c) PSU BONDS — e.g., REC, PFC, HUDCO. (d) CORPORATE BONDS — private/listed firms. (e) MUNICIPAL BONDS — city governments. (II) BY FEATURE: ZERO-COUPON (no interim coupon, sold at discount); CALLABLE (issuer can redeem early); PUTTABLE (holder can redeem); CONVERTIBLE (can convert to equity — FCCB Foreign Currency Convertible, Optionally Convertible Debentures); PERPETUAL / AT-1 bonds (no maturity, Basel III bank tier-1 capital); GREEN bonds (funds environmental projects); SOCIAL bonds; SDG-linked; MASALA BONDS (rupee-denominated offshore bonds). INVERSE PRICE-YIELD: BOND prices move OPPOSITE to interest rates. When RBI raises rates, bond prices FALL (old bonds' fixed coupon less attractive); when rates fall, prices RISE. DURATION measures price sensitivity to rate changes. INDIAN BOND MARKET: (a) G-Secs market is well-developed, ~₹170 lakh crore outstanding; (b) Corporate bond market small (~₹45 lakh crore) but growing post-Ratan Tata Committee + SEBI reforms; (c) RBI RETAIL DIRECT (2021) — allows retail investors to buy G-Secs directly; (d) Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs, started 2015) — gold-denominated; 2.5% coupon; 8-year tenure; tax-free LTCG at maturity; paused in 2024-25 amid high gold prices; (e) JP Morgan + Bloomberg index INCLUSION of Indian G-Secs (June 2024) brings $25-40 billion inflows over 18 months. Taxation: interest on bonds taxed at slab rate; sovereign gold bonds tax-free at maturity. issuer pays periodic COUPON (interest) + returns PRINCIPAL at maturity; lower risk than equity; regulated by SEBI (corporate bonds) + RBI (G-Secs); government or company.

cards.front:
FIRST FIVE YEAR PLAN of India (1951-56) gave priority to:

(A) Agriculture + irrigation (Harrod-Domar model)
(B) Heavy industries (Mahalanobis model later)
(C) IT + services sector (came much later)
(D) Defence + nuclear programme alone
cards.back:
(A) Agriculture + irrigation (Harrod-Domar model)

Planning & Poverty — FIRST PLAN (1951-56) — focused on AGRICULTURE + IRRIGATION + power (recovery from Partition + Bengal famine 1943). Based on HARROD-DOMAR growth model (savings → investment → output → growth). Targets: ~2.1% GDP growth (achieved 3.6%, exceeded target). KEY PROJECTS: Bhakra-Nangal (Punjab), Hirakud (Odisha), Damodar Valley Corp (DVC, WB-Jharkhand). 2nd PLAN (1956-61) — MAHALANOBIS MODEL — heavy industry focus (steel, machine tools, electricity). cards.front:
GREEN REVOLUTION in India (1960s-70s) is primarily associated with:

(A) M.S. Swaminathan (father of GR in India)
(B) Verghese Kurien (White Revolution dairy)
(C) Hargobind Khorana (genetics, Nobel)
(D) C.N.R. Rao (chemistry, Bharat Ratna)
cards.back:
(A) M.S. Swaminathan (father of GR in India)

Planning & Poverty — GREEN REVOLUTION (1960s-70s) — dramatic increase in food grain output. Pioneered globally by NORMAN BORLAUG (American agronomist, Nobel Peace 1970, dwarf wheat varieties); brought to INDIA by M.S. SWAMINATHAN (father of Green Revolution in India; Bharat Ratna 2024 posthumous). KEY ELEMENTS: HYV seeds (high-yield variety, Mexican wheat + IRRI rice), CHEMICAL FERTILIZERS, IRRIGATION, mechanisation (tractors, threshers). FOCUS STATES: Punjab, Haryana, Western UP — mostly wheat; later rice in Andhra, TN. RESULT: India self-sufficient in grain by mid-1970s; PL 480 wheat imports from USA stopped. WHITE REVOLUTION = MILK production (Verghese Kurien, AMUL, Operation Flood, ~1970+). BLUE = fish; YELLOW = oilseed; PINK = onion; SILVER = poultry/eggs.

(A) Heavy industry + capital goods first
(B) Agriculture + small-scale only
(C) Services sector exports primarily
(D) Foreign direct investment as priority
cards.back:
(A) Heavy industry + capital goods first

Planning & Poverty — P.C. MAHALANOBIS — Indian statistician, founder of INDIAN STATISTICAL INSTITUTE (ISI, 1931). Designed 2ND PLAN (1956-61). Logic: build CAPITAL GOODS (machines that make machines) first → enables faster long-term growth than starting with consumer goods. Inspired by Soviet planning (Feldman model). PHASE 1: heavy + machine-building industry. PHASE 2: consumer goods. CRITICISM: ignored demand-side, agricultural neglect, foreign exchange shortage. INDIA's stable BUT slow 'HINDU RATE OF GROWTH' (~3.5% annual, 1950-80) often blamed on this. PROFESSIONALLY he's known for MAHALANOBIS DISTANCE (statistics). 'PLANNED ECONOMY' phase ended ~1991 with LPG reforms. POLICY trade-off question: should developing economies focus on heavy industry first or agri/services? — debated still.

cards.front:
PLAN HOLIDAY (1966-69) — period when normal Five-Year Plans were SUSPENDED — was due to:

(A) 1965 Indo-Pak war + drought + economic crisis
(B) Indira Gandhi's 1975 Emergency declared
(C) 1991 BoP crisis when reserves crashed
(D) Demonetisation of currency in 2016
cards.back:
(A) 1965 Indo-Pak war + drought + economic crisis

Planning & Poverty — PLAN HOLIDAY (1966-1969) — three ANNUAL PLANS replaced 4th FYP. CAUSES: (1) 1965 INDO-PAK WAR (drained resources); (2) successive DROUGHTS (1965, 1966) → near-famine; (3) DEVALUATION OF RUPEE (June 1966, INR/$ from 4.76 to 7.50 — 36% devaluation, controversial); (4) PL 480 wheat imports from USA → political dependency under LBJ's 'short-tether' policy. 4th PLAN (1969-74) under Indira → focus on POVERTY ALLEVIATION + self-reliance. 'GARIBI HATAO' (1971 Indira election slogan). Other notable plan disruptions: ROLLING PLAN (1978-80) under Janata govt (1979-80 Annual Plan). PLAN ALMOST TERMINATED 1990 (BoP crisis); 9th Plan (1997-2002) only after delay.

(B) Self-reliance + heavy industry only

(D) Defence-only spending without anything else
cards.back:

(B) MONTHLY PER CAPITA CONSUMPTION EXPENDITURE
(C) Only land holding
(D) Caste alone
cards.back:
(B) MONTHLY PER CAPITA CONSUMPTION EXPENDITURE

Planning & Poverty — INDIA's POVERTY MEASUREMENT — multiple approaches over years. (1) DANDEKAR + RATH (1971) — first study; defined poverty based on calorie intake (2,250 kcal/day rural + urban), expenditure terms. (2) TASK FORCE (Planning Commission 1979) — calorie norms revised: 2,400 kcal RURAL + 2,100 kcal URBAN. (3) LAKDAWALA COMMITTEE (1993) — CPI deflators by state; retained calorie norms. (4) TENDULKAR COMMITTEE (2009, Chair Suresh Tendulkar) — dropped calorie link; ALL-INDIA POVERTY LINE based on MPCE (Monthly Per Capita Consumption Expenditure) @ 2011-12 prices: ₹816 rural + ₹1000 urban per month (~₹27 rural, ₹33 urban per DAY). Broader consumption basket. Used till 2015. 21.9% poverty in 2011-12 (PC 27% rural, 13.7% urban). (5) RANGARAJAN COMMITTEE (2014) — widened poverty line: ₹972 rural + ₹1407 urban (2011-12). 29.5% poverty in 2011-12. But GOVT never formally adopted Rangarajan; Tendulkar still official. (6) NO NEW OFFICIAL LINE since 2011-12 NSSO consumer expenditure survey data; 2017-18 survey SUPPRESSED by govt citing quality issues. 2022-23 HCES (Household Consumption Expenditure Survey) released Feb 2024 + Aug 2024 (full). MULTIDIMENSIONAL POVERTY INDEX (MPI) — developed by OPHI (Oxford Poverty + Human Development Initiative) + UNDP. India uses NITI Aayog's national MPI (since 2021). COVERS 12 INDICATORS across 3 DIMENSIONS: (a) HEALTH (3 indicators: nutrition, child + adolescent mortality, maternal health). (b) EDUCATION (2: years of schooling, school attendance). (c) STANDARD OF LIVING (7: cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account). Deprivation in 1/3 of weighted indicators = MULTIDIMENSIONALLY POOR. India's MPI HEADCOUNT: (a) 2015-16 = 24.85% (NFHS-4). (b) 2019-21 = 14.96% (NFHS-5). 13.5 CRORE Indians lifted out of multi-dim poverty in 5 years. Latest NITI Aayog estimate Jan 2024: 11.28% MPI poor (2022-23). Targets SDG 1 halving national poverty by 2030. GLOBAL COMPARISON (Global MPI UNDP): India still has LARGEST absolute number of poor (~230 million), but trajectory improving. WORLD BANK POVERTY LINES (global): (1) EXTREME poverty — $2.15/day (PPP, 2017 revision); India ~10% (2019-20 estimates). (2) Lower-middle income line — $3.65/day. (3) Upper-middle income — $6.85/day. India has risen from lower-middle to solidly middle-income trajectory. SCHEMES TO REDUCE POVERTY: (1) MGNREGA (2005). (2) PMAY — rural + urban housing. (3) PMJAY / Ayushman Bharat — health insurance ₹5 lakh cover. (4) PM-KISAN — ₹6000/yr farmer income support. (5) PM GARIB KALYAN ANNA YOJANA (GRATIS food 5kg/person/month post-COVID; extended 2023-28 for 80 crore). (6) Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile (JAM Trinity) — financial inclusion. (7) Targeted PDS (Public Distribution System; fair-price shops; 75 crore beneficiaries post-NFSA 2013). (8) NRLM (National Rural Livelihoods Mission — SHGs). (9) UJJWALA — free LPG. (10) JJM — piped water. (11) Swachh Bharat toilets. (12) Saubhagya — electricity. (13) ASPIRATIONAL DISTRICTS PROGRAMME (2018). (14) POSHAN ABHIYAAN (nutrition). India's POVERTY has declined from 40%+ (1990s) to sub-15% (2023) on consumption metric — BIGGEST POVERTY REDUCTION in human history (per World Bank data). ₹816 rural / ₹1000 urban (2011-12 prices); multidimensional metrics used by NITI Aayog since 2021.

cards.front:
PERIODIC LABOUR FORCE SURVEY (PLFS), which replaced NSSO employment-unemployment surveys in 2017, is conducted by:

(A) Reserve Bank of India
(B) NATIONAL STATISTICAL OFFICE (NSO) under MoSPI
(C) Labour Bureau
(D) Census Office
cards.back:
(B) NATIONAL STATISTICAL OFFICE (NSO) under MoSPI

Planning & Poverty — PERIODIC LABOUR FORCE SURVEY (PLFS) — India's primary labour force survey since 2017-18. Conducted by NATIONAL STATISTICAL OFFICE (NSO; formerly NSSO — merged with CSO in 2019 to form NSO) under MINISTRY OF STATISTICS + PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (MoSPI). REPLACED earlier NSSO quinquennial rounds (last 2011-12). FREQUENCY: (1) ANNUAL REPORTS (covering rural + urban). (2) QUARTERLY REPORTS (urban only). KEY METRICS: (1) LABOUR FORCE PARTICIPATION RATE (LFPR) — % of POPULATION aged 15+ who are either WORKING or SEEKING work. India 2022-23: ~57.9%; very LOW by global standards (~75% in China, 62% US, 66% UK). Especially low WOMEN LFPR (~37% India vs ~67% China, 56% US). Rising slightly. (2) WORKER POPULATION RATIO (WPR) — % of population aged 15+ who are employed. 2022-23: ~56.0%. (3) UNEMPLOYMENT RATE (UR) = (unemployed / labour force) × 100. 2022-23: ~3.2% overall; but YOUTH (15-29 yrs) UR ~10% (higher). URBAN UR (~5%) > RURAL UR (~2%). FEMALE UR historically higher but narrowing recently. MEASUREMENT approaches: (a) USUAL STATUS — employment status for previous 365 days. (b) CURRENT WEEKLY STATUS (CWS) — status in previous 7 days; more dynamic. PLFS reports both. NEW JOB INDICATORS: (1) FORMAL vs INFORMAL work — PLFS estimates ~85% of India's workforce is INFORMAL (no social security, contracts); only ~15% formal. EPFO (Employees Provident Fund Organisation) + ESIC (Employees' State Insurance Corporation) track formal sector — ~7-8 crore subscribers. (2) SELF-EMPLOYED (~55-58%) + CASUAL labourers (~23%) + REGULAR wage/salaried (~20%). (3) MSME sector employs ~110M; agri ~46% of workforce; services ~32%; industry ~22%. RECENT TRENDS: (1) COVID-19 shock 2020 — UR spiked to ~24% in April 2020 (CMIE data; PLFS less volatile) + quickly recovered. (2) Post-COVID AGRI employment rose (reverse migration during lockdown); since tapered. (3) FEMALE LFPR rose from 22% (2017-18) to 37% (2022-23) — partly due to unpaid domestic + subsistence work being recounted; partly real. (4) Youth unemployment particularly concerning — SKILL GAPS despite degrees. NEW LABOUR CODES: (1) CODE on WAGES 2019. (2) Industrial Relations Code 2020. (3) Social Security Code 2020. (4) Occupational Safety, Health + Working Conditions Code 2020. Amalgamate + modernise 29 old labour laws. Implementation in progress; Rules notified by states. Labour is CONCURRENT list subject. UNEMPLOYMENT TYPES: (1) FRICTIONAL — between jobs. (2) STRUCTURAL — skill mismatch. (3) CYCLICAL — recession-driven. (4) SEASONAL — agri, tourism. (5) DISGUISED — underemployment (too many on same work, common in agri). (6) EDUCATED unemployment — big India problem; degree without skills. Skill India Mission + PMKVY (PM Kaushal Vikas Yojana) + NSDC (National Skill Development Corporation) programmes. Also the MUDRA + Startup India to create jobs. CMIE (Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy) — private think tank; publishes monthly unemployment data; often differs from PLFS (CMIE typically higher). Two private indicators. AGRI → NON-AGRI transition slow in India; China shifted 60%+ in 30 years via manufacturing; India stuck in 'SERVICES-LED' model. annual reports + quarterly (urban); tracks LFPR, UR, WPR + gender-disaggregated data.

cards.front:
HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI), published annually by UNDP, measures:

(A) Military strength only
(B) LIFE EXPECTANCY + EDUCATION (mean + expected years of schooling) + GNI PER CAPITA (PPP); India ranked 134/193 in 2024 HDR
(C) Only GDP
(D) Population size
cards.back:
(B) LIFE EXPECTANCY + EDUCATION (mean + expected years of schooling) + GNI PER CAPITA (PPP); India ranked 134/193 in 2024 HDR

Planning & Poverty — HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI) — composite statistic of life EXPECTANCY + EDUCATION + PER-CAPITA INCOME; developed by MAHBUB UL HAQ (Pakistani economist) + AMARTYA SEN (Indian Nobel laureate) in 1990 for UNDP HUMAN DEVELOPMENT REPORT (HDR). PUBLISHED ANNUALLY by UNDP. ~190 countries ranked. FORMULA: HDI = geometric mean of 3 dimensional indices: (1) HEALTH — LIFE EXPECTANCY at birth (range 20-85 years). (2) EDUCATION — combines MEAN YEARS of SCHOOLING (adults 25+) + EXPECTED YEARS of schooling (children entering school). (3) INCOME — GNI per capita (in PPP $, natural log used). Normalised 0 to 1. Rankings: > 0.800 = VERY HIGH human development; 0.700-0.799 = HIGH; 0.550-0.699 = MEDIUM; < 0.550 = LOW. HDR 2024 (covering 2022 data, released March 2024): INDIA RANK 134 out of 193 countries with HDI 0.644 (MEDIUM). Previous 132 out of 191 (2021 data, 2022 report). China rank 75 (High, 0.788); Sri Lanka 78; Bangladesh 129; Bhutan 125; Nepal 143; Pakistan 164; Afghanistan 182. TOP: (1) Switzerland 0.967; (2) Norway 0.966; (3) Iceland 0.959; Denmark, Hong Kong, Sweden, Germany, Ireland, Singapore, Australia. BOTTOM: Somalia, South Sudan, CAR, Chad, Niger. INDIA's HDI HISTORY: 1990 = 0.434 → 2022 = 0.644. Steadily rising. Life expectancy rose from 58 → 67+ years; mean schooling 3 → 6.6 years. Better than most SAARC (except Sri Lanka which has long led human development in region). RELATED INDICES: (1) INEQUALITY-ADJUSTED HDI (IHDI) — HDI adjusted for inequality within country; India IHDI = 0.475 (rank drops). (2) GENDER DEVELOPMENT INDEX (GDI) — ratio of female HDI to male HDI; India = 0.852 (high gap). (3) GENDER INEQUALITY INDEX (GII) — India rank 108 in 2022 (out of 166); improvement needed. (4) MULTIDIMENSIONAL POVERTY INDEX (MPI) — India down from 24.85% (2015-16) to 14.96% (2019-21) per NITI Aayog + 11.28% (2022-23). OTHER KEY INTERNATIONAL INDICES: (1) GLOBAL HUNGER INDEX (GHI) — by Concern Worldwide + Welthungerhilfe; India rank 105/127 (2024) — SERIOUS; GoI criticises methodology. (2) WORLD HAPPINESS REPORT — India rank 126/143 in 2024 (declined); Finland #1 (7th yr); US at 23. (3) DEMOCRACY INDEX (EIU) — India 'flawed democracy' rank 41; Norway #1. (4) CORRUPTION PERCEPTIONS INDEX (CPI) by Transparency Intl — India rank 93 in 2023 (score 39/100). (5) GLOBAL INNOVATION INDEX (GII) — India rank 39/132 in 2024 (UP from 81 in 2015; major improvement). (6) EASE OF DOING BUSINESS (World Bank, discontinued 2021 after methodology scandal); revived as B-READY. (7) GENDER GAP INDEX (WEF) — India rank 129/146 in 2024. (8) GLOBAL FIREPOWER INDEX — India rank 4 military strength. (9) NYT's COUNTRY OF YEAR. (10) PRESS FREEDOM INDEX (RSF) — India rank 159/180 in 2024. (11) HUMAN CAPITAL INDEX (World Bank) — India 0.49. (12) PISA (OECD education) — India participated 2009 (Tamil Nadu + Himachal poor ranks); skipping since. India generally shows MIXED picture — economic rise but social indicators lagging; critical EDUCATIONAL + HEALTH investments needed. Medium category.

cards.front:
The GINI COEFFICIENT, measuring INCOME / WEALTH INEQUALITY, ranges from:

(A) -1 to +1
(B) 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality — one person has everything); India's income Gini ~0.35-0.40; wealth Gini ~0.83
(C) 0 to 100 only
(D) No fixed range
cards.back:
(B) 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality — one person has everything); India's income Gini ~0.35-0.40; wealth Gini ~0.83

Planning & Poverty — GINI COEFFICIENT — most common measure of INCOME + WEALTH INEQUALITY. Developed by Italian statistician CORRADO GINI in 1912 paper 'Variabilità e mutabilità'. RANGE: 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100 if expressed as percentage). (1) Gini = 0 → PERFECT EQUALITY (everyone has same income/wealth). (2) Gini = 1 → PERFECT INEQUALITY (one person has everything, others have nothing). DERIVED from LORENZ CURVE (plot of cumulative income share vs cumulative population share). Gini = area between Lorenz curve + line of equality (45° diagonal), divided by total area below 45° line. INCOME GINI (world): (1) MOST EQUAL — Slovakia 0.23, Slovenia 0.24, Czech Republic 0.25, Denmark, Norway, Netherlands — Nordic + European welfare states. (2) MOST UNEQUAL — South Africa 0.63 (worst among major economies), Namibia, Zambia, CAR, Brazil, Colombia. (3) INDIA income Gini ~0.35-0.38 (relatively modest — but rising). (4) CHINA ~0.46. (5) USA ~0.41. WEALTH GINI (typically much higher than income Gini): (1) INDIA ~0.83 (very high). (2) USA ~0.85. (3) Brazil, South Africa ~0.80-0.85. (4) Most equal — Japan, Scandinavia ~0.60. INDIA's INCOME + WEALTH INEQUALITY: (a) OXFAM 2024 report: TOP 1% of India owns ~40% of national wealth; BOTTOM 50% owns 3%. (b) Billionaire count — India has 185+ billionaires (3rd after US + China). (c) 'Inequality Inc.' report. (d) WORLD INEQUALITY DATABASE (Chancel + Piketty): India's top 1% income share 22% (2022 vs world 11%). (e) Wealth MUCH more concentrated — Ambani + Adani families alone own wealth equivalent to bottom ~10-15% of India's population. DEBATES: (a) POVERTY reduction + inequality rise can co-occur — absolute welfare improves for poor while top gains dominate growth; (b) Rural-urban + caste + gender dimensions of inequality in India; (c) Privatisation + automation may exacerbate. KUZNETS CURVE — Simon Kuznets 1955 hypothesis — inequality rises in early industrialisation, peaks, then falls as country becomes richer. India in rising phase; unclear if will peak + decline. OTHER inequality measures: (1) PALMA RATIO (income share top 10% / bottom 40%) — India ~1.4. (2) 20:20 ratio. (3) THEIL INDEX. (4) ATKINSON index. POLICIES to ADDRESS INEQUALITY: (a) PROGRESSIVE TAXATION (income tax slabs; luxury surcharge). (b) Wealth tax (India abolished 2015; debate continues); (c) INHERITANCE tax (India abolished 1985; Congress 2024 manifesto floated reintroducing; politically fraught). (d) SOCIAL SPENDING — health, education, sanitation, housing, food subsidies. India spends ~2% GDP on health, 3% on education (both below global norms ~6% each). (e) MGNREGA + minimum wages. (f) Direct Benefit Transfer schemes. (g) UNIVERSAL BASIC INCOME (proposed by Economic Survey 2017; Sikkim pilot). (h) Financial inclusion (Jan Dhan + Mudra). (i) Affirmative action — reservation for SC/ST/OBC. (j) Land reforms (pending in many states). (k) Regional balancing — Aspirational Districts Programme. India's challenges: informal labour, low tax-GDP (~12% vs OECD 34%); growing divergence between rich states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, TN, Karnataka) + poor (Bihar, UP, MP, Odisha). highly unequal.

DEBATES: (a) POVERTY reduction + inequality rise can co-occur — absolute welfare improves for poor while top gains dominate growth; (b) Rural-urban + caste + gender dimensions of inequality in India; (c) Privatisation + automation may exacerbate. KUZNETS CURVE — Simon Kuznets 1955 hypothesis — inequality rises in early industrialisation, peaks, then falls as country becomes richer. India in rising phase; unclear if will peak + decline. OTHER inequality measures: (1) PALMA RATIO (income share top 10% / bottom 40%) — India ~1.4. (2) 20:20 ratio. (3) THEIL INDEX. (4) ATKINSON index. POLICIES to ADDRESS INEQUALITY: (a) PROGRESSIVE TAXATION (income tax slabs; luxury surcharge). (b) Wealth tax (India abolished 2015; debate continues); (c) INHERITANCE tax (India abolished 1985; Congress 2024 manifesto floated reintroducing; politically fraught). (d) SOCIAL SPENDING — health, education, sanitation, housing, food subsidies. India spends ~2% GDP on health, 3% on education (both below global norms ~6% each). (e) MGNREGA + minimum wages. (f) Direct Benefit Transfer schemes. (g) UNIVERSAL BASIC INCOME (proposed by Economic Survey 2017; Sikkim pilot). (h) Financial inclusion (Jan Dhan + Mudra). (i) Affirmative action — reservation for SC/ST/OBC. (j) Land reforms (pending in many states). (k) Regional balancing — Aspirational Districts Programme. India's challenges: informal labour, low tax-GDP (~12% vs OECD 34%); growing divergence between rich states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, TN, Karnataka) + poor (Bihar, UP, MP, Odisha). highly unequal.

cards.front:
The NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY ACT (NFSA) 2013 provides subsidised food grains to approximately what fraction of India's population?

(A) 25%
(B) ~67%
(C) 10%
(D) 100%
cards.back:
(B) ~67%

Planning & Poverty — NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY ACT (NFSA) 2013 — landmark legislation enshrining FOOD SECURITY as a LEGAL RIGHT. Enacted 12 September 2013 under UPA-II. Aim: 'to provide for food + nutritional security in human life cycle approach, by ensuring access to adequate quantity of quality food at affordable prices'. COVERAGE: UP TO 75% of RURAL + 50% of URBAN population = ~67% overall = ~81.35 CRORE people (out of then 121 cr); currently ~80 cr after Census 2011 base used (needs update post-2021 Census when held). BENEFITS: (1) PRIORITY HOUSEHOLDS (PHH) — 5 KG/PERSON/MONTH of food grains at ISSUE PRICES: ₹3/kg rice, ₹2/kg wheat, ₹1/kg coarse grains. 75% of NFSA beneficiaries are PHH. (2) ANTYODAYA ANNA YOJANA (AAY) — 'poorest of poor' category — 35 kg PER HOUSEHOLD PER MONTH (not per person) at same prices; ~2.3 crore AAY households. (3) MATERNITY — pregnant women + lactating mothers ₹6,000 maternity benefit (PM Matru Vandana Yojana) + take-home rations (1 kg/month) + one hot cooked meal at Anganwadi. (4) CHILDREN — 6 mo to 6 yrs — hot cooked meal/take-home rations at Anganwadi (Integrated Child Development Services, ICDS). Children 6-14 — mid-day meal in schools (PM POSHAN, est 1995; renamed 2021). ELIGIBILITY: States/UTs identify beneficiaries using SECC (Socio-Economic Caste Census) 2011 data + other criteria; cap on eligible population fixed. RATION CARDS updated; BPL / APL distinction obsoleted. IMPLEMENTATION: (1) FAIR PRICE SHOPS (FPS) — ~5.4 LAKH across India; mostly Panchayat/cooperative run. (2) FOOD CORPORATION OF INDIA (FCI, est 1965) — procures, stores, distributes; buffer stocks. (3) CMRs (central pool) + state pools. (4) Food grain procured via MSP at ~23 crops. COSTS: Centre bears ~₹2.1 lakh crore annually for food subsidy (largest budget item after defence + interest + transfer to states). PM GARIB KALYAN ANNA YOJANA (PMGKAY) — launched March 2020 during COVID; ADDITIONAL 5 kg food grains FREE per person over + above NFSA. Continued + extended; now MERGED into NFSA since Jan 2023 — i.e., NFSA allocation FREE (₹0 instead of ₹1-3/kg) till Dec 2028 (5-year extension announced by PM Nov 2023). 81 crore beneficiaries get FREE food grains. ONE NATION ONE RATION CARD (ONORC) — launched 2020; portable ration cards; beneficiaries can access grains anywhere in India via biometric authentication. 100% implementation achieved 2022. Benefits migrants esp. ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) India has been FOOD SURPLUS nation since mid-1970s (Green Revolution). (2) Hunger headcount way down. (3) Maternal + child nutrition improved (but still concerns — stunting 35%, wasting 19% per NFHS-5). CRITIQUES: (1) LEAKAGES — 25-35% historically (reduced with Aadhaar seeding + ePoS machines). (2) INCLUSION / EXCLUSION errors. (3) FISCAL burden high. (4) URBAN poor often excluded. (5) 'Pulses + oils' not covered (only cereals). (6) Inactivity about QUALITY + nutritional adequacy. GLOBAL HUNGER INDEX places India poorly (105/127 in 2024 — 'serious'); GoI disputes methodology. FORTIFICATION: rice fortification under NFSA/PDS (iron + folate + B12) rolled out nationwide by 2024. MILLETS included in NFSA as coarse grains. 75% rural + 50% urban; ~81 crore people eligible; 5 kg/person/month at ₹1/2/3/kg (coarse grains/wheat/rice); world's largest food security programme.

cards.front:
The SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (SDGs) consist of how many goals, set for achievement by 2030?

(A) 10
(B) 17 GOALS + 169 TARGETS + 232 indicators
(C) 100
(D) 5
cards.back:
(B) 17 GOALS + 169 TARGETS + 232 indicators

Planning & Poverty — SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (SDGs) / 'AGENDA 2030' — 17 INTEGRATED GOALS + 169 TARGETS + 232 indicators, adopted by UN General Assembly on 25 SEPTEMBER 2015 in New York. Timeline: 2016-2030. Replaced MDGs (Millennium Development Goals, 2000-2015 — had 8 goals). ALL 193 UN member states signed. 17 SDGs: (1) NO POVERTY — end all forms globally. (2) ZERO HUNGER. (3) GOOD HEALTH + WELL-BEING. (4) QUALITY EDUCATION — inclusive + equitable. (5) GENDER EQUALITY. (6) CLEAN WATER + SANITATION. (7) AFFORDABLE + CLEAN ENERGY. (8) DECENT WORK + ECONOMIC GROWTH. (9) INDUSTRY, INNOVATION + INFRASTRUCTURE. (10) REDUCED INEQUALITIES — within + between countries. (11) SUSTAINABLE CITIES + COMMUNITIES. (12) RESPONSIBLE CONSUMPTION + PRODUCTION. (13) CLIMATE ACTION. (14) LIFE BELOW WATER (oceans, seas, marine). (15) LIFE ON LAND (terrestrial ecosystems, forests, biodiversity). (16) PEACE, JUSTICE + STRONG INSTITUTIONS. (17) PARTNERSHIPS for the GOALS. Characterised by 'LEAVING NO ONE BEHIND' principle. Universal — applies to ALL countries (developed + developing), unlike MDGs focused on developing. KEY FEATURES: integrated + interconnected; evidence-based; multi-stakeholder (govt + private + civil society + academia). TRACKING: UN Global Monitoring via SDG Indicators Database; annual VOLUNTARY NATIONAL REVIEWS (VNRs) at UN High-Level Political Forum (HLPF). SDG PROGRESS (2024): world LAGGING on most goals; COVID-19 set back progress. Only 17% of targets on track. Climate action + inequality + biodiversity particularly off-track. INDIA + SDGs: (1) NITI AAYOG is nodal agency; tracks via SDG INDIA INDEX (annual since 2018, 5 editions by 2024). (2) LOCALIZATION — state + district-level SDG integration; SDG Cell in every state. (3) 2023-24 SDG India Index: Kerala + Tamil Nadu lead (72 + 71 scores); Bihar + Jharkhand lag (52 + 56). Overall 71/100 for India (Performer category). (4) INDIA's NDC + Panchamrit aligns with SDG 13. (5) Ayushman Bharat + NFSA + MGNREGA + Swachh Bharat align with multiple SDGs. SDG CHALLENGES for INDIA: (a) POVERTY reduction (SDG 1) — achieving with MPI dropping. (b) Hunger (SDG 2) — still major; stunting 35%. (c) Gender equality (SDG 5) — LFPR gap, safety, education gap. (d) Inequality (SDG 10) — rising. (e) Climate (SDG 13) — coal phase-down slow. (f) Biodiversity (SDG 14 + 15) — habitat loss. MDGs (2000-2015): 8 goals — (1) Extreme poverty; (2) Universal primary education; (3) Gender equality; (4) Child mortality; (5) Maternal health; (6) HIV/AIDS, malaria; (7) Environmental sustainability; (8) Global partnership. Mixed but substantial success globally — extreme poverty halved, child mortality down 50%, HIV down; education gains. SDGs DIFFERENCES from MDGs: (a) more numerous + integrated; (b) universal (all countries); (c) covers inequality, climate, cities, oceans (new); (d) includes peace + governance; (e) embraces multi-stakeholder partnership model. POST-2030 discussions already starting — 'Beyond 2030' agenda. Global South concerns: financing gap ($4-7 trillion/year needed vs actual flows), developed country commitment shortfalls, climate finance $100 bn pledge met late + inadequate. UN SDG Summit 2023 midpoint review called for ACCELERATED action.

cards.front:
The 'INDIA'S CHILD STUNTING RATE' according to NFHS-5 (2019-21) is:

(A) Below 10%
(B) ~35.5% of under-5 children
(C) 80%
(D) ~1%
cards.back:
(B) ~35.5% of under-5 children

Planning & Poverty — CHILD MALNUTRITION indicators in INDIA (per NFHS-5, National Family Health Survey 2019-21, latest published; NFHS-6 fieldwork underway). (1) STUNTING (LOW HEIGHT-FOR-AGE) = chronic undernutrition: 35.5% of under-5 children stunted (NFHS-5); down from 38.4% (NFHS-4, 2015-16); BIG decline from 48% (NFHS-3, 2005-06) + 52% (NFHS-2, 1998-99). But STILL HIGH by global norms (Africa ~30%, China ~7%). (2) WASTING (LOW WEIGHT-FOR-HEIGHT) = acute undernutrition: 19.3%. (3) SEVERE WASTING: 7.7% (up from 7.5% NFHS-4 — DID NOT IMPROVE; a concern). (4) UNDERWEIGHT (low weight-for-age): 32.1% (vs 35.8% NFHS-4). Overall ~1/3 children chronically undernourished — alarming for a rising economy. GLOBAL HUNGER INDEX 2024: India 105/127 — 'SERIOUS' hunger. GoI disputes methodology. NUTRITION ISSUES: (a) iron-deficiency ANAEMIA — 67% under-5 children, 57% women 15-49, 25% men; MASSIVE burden. (b) Vitamin A, B12, D deficiencies common. (c) STUNTING linked to first 1000 DAYS (conception to 2 years) — irreversible impact on cognitive + physical development. Long-term economic cost: ~2-3% of GDP from lost productivity. GOVT SCHEMES: (1) INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS, 1975) — 14 LAKH Anganwadis (world's largest child nutrition programme); hot cooked meal + take-home rations + preschool + health checkups + immunisation; 8.8 CRORE children covered. (2) MID-DAY MEAL / PM POSHAN (1995, renamed 2021) — free cooked midday meal for Classes 1-8 in govt + aided schools; 11.8 CRORE children covered. TN pioneered (Kamaraj 1956, then MGR expanded 1982). (3) POSHAN ABHIYAAN (National Nutrition Mission, 2018) — 'Nutrition Mission'; aims at reducing stunting by 6% + underweight by 6% by 2022 (targets extended). Integrated approach: ICDS + POSHAN Tracker app + Village Health + Nutrition Days + behaviour change. (4) NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY ACT 2013 — ensures entitlement to food. (5) RAJMATA JIJAU MOTHER-CHILD HEALTH + NUTRITION MISSION (Maharashtra). (6) MAMATA SCHEME (Odisha), Anna Amrutham (Telangana) — state variants. (7) PM MATRU VANDANA YOJANA (PMMVY, 2017) — ₹5,000 maternity benefit for first child + ₹6,000 additional under JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana). (8) ANAEMIA MUKT BHARAT (2018) — iron-folic acid supplementation for 6-groups (kids, adolescents, pregnant, lactating, WRA, men); 6×6×6 strategy. (9) RICE FORTIFICATION in PDS (iron, B12, folate) — rolled out 2022-24. (10) SUPER 75% beneficiaries. GLOBAL benchmarks: WHO 2025 targets = 40% REDUCTION in stunting; India unlikely to meet. India's MATERNAL MORTALITY RATIO (MMR): NFHS-5 — 97/1,00,000 (down from 130 in 2014-16; down from 556 in 1990) — remarkable progress; SDG target 70 by 2030. Kerala has lowest MMR (19); Assam highest (205). IMR (Infant Mortality Rate): 35 per 1000 live births (down from 78 in 1990; 2030 target 12). U5MR: 42 (down from 125). LIFE EXPECTANCY at birth: 70 years (2022, up from 60 in 1990). Major gains but gaps persist. NUTRITION-economic growth PARADOX of India = much-debated (contrast China which reduced stunting from 34% → 7% over same period). still high; down from 38.4% in NFHS-4 (2015-16); reflects chronic undernutrition; stuck despite economic growth.

cards.front:
India's POPULATION overtook China in:

(A) 2010
(B) April 2023
(C) Never
(D) 1991
cards.back:
(B) April 2023

Planning & Poverty — INDIA's POPULATION surpassed CHINA's in APRIL 2023 per UN Department of Economic + Social Affairs (UN DESA) estimates — India became the WORLD's MOST POPULOUS COUNTRY. CURRENT (mid-2024): India ~144 crore (1.44 billion); China ~141 crore (1.41 billion, DECLINING); World ~810 crore (8.1 billion, Nov 2022 milestone). India hosts 17.5% of humanity on 2.4% of land area. INDIA's POPULATION HISTORY (Census data): (a) 1901 — 23.8 crore. (b) 1951 (first post-independence census) — 36.1 cr. (c) 1981 — 68.3 cr. (d) 2001 — 102.9 cr (crossed 100 cr). (e) 2011 — 121 cr (LAST CENSUS CONDUCTED). 2021 CENSUS POSTPONED due to COVID + delay continues (pending 2025-26 or later); unprecedented. POPULATION GROWTH RATE: declining dramatically — 2.15% (1981-91) → 1.97% (1991-2001) → 1.64% (2001-11) → now ~1% or less. TOTAL FERTILITY RATE (TFR) — children per woman: (a) 1951: ~6.0; (b) 1991: ~3.8; (c) 2011: ~2.4; (d) NFHS-5 (2019-21): 2.0 — BELOW REPLACEMENT LEVEL (2.1) for first time. Urban TFR 1.6; rural 2.1. STATE-WISE TFR: Sikkim 1.1 (lowest), Goa 1.3, Andaman 1.3, J&K 1.4, Kerala 1.7, TN 1.8, Delhi 1.6, Maharashtra 1.7. HIGH TFR: Bihar 3.0, Meghalaya 2.9, UP 2.4, Jharkhand 2.3, Rajasthan 2.0, MP 2.0. SOUTH + WEST + NE below replacement; NORTH still higher. DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND: India's median age ~28 years; 65% of pop under 35; massive WORKING-AGE population (15-59) — ~62% of total. Advantage for economic growth IF adequate jobs + skills + education. Expected to last 2055-60 before aging begins. CHINA DECLINE: TFR crashed to 1.0 (2023); started declining 2022; Communist Party's 1-Child Policy (1979-2015) aggressive effect now evident. Population to drop to 1 bn by 2080. Many Chinese elderly, labour shortages, care crisis looming. ASIAN TIGERS (Japan, S Korea, Taiwan) similar. INDIA's DEMOGRAPHIC STRUCTURE (2023 estimates): (a) 0-14: 24.9%; (b) 15-64: 68.3%; (c) 65+: 6.8% (growing fast). SEX RATIO (females per 1000 males): (a) 2011 Census: 943 (overall), 919 (child sex ratio 0-6 — decline from 927 in 2001; concerning). (b) NFHS-5: 1,020 (overall, FIRST TIME over 1000 in India's history) + 929 (child sex ratio). (c) Kerala best (1,084); Haryana worst (879). SEX-SELECTIVE ABORTION issue — PC-PNDT Act 1994 (Pre-Conception + Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act) bans sex determination + selective abortion — stringent enforcement. URBANISATION: ~35% URBAN (Census 2011 + projections) vs China's 65% + world avg 55%. Slow urbanisation due to migration flows, push + pull, land laws. STATES by population (2011): (1) UP 199.8M (16.5%, if state = country = 5th largest); (2) Maharashtra 112M; (3) Bihar 104M; (4) WB 91M; (5) MP 72.6M; (6) TN 72M; (7) Rajasthan 68M; (8) Karnataka 61M; (9) Gujarat 60M; (10) AP (undivided) 84M (now AP 50 + Telangana 35). India's + Pakistan's combined population ~166 crore > China's 141 crore. ACTUAL DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND capture demands: EMPLOYMENT generation, SKILLS, education, health, women's participation, urbanisation — India's CHALLENGES. AGEING will be a reality post-2050 — health care systems, pensions, elderly care need preparation. 142.8 crore India vs 142.6 crore China; India is world's MOST POPULOUS country; 17.5% of humanity on 2.4% of land; per UN estimates.

cards.front:
The FIRST FIVE-YEAR PLAN of India (1951-56) was based on the:

(A) Mahalanobis model
(B) HARROD-DOMAR MODEL
(C) Gandhian model
(D) Nehruvian only
cards.back:
(B) HARROD-DOMAR MODEL

Planning & Poverty — FIRST FIVE-YEAR PLAN of INDIA (1951-56) — first of 12 Five-Year Plans. Launched by PM Jawaharlal Nehru; based on HARROD-DOMAR MODEL (British + American economists' work; focused on SAVINGS + CAPITAL accumulation for growth). FOCUS: AGRICULTURE + IRRIGATION + POWER — critical after Partition (which had put India's food-surplus areas in Pakistan) + famines + refugee crisis. MAJOR PROJECTS + ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) BHAKRA NANGAL DAM (Punjab/HP) — inaugurated 1963 but work in 1st plan; Nehru's 'TEMPLES OF MODERN INDIA'; irrigates 1M hectares of Punjab/Haryana/Rajasthan. (2) HIRAKUD DAM (Odisha, Mahanadi) — world's longest earthen dam; commissioned 1957. (3) DAMODAR VALLEY CORP (DVC 1948) — multi-purpose projects. (4) Community Development Programme 1952 (2 Oct — birthday of Gandhi). (5) National Extension Service 1953. (6) UGC (University Grants Commission) 1953. (7) Five STEEL PLANTS planned (Bhilai + Rourkela + Durgapur realised later). (8) Delhi → Chandigarh as Punjab capital (post 1947 partition, Lahore was lost). GROWTH TARGET 2.1% achieved 3.6% — unexpectedly good. 12 FIVE-YEAR PLANS (1951-2017): (1) 1st 1951-56 (Harrod-Domar, agri + irrigation focus; 3.6% growth). (2) 2nd 1956-61 (MAHALANOBIS MODEL — heavy industry; PSUs born — Steel Authority + BHEL + ONGC + Indian Oil all in this era; Bhilai + Rourkela + Durgapur steel plants; 4.1% growth vs 4.5% target). (3) 3rd 1961-66 (self-sustaining growth; FAILED due to Indo-China War 1962 + 1965 Indo-Pak + severe droughts 1965-66; only 2.4% vs 5.6% target). Three ANNUAL PLANS 1966-69 ('PLAN HOLIDAY'). (4) 4th 1969-74 — Indira's 'GARIBI HATAO'; Bank Nationalisation 1969; BANGLADESH WAR 1971; Green Revolution intensified; 3.3% vs 5.7%. (5) 5th 1974-79 — Emergency era; Minimum Needs Programme; TRUNCATED by Janata Party Govt 1978 for new 'Rolling Plan'. (6) ROLLING PLANS (1978-80, Janata). (7) 6th 1980-85 — Indira returned; IRDP; NREGP (Rural Employment Guarantee predecessor); growth 5.7%. (8) 7th 1985-90 — Rajiv Gandhi; emphasis on productivity + modernisation + TELECOM; growth 6.0%. TWO ANNUAL PLANS 1990-92. (9) 8th 1992-97 — under MANMOHAN-RAO LPG reforms; growth 6.8% (best of any plan till then). (10) 9th 1997-2002 — growth + equity + distributive justice; 5.4% actual. (11) 10th 2002-07 — growth 7.8% + poverty reduction focus; Vajpayee/Manmohan transition. (12) 11th 2007-12 — INCLUSIVE growth; 8.1% actual; financial crisis dampened. (13) 12TH 2012-17 — LAST PLAN ('Faster, More Inclusive + Sustainable Growth'); 8% target; actual 6.9%. PLANNING COMMISSION + FIVE-YEAR PLANS SCRAPPED 2014-15; replaced by NITI AAYOG (1 Jan 2015) + 3-yr Action Agenda + 7-yr strategy + 15-yr vision + annual budgets. MAHALANOBIS MODEL (P.C. Mahalanobis, eminent statistician of ISI Kolkata) — 2-sector (consumer + capital goods) model advocating HEAVY INDUSTRY-first strategy (Soviet-inspired). CRITIQUED for neglecting agriculture + consumer goods. 2nd Plan was INDIA's most distinctive planning moment. OTHER PLANNERS: V.T. Krishnamachari, Charan Singh (critical of industry bias), P.C. Mahalanobis, Tarlok Singh, Asoka Mehta, D.R. Gadgil, K.N. Raj, Jagdish Bhagwati (later critic). PLANNING gave India ~10 MAJOR IITs + IIMs + RECs + AIIMS + ICAR + IISc + CSIR labs + ISRO + DAE + DRDO + DVC + FCI + RBI expansion. Keynesian capital-output-ratio model; focus on AGRICULTURE + IRRIGATION (post-Partition food crisis); Bhakra-Nangal + Hirakud dams.

cards.front:
INDIA is targeting to become a 'DEVELOPED NATION' ('VIKSIT BHARAT') by:

(A) 2030
(B) 2047
(C) 2040
(D) 2050
cards.back:
(B) 2047

Planning & Poverty — 'VIKSIT BHARAT 2047' — PM NARENDRA MODI's vision to transform INDIA into a DEVELOPED NATION by 100TH YEAR OF INDEPENDENCE (15 AUG 2047). Announced in his 15 AUG 2022 Red Fort speech; reiterated regularly. 'AMRIT KAAL' — 'era of nectar' — the 25-year period 2022-2047 framed as opportunity. TARGETS (broad, not exhaustive): (1) ECONOMY: GDP to $30-35 TRILLION (from ~$4T in 2024); per-capita income to $20,000+ (from ~$2,700); among top-2 world economies (China rival by 2035; US by 2047). (2) DEMOGRAPHY + EMPLOYMENT: create ~20 CR quality jobs (urban + rural); FORMAL employment 25%+ (from ~15%); harness demographic dividend before ageing begins 2055. (3) EDUCATION + SKILLS: universal literacy; 50%+ gross enrolment in higher ed (from 28%); top-quality universities globally; implement NEP 2020. (4) HEALTH: life expectancy 80+ (from 70); universal health coverage; adequate doctors/1,000; eliminate TB, malaria, HIV. (5) INFRASTRUCTURE: 100% electrification + piped water (largely done by 2024); world-class road + rail + air networks; all villages internet (Bharatnet); smart cities; 500+ mass-transit systems. (6) ENERGY: NET-ZERO by 2070 (COP-26 commitment); 500 GW non-fossil by 2030; 100 GW nuclear; green hydrogen economy; full EV for 2-3-wheelers + buses by 2030. (7) AGRICULTURE: DOUBLE farmer incomes; agri-processing + exports; sustainable farming. (8) MANUFACTURING: 25% of GDP (from 15-16%); PLI sectors (semiconductors, EVs, drones, solar, pharma). (9) SERVICES + TECH: AI + quantum + biotech + space + fin-tech leadership; 10+ CR people working in tech. (10) GOVERNANCE: digital governance; least corruption; top-5 on Human Development Index. (11) POVERTY: MPI poverty <5%; inequality reduced via progressive policies. (12) GEO-POLITICAL: UNSC permanent seat; G3 of G20; $1 trillion exports; STRATEGIC autonomy. CHALLENGES / RISKS: (1) MIDDLE-INCOME TRAP — countries like Brazil, Mexico, S Africa stagnated after reaching $10-15K per capita; can India escape? (2) HUMAN CAPITAL gaps — stunting, literacy gaps, skill deficit; 50% of graduates unemployable. (3) EMPLOYMENT crisis — jobless growth concern; agri employs 46% but 17% of GDP. (4) INEQUALITY + SOCIAL COHESION — caste + religious + regional tensions. (5) CLIMATE vulnerability — heat waves, monsoon shifts, cyclones; coastal cities submergence risk. (6) INFRASTRUCTURE deficit — $1.4 trillion needed over 10 years (NIP). (7) GOVERNANCE — institutional strength, rule of law, judicial efficiency. (8) MANUFACTURING — hasn't grown fast enough; stuck at 15-16% GDP. (9) HEALTH EXPENDITURE only 2% of GDP (vs OECD 8-10%). (10) EDUCATION SPEND 3% (vs needed 6%). INSTITUTIONAL ROADMAP: (1) NITI AAYOG's 'STRATEGY FOR NEW INDIA @ 75' (2018) — 41 chapters covering drivers, infrastructure, inclusion, governance; pre-cursor. (2) INDUSTRIAL POLICY 2024-25 revamped. (3) NATIONAL INFRASTRUCTURE PIPELINE (NIP, 2020) — ₹111 lakh crore projects. (4) PM Gati Shakti — multi-modal transport + logistics integration. (5) DIGITAL INDIA + UPI + Aadhaar + DPI = foundational. (6) SKILL INDIA, Make in India, Startup India, Stand-Up India. (7) STATES' role — cooperative + competitive federalism; state strategies for Viksit Bharat. (8) INTERMEDIATE milestones: $5 TR by 2027, $7 TR by 2030-32, $10 TR by 2035. INDIA has outpaced most emerging economies 2014-24; if current trajectory continues + reforms accelerate, Viksit Bharat 2047 is within reach — but requires sustained effort + good fortune on climate + geopolitics. 100th year of Independence; PM Modi's 'Amrit Kaal' target; requires GDP to reach $30-35 trillion (vs current ~$4T); HCI + infra + jobs + innovation.

cards.front:
MGNREGA — India's flagship rural employment scheme — guarantees how many days of work per household per year?

(A) 50 days
(B) 100 days
(C) 180 days
(D) 365 days
cards.back:
(B) 100 days

Planning & Poverty — MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005) — legal right to 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household per year, on demand. World's largest public works scheme. During Covid (2020-21), the limit was raised to 150 days in drought-notified areas. Administered by the Ministry of Rural Development; wages are paid directly to bank accounts via DBT.

cards.front:
'Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana' (PMJDY), launched in August 2014, is a flagship scheme for:

(A) Housing for all
(B) Financial inclusion (universal bank-account access)
(C) Skill development
(D) Road construction
cards.back:
(B) Financial inclusion (universal bank-account access)

Planning & Poverty — PMJDY — launched 28 August 2014 — brings every household into the formal banking system: a zero-balance savings account, RuPay debit card, overdraft facility, accident insurance. Over 50 crore accounts have been opened, ~₹2 trillion deposits (2024). The Jan-Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile (JAM) trinity underpins Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) for subsidies, reducing leakages.

cards.front:
'Ayushman Bharat — Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana' (PM-JAY) offers beneficiary families annual health cover up to:

(A) ₹1 lakh
(B) ₹5 lakh
(C) ₹10 lakh
(D) ₹2 lakh
cards.back:
(B) ₹5 lakh

Planning & Poverty — PM-JAY (launched 2018) — ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalisation. Targets the bottom ~40 % of the population (identified via SECC 2011 deprivation criteria). World's largest government-funded health assurance scheme by coverage. Complemented by Ayushman Bharat Health & Wellness Centres (HWCs, for primary care) and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM).

cards.front:
The 'Multidimensional Poverty Index' used globally (and the Indian equivalent published by NITI Aayog) measures poverty across how many dimensions?

(A) Two
(B) Three
(C) Five
(D) Seven
cards.back:
(B) Three

Planning & Poverty — MPI's three dimensions — Health, Education, Standard of Living — covered by 10 indicators (nutrition, child mortality; years of schooling, school attendance; cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets). Developed by OPHI and UNDP's HDRO. NITI Aayog's National MPI adds bank account + maternal health. India's national MPI fell from ~25 % (2015-16) to ~15 % (2019-21) according to NITI Aayog.

cards.front:
India's 'Direct Benefit Transfer' (DBT) system depends on the JAM trinity. 'JAM' stands for:

(A) Jobs, Agriculture, Markets
(B) Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile
(C) Justice, Administration, Media
(D) Judiciary, Army, Ministry
cards.back:
(B) Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile

Planning & Poverty — JAM trinity — Jan Dhan (bank account) + Aadhaar (biometric identity) + Mobile (SIM-linked) — enables secure, leakage-free Direct Benefit Transfer of subsidies (LPG, PM-KISAN, scholarships, etc.). Rolled out via DBT-Mission from 2013. Has cumulatively saved lakhs of crores from fake-beneficiary leakages.

cards.front:
'Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana' (PMAY) is a scheme for:

(A) Skill development
(B) Housing for all
(C) Old-age pensions
(D) Free electricity
cards.back:
(B) Housing for all

Planning & Poverty — PMAY — launched 2015 — aims at 'Housing for All' through two sub-schemes: PMAY-Urban (for urban poor) and PMAY-Gramin (rural). Central assistance + CLSS (Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme) interest subsidies + pucca-house construction. Targets EWS, LIG, MIG groups. Goals refreshed for the 2024-29 period to build another 3 crore houses.

cards.front:
The National Food Security Act, 2013, covers approximately what percentage of India's population?

(A) 25 %
(B) 67 %
(C) 50 %
(D) 90 %
cards.back:
(B) 67 %

Planning & Poverty — NFSA 2013 entitles 75 % of rural + 50 % of urban population — ~67 % overall (~81 crore people) — to subsidised food grains (5 kg/person/month at ₹3/rice, ₹2/wheat, ₹1/coarse). Under PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (launched April 2020 during Covid), additional free grains were distributed; from Jan 2023, regular NFSA entitlement was made fully free for 5 years.

cards.front:
The MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) guarantees:

(A) 100 days of unskilled manual labour per rural household per financial year
(B) Minimum wage for all Indians
(C) Subsidised food grains at ration shops
(D) Free healthcare up to ₹5 lakh per family
cards.back:
(A) 100 days of unskilled manual labour per rural household per financial year

Agriculture & Schemes — MGNREGA — enacted SEPTEMBER 2005 as NREGA, renamed MGNREGA in 2009. World's largest employment guarantee programme. Provides 100 DAYS of guaranteed wage employment per financial year to ADULT MEMBERS of any rural household willing to do UNSKILLED manual work. Work must be provided within 5 km radius or compensation (wage + travel). If no work within 15 days → UNEMPLOYMENT ALLOWANCE. Wages paid within 15 days (DBT to bank accounts). State wage rates vary (~₹200-350/day). Typical works: water conservation, drought-proofing, flood management, rural connectivity, land development. Nodal ministry: RURAL DEVELOPMENT. 100% central funded for unskilled wages; 75:25 for materials/equipment. COVID-era: 100 days boosted to 150 in some states. Job card = ID. Social audit is mandatory.

Tri-ministerial: Ministry of Women and Child Development (nodal) + Health & Family Welfare + Education. Objectives: (1) prevent gender-biased sex-selective elimination (female foeticide); (2) ensure survival & protection of girl child; (3) education & participation. Linked schemes: SUKANYA SAMRIDDHI YOJANA (Jan 2015 — savings for girl child, highest interest rate among small savings at 8.2%), Mahila Samman Savings Certificate (2023, 2-year 7.5%). CSR improved to 929 per 2022 SRS data. Additional: One Stop Centre (OSC) for women in distress — 'Sakhi' scheme.

Trade & International Finance — Balance of Payments has TWO principal accounts: (1) CURRENT ACCOUNT — records trade in goods and services plus primary income (investment income, compensation of employees) and secondary income (current transfers, remittances); (2) CAPITAL ACCOUNT / FINANCIAL ACCOUNT — records transactions in financial assets/liabilities (FDI, FPI, loans, reserves). Option D is close but 'Trade Account' (goods only) and 'Invisibles Account' are SUB-PARTS of the Current Account, not the principal accounts themselves. 'Revenue Account' (option A) is a budget/government-accounting term, not BoP. Option C conflates fiscal vs monetary policy — different concept entirely.

cards.front:
In India's Balance of Payments accounting, which of the following is recorded under the CURRENT ACCOUNT (not the Capital Account)?

(A) Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflow
(B) Remittances sent by an NRI in the USA to family in India
(C) External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) taken by an Indian company
(D) Sale of a real-estate property abroad by an Indian resident
cards.back:
(B) Remittances sent by an NRI in the USA to family in India

Trade & International Finance — Remittances (private transfers) are classified under the Current Account's SECONDARY INCOME (also called Current Transfers) sub-heading — they don't create any claim or liability, so they aren't capital-account items. FDI (option A) creates an ownership stake → capital account. ECB (option C) creates a debt liability → capital account. Sale of overseas real estate (option D) is a disposal of an asset → capital account. India is historically the world's largest recipient of remittances (~USD 125 billion in recent years from migrant workers in Gulf, USA, UK) — a crucial BoP cushion.

cards.option3: Sale of a real-estate property abroad by an Indian resident

cards.front:
India's MERCHANDISE TRADE DEFICIT (goods imports > goods exports) is persistently financed by which category of Current-Account INFLOWS?

(A) FDI inflows only
(B) Net INVISIBLES
(C) RBI's sale of government securities to foreign buyers
(D) Sovereign gold bonds floated domestically
cards.back:
(B) Net INVISIBLES

Trade & International Finance — India structurally runs a MERCHANDISE (goods) trade deficit — roughly USD 250 bn/year in recent years, driven by crude-oil imports. The deficit is LARGELY financed by strong NET INVISIBLES EARNINGS (services + remittances): (i) IT/BPM services exports (~USD 200 bn/year); (ii) remittances (~USD 125 bn); (iii) tourism. Combined, these offset most of the goods deficit and keep the overall Current Account Deficit (CAD) manageable (~1-2 % of GDP in normal years). FDI (option A) is Capital Account, not Current. Option C is a Capital Account transaction. Option D is a domestic instrument — not a BoP item. primarily remittances, software services exports, and tourism earnings.

cards.front:
If India's Current Account Deficit (CAD) + Capital Account Surplus = positive overall balance, the RBI typically responds by:

(A) Selling foreign exchange reserves to tighten forex supply
(B) Buying foreign exchange from the market, ADDING to its forex reserves
(C) Printing INR to match the dollar inflow
(D) Mandating all Indian exporters to convert to INR immediately
cards.back:
(B) Buying foreign exchange from the market, ADDING to its forex reserves

Trade & International Finance — BoP identity: Current Account + Capital Account = 0 (when you include the official reserve transactions). If CAD (−) is MORE THAN OFFSET by Capital Account Surplus (+), there's a net dollar inflow into the economy. To prevent excessive INR appreciation, RBI INTERVENES by BUYING the excess USD from the market, accumulating forex reserves. The reverse happens when CAD exceeds inflows — RBI sells reserves to protect the INR. India's forex reserves crossed USD 650 bn in 2024, among the world's largest. Option A is the opposite response. Option C describes naive monetary expansion — RBI sterilises such INR creation via OMOs. Option D is not a policy tool.

cards.option2: Printing INR to match the dollar inflow
cards.option3: Mandating all Indian exporters to convert to INR immediately

cards.front:
Which of the following transactions would IMPROVE (increase the surplus / reduce the deficit of) India's CURRENT account?

(A) An Indian auto company imports machinery from Germany
(B) An Indian software firm exports services to a US client
(C) Foreign investors buy Indian government bonds
(D) The government takes a loan from the IMF
cards.back:
(B) An Indian software firm exports services to a US client

Trade & International Finance — Services exports = Current Account CREDIT (inflow of foreign exchange for services rendered) → improves CAD. Option A is a merchandise import → Current Account DEBIT → WORSENS the deficit. Options C and D are CAPITAL Account transactions (bond purchases and loans create liabilities) → don't directly affect the Current Account (though they finance it). The Current Account cares about 'real' flows — goods, services, income, transfers. Capital Account cares about changes in asset positions.

cards.front:
Match each BoP sub-component with the correct principal account and pick the correct pairing:
(i) Merchandise trade — Current Account
(ii) Software services exports — Current Account
(iii) Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) — Capital Account
(iv) NRI remittances — Current Account

(A) Only (i) and (ii) correctly paired
(B) Only (i), (ii), (iii) correctly paired
(C) All four (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) correctly paired
(D) Only (iii) correctly paired
cards.back:
(C) All four (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) correctly paired

Trade & International Finance — ALL four pairings are correct. CURRENT Account: merchandise trade (goods), services (incl. software exports), primary income (compensation, investment income), secondary income (remittances, grants). CAPITAL Account (or Financial Account in IMF terminology): FDI, FPI, External Commercial Borrowings, loans, banking capital, changes in reserves. Memorising 'which side of the BoP does X go on' is the #1 drill for Economics GK in Bank exams. Classic confusion: remittances feel like money transfer (capital-ish), but they're UNREQUITED transfers with no asset-liability creation, so Current Account.

cards.front:
The term 'TWIN DEFICIT' — a recurring concern in Indian macroeconomic discussions — refers to simultaneous:

(A) Fiscal deficit (Revenue + Capital expenditure > Revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) AND Current Account Deficit
(B) Current Account Deficit AND Capital Account Deficit
(C) Trade Deficit AND Invisibles Deficit
(D) Primary Deficit AND Revenue Deficit
cards.back:
(A) Fiscal deficit (Revenue + Capital expenditure > Revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) AND Current Account Deficit

Trade & International Finance — TWIN DEFICIT = FISCAL DEFICIT + CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT occurring together. The concern: a government running a fiscal deficit borrows → if borrowing is large and savings are low, the economy has to attract foreign capital → pressures INR → can push the CAD up. Worst case: a 'spiral' where both deficits self-reinforce. Notable Indian episodes: 1991 BoP crisis, 2013 'taper tantrum' crisis. Option B is rare/impossible structurally — a CAD is typically FINANCED by a Capital Account Surplus, so they're usually opposite signs. Options C and D describe other fiscal-terminology deficits.

cards.front:
In the IMF's BoP Manual (BPM6) — which India follows — the CAPITAL ACCOUNT and the FINANCIAL ACCOUNT are treated as:

(A) Completely identical terms used interchangeably
(B) Distinct — 'Capital Account' covers capital transfers (e.g. debt forgiveness) and non-produced non-financial assets; 'Financial Account' covers financial asset/liability transactions (FDI, FPI, loans, reserves)
(C) 'Capital Account' was renamed to 'Current Transfer Account' in BPM6
(D) 'Financial Account' refers to purely domestic banking
cards.back:
(B) Distinct — 'Capital Account' covers capital transfers (e.g. debt forgiveness) and non-produced non-financial assets; 'Financial Account' covers financial asset/liability transactions (FDI, FPI, loans, reserves)

Trade & International Finance — Under IMF BPM6 (used by the RBI): CAPITAL ACCOUNT is narrow — it covers (a) capital transfers like debt forgiveness, migrants' transfers, government-to-government grants; (b) non-produced non-financial assets (e.g. patents sold to a foreign party). FINANCIAL ACCOUNT is much larger — FDI, FPI, External Debt, Banking Capital, Rupee Debt Service, Other Capital, and changes in RBI Reserves. Many Indian textbooks (pre-BPM6) used 'Capital Account' loosely to mean what is now 'Financial Account' — this is a common exam trap. RBI's monthly BoP release uses the modern BPM6 definitions.
cards.option2: 'Capital Account' was renamed to 'Current Transfer Account' in BPM6
cards.option3: 'Financial Account' refers to purely domestic banking

cards.front:
The 1991 BALANCE OF PAYMENTS CRISIS in India was famously resolved after the government pledged GOLD to secure a short-term loan from which international authority?

(A) The World Bank
(B) The Bank of England (and later the Bank of Japan) against a physical gold pledge
(C) The Asian Development Bank
(D) The Federal Reserve Bank of the United States
cards.back:
(B) The Bank of England (and later the Bank of Japan) against a physical gold pledge

Trade & International Finance — In 1991, India's forex reserves had crashed to ~USD 1.2 bn (about 2 weeks of imports). The Chandra Shekhar government (May 1991) pledged 47 tonnes of gold to the Bank of England; the subsequent Rao-Manmohan Singh government (July 1991) pledged another 20 tonnes to the Bank of Japan — raising ~USD 600 mn to avert default. The crisis triggered the 1991 economic reforms (LPG — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation). The IMF ALSO provided a Stand-By Arrangement but the short-term gold-pledge was the immediate rescue. World Bank and ADB gave longer-term project finance but weren't the emergency bridge. This episode is a GA staple — memorise 1991, gold, and 'LPG reforms'.
cards.option3: The Federal Reserve Bank of the United States

cards.front:
Which of the following is the CORRECT definition of 'BoP SURPLUS' under a floating exchange-rate regime like India's?

(A) An ACCOUNTING impossibility — BoP always balances to zero by construction
(B) The situation where total autonomous transactions produce a net inflow, leading to RESERVE ACCUMULATION by the central bank
(C) The situation where the government runs a fiscal surplus
(D) The situation where exports exactly equal imports
cards.back:
(B) The situation where total autonomous transactions produce a net inflow, leading to RESERVE ACCUMULATION by the central bank

Trade & International Finance — Conceptually the BoP is split into AUTONOMOUS (voluntary, profit-motivated) transactions and ACCOMMODATING (balancing, via official reserves) transactions. A 'BoP surplus' is informally the excess of autonomous inflows over outflows — which the central bank accommodates by buying forex and INCREASING reserves. Technically, when reserves are included, the BoP sums to zero (accounting identity). Option A confuses the identity with economic meaning. Option C conflates fiscal policy with BoP. Option D describes balanced trade, not BoP surplus (services, transfers, capital flows all matter too).

cards.option2: The situation where the government runs a fiscal surplus
cards.option3: The situation where exports exactly equal imports

(A) Ministry of Finance only
(B) Reserve Bank of India (BoP data) and Ministry of Finance
(C) Ministry of Commerce and NITI Aayog
(D) SEBI and IRDAI

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a determinant typically used to assess if a country's Current Account Deficit is 'SUSTAINABLE'?

(A) CAD as % of GDP (commonly safe threshold < 3 %)
(B) Composition of deficit financing (FDI preferred over 'hot money' FPI)
(C) Stock of forex reserves (months of imports covered)
(D) The domestic unemployment rate among PhD holders
cards.back:
(D) The domestic unemployment rate among PhD holders

Trade & International Finance — The three canonical sustainability tests for CAD: (i) CAD as % of GDP — below 3 % is considered manageable in emerging markets; (ii) QUALITY of financing — stable FDI (long-term, equity) better than FPI (short-term, 'hot money' that can reverse suddenly); (iii) Forex reserve adequacy — reserves covering 6-9 months of imports provide a cushion. Unemployment of PhDs (option D) has NO direct BoP-sustainability linkage — pure distractor. India's CAD was 1.2 % of GDP in FY24, financed largely by stable FDI + remittances — currently comfortable.

cards.front:
'Balance of Trade' (BoT) is the difference between a country's:

(A) Gross income and expenditure
(B) Visible exports and visible imports of goods (NOT services)
(C) Foreign reserves and foreign debt
(D) Government revenue and expenditure
cards.back:
(B) Visible exports and visible imports of goods (NOT services)

Trade & International Finance — BoT considers ONLY visible (merchandise/goods) trade. Balance of Payments (BoP) is broader: BoT + invisible trade (services, transfers, factor income) + capital account. India typically runs a TRADE DEFICIT (imports goods worth more than it exports — oil + gold + electronics drive imports). But a SURPLUS in services (IT, BPO, consultancy) helps narrow Current Account Deficit. CAD = BoT + Invisibles. India's CAD usually 1-3% of GDP.

cards.front:
India's BIGGEST single import item by value (typically) is:

(A) Gold
(B) Crude petroleum (and petroleum products)
(C) Coal
(D) Electronics
cards.back:
(B) Crude petroleum (and petroleum products)

Trade & International Finance — Crude oil — India's largest single import (~25-30% of total imports by value, ~$130-150 B/year). India imports ~85% of its crude oil needs. Top suppliers in 2024-25: Russia (largest after Ukraine war discounts), Iraq, Saudi Arabia, UAE, USA. Other major imports: gold (~$40-50 B), electronics (smartphones, semiconductors), coal & coke, petroleum products, fertilisers. The trade deficit shrinks when crude prices fall or rupee strengthens.

India's foreign exchange reserves are managed by:

(B) Reserve Bank of India (under FEMA, 1999)

cards.back:

cards.front:
The 'Most Favoured Nation' (MFN) principle of the WTO requires that:

(A) Members trade only with their favoured allies
(B) Any trade concession given to one WTO member must be extended to ALL other members on equal terms (no discrimination among trading partners)
(C) Most countries get preferential rates
(D) MFN status is awarded only to developed countries
cards.back:
(B) Any trade concession given to one WTO member must be extended to ALL other members on equal terms (no discrimination among trading partners)

Trade & International Finance — MFN — Article I of GATT, the cornerstone non-discrimination principle. If country A gives B a 5% tariff on a product, A must extend the same 5% to ALL other WTO members. Exceptions: (1) Free Trade Agreements / Customs Unions (NAFTA, EU, ASEAN) — preferential treatment within bloc allowed; (2) Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) — developed countries can give better access to developing countries; (3) National-security exceptions. NATIONAL TREATMENT (Art III) — once goods are imported, they must be treated the same as domestic goods (no discriminatory taxes/regulations). India revoked Pakistan's MFN status after Pulwama attack (Feb 2019); Pakistan never granted India MFN status post 1996.

(B) Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets)
(C) Travel and tourism

Trade & International Finance — TRIPS (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) — adopted 1995 alongside WTO. Sets MINIMUM IP standards: patents 20 years; copyright life of author + 50 years (often extended); trademarks renewable. India had to amend its 1970 Patents Act in 2005 to introduce product patents on pharmaceuticals (had been process patents only — that's how Indian generics industry like Cipla, Dr Reddy's grew). DOHA DECLARATION 2001 — TRIPS + Public Health: countries can issue compulsory licences for affordable access to essential medicines (HIV, TB, etc.). Section 3(d) of Indian Patents Act — prevents 'evergreening' (Novartis Glivec case 2013, SC ruled against Novartis). Other key WTO agreements: GATS (services), AoA (agriculture), SPS (sanitary measures), TBT (technical barriers).

(A) Tokyo round
(B) Doha Development Agenda
(C) Bretton Woods round
(D) Geneva accord
cards.back:
(B) Doha Development Agenda

Trade & International Finance — Doha Round (2001-) — formally the DOHA DEVELOPMENT AGENDA (DDA), launched at the 4th Ministerial Conference in Doha, Qatar. Focus: development concerns of poor countries, especially in agriculture, services, IPR. Major sticking points: (1) Agricultural subsidies — developed countries (US, EU) heavily subsidise farms (~$300 bn/year); developing countries demand cuts. India + China — peace clause for public food stockholding (e.g., MSP-based PDS). (2) Special + Differential Treatment for developing countries. (3) NAMA — non-agricultural market access. After 20+ years, Doha Round is largely STALLED — not formally concluded; the multilateral path has yielded to bilateral / plurilateral FTAs (TPP, RCEP, etc.). India has historically resisted reduction in its food subsidies, leveraging the food security argument.

Trade & International Finance — WTO Dispute Settlement Body — long considered the 'crown jewel' of the WTO (binding dispute resolution, unlike most international bodies). (B) AoA — Agreement on Agriculture (with Green / Amber / Blue boxes for different subsidy types)

Trade & International Finance — AoA — entered force 1995. Classifies subsidies into BOXES: GREEN BOX (non/minimally trade-distorting — research, environmental, infrastructure; allowed without limit); AMBER BOX (trade-distorting — direct price support, input subsidies; capped at 10% of value of agricultural production for developing countries — the 'de minimis' level); BLUE BOX (production-limiting, with restrictions). India's MSP + PDS system risks crossing the de minimis threshold. BALI MINISTERIAL 2013 — peace clause for India: developing countries can exceed AMBER limits for public stockholding for food security WITHOUT being challenged at WTO, until a permanent solution. The 'PERMANENT SOLUTION' on PSH remains India's key demand at MC13 (2024) and beyond. SCM — Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (industrial subsidies).

cards.front:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) was established under the:

(A) RBI Act, 1934
(B) IRDA Act, 1999
(C) LIC Act, 1956
(D) Insurance Act, 1938
cards.back:
(B) IRDA Act, 1999

Insurance & Miscellaneous — IRDA Act 1999 — set up IRDAI in April 2000 to regulate the insurance sector following its opening to private players (Malhotra Committee, 1994). Headquartered in Hyderabad. Renamed IRDAI in 2014. Issues licences, monitors solvency, prescribes rules, settles disputes. Reports to MoF. Currently chaired by Debasish Panda (since 2022). Insurance Act 1938 is the basic insurance legislation; LIC Act 1956 nationalised life insurance (245 private insurers merged into LIC).

cards.front:
LIC of India was nationalised on:

(A) 26 January 1950
(B) 1 September 1956 (LIC Act 1956)
(C) 15 August 1947
(D) April 2000
cards.back:
(B) 1 September 1956 (LIC Act 1956)

Insurance & Miscellaneous — LIC Act 1956 — nationalised 245 private life insurers into LIC. Operations began 1 September 1956. Headquartered in Mumbai (Yogakshema Building). LIC IPO — May 2022 — government divested 3.5% stake; 2nd largest IPO ever in India (₹21,000 crore). Currently 32 life insurers in India (1 public + 31 private) and 26 general insurers + 4 specialised + several health insurers. General Insurance Corporation (GIC) — 1972, holds 4 subsidiaries (now separated): NIA, OIC, NIC, UIIC. Disinvested 2023.

cards.front:
FDI cap in insurance sector — most-recently set at:

(A) 26%
(B) 74% (raised from 49% in Budget 2021)
(C) 100% with conditions
(D) 20%
cards.back:
(B) 74% (raised from 49% in Budget 2021)

Insurance & Miscellaneous — FDI history in insurance: 26% (2000, on opening), 49% (2015 Insurance Amendment Act), 74% (Budget 2021, Finance Act 2021). Up to 74% under automatic route, with conditions on Indian-controlled board. Insurance intermediaries (brokers, agents) → 100%. Lloyds India, reinsurance branches allowed. Budget 2024-25 hinted at allowing 100% FDI in insurance, possibly via Ins. Amendment Bill — under consideration.

(A) ₹1 lakh
(B) ₹2 lakh — at premium ~₹436/year (revised from ₹330)

cards.back:

Insurance & Miscellaneous — PMJJBY — launched 9 May 2015. Life insurance cover ₹2 lakh, available to individuals 18-50 with savings bank account, paid via auto-debit. Annual premium ~₹436 (raised in 2022 from ₹330). Underwritten by LIC (also private insurers). PMSBY (Suraksha Bima Yojana) — accident + disability insurance ₹2 lakh, premium just ₹20/yr (raised from ₹12 in 2022). APY (Atal Pension Yojana) — pension scheme. Together — JANSURAKSHA suite providing financial security to underprivileged.

cards.front:
Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) — crop-insurance scheme launched 2016 — replaced:

(A) PMJDY
(B) NAIS (National Agricultural Insurance Scheme) and MNAIS
(C) Atal Pension Yojana
(D) PMSBY
cards.back:
(B) NAIS (National Agricultural Insurance Scheme) and MNAIS

Insurance & Miscellaneous — PMFBY — launched 13 January 2016 (Sehore, MP). Replaced NAIS (1999) and MNAIS (2010). Aims to provide affordable crop insurance for farmers — premium just 1.5% (rabi), 2% (kharif), 5% (commercial) of insured sum; rest subsidised by Centre + State. AY 2020 — voluntary participation (was mandatory for loanee farmers earlier). Implemented by AIC (Agriculture Insurance Company of India) + private insurers. Covers natural calamities, pests, diseases. Around 5-6 crore farmers enrolled annually. PMFBY is the largest crop-insurance program in the world by area covered.

cards.front:
AYUSHMAN BHARAT — Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), launched 2018 — provides annual health cover up to:

(A) ₹1 lakh per family
(B) ₹5 lakh per family per year (secondary + tertiary care)
(C) ₹50,000
(D) ₹10 lakh
cards.back:
(B) ₹5 lakh per family per year (secondary + tertiary care)

Insurance & Miscellaneous — PM-JAY (launched 23 September 2018, Ranchi) — health cover ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary + tertiary care hospitalisation. Beneficiaries identified via SECC 2011 — ~10.74 crore poor + vulnerable families = ~50 crore people. World's largest government-funded health insurance scheme. Cashless + paperless treatment at ~28,000 empanelled hospitals (PMJAY portal). National Health Authority (NHA) implements. Senior citizens (70+) added September 2024 — irrespective of income/SECC eligibility.

cards.front:
Insurance penetration in India (premiums as % of GDP) currently is approximately:

(A) 0.5%
(B) ~4% (India 4.0% in 2023; global average ~7%)
(C) 20%
(D) 0.1%
cards.back:
(B) ~4% (India 4.0% in 2023; global average ~7%)

Insurance & Miscellaneous — Insurance Penetration: Premiums / GDP. India's penetration (Swiss Re Sigma 2023): Total ~4.0%; Life ~3.0%; Non-life ~1.0%. Global average ~7% (advanced economies typically 8-10%). India ranks ~10th in life insurance worldwide by premium volume. Insurance density (premium per capita) much lower in India ($90) vs US ($8,000). IRDAI's 'Insurance for All by 2047' vision aims to dramatically raise penetration via simpler products, regulatory ease (Bima Sugam, Bima Vahak), and digital onboarding.
